claims.scope: Preconditions and dual evidentiary requirements for direct substitution in PEF Step 2

claims.text: A hypothetical material case clarifies what each piece of evidence establishes. Suppose a study meets all other general ILCD prerequisites, a dependent product Y has two active equivalent alternatives (Alpha and Beta), and market absorption has been verified against the ILCD criterion. Those records can support ILCD's conditional consumption-mix approximation, yet they cannot by themselves qualify for a PEF direct-substitution credit. Adding procurement records showing that a specific user actually switched to Y and reduced purchases of Alpha supplies evidence of the direct effect and displaced target—but if the available inventory still does not represent the affected Alpha supply, the second PEF condition remains unmet. The example contrasts what different evidence layers authorize rather than computing two compliant PEF and ILCD scores for the same case; PEF's prior hierarchy steps would also remain to be checked.
claims.scope: Hypothetical incremental evidence illustration without empirical procurement, output, or environmental observations
caveats: Introduces no new environmental values and does not certify the chapter's worked batch example under any PEFCR.

claims.text: Lacking sufficient proof for direct substitution neither sets the credit to zero nor forces an automatic jump to economic allocation. PEF Step 2 still permits other justified underlying physical relationships; moving to Step 3 requires documenting why Steps 1 and 2 were excluded and why the chosen Step 3 rule fits. Using indirect substitution in Step 3 still requires identifying an indirect substitution effect and modeling the displaced product with a reasonably representative inventory—"not knowing exactly who was displaced" is not evidence of indirect substitution—or applying another valid allocation relationship. ILCD handles insufficient alternative scale differently: it first checks a broader equivalent function and, if still insufficient, shifts to Situation B—a distinct branch from falling back to allocation when substitution modeling is infeasible and generic data are not sufficiently accurate.
claims.scope: Fallback branches in EU PEF and ILCD when direct substitution or alternative scale criteria are unmet
caveats: Formal ILCD Provision I.a.iv.4 additionally requires that substitution modeling is infeasible and generic data are insufficiently accurate, while retaining conditions against materially favoring the studied system and requiring disclosure of accuracy loss; broader explanatory wording on p. 83 does not expand the formal permission here.
PEF Step 3 is not unconditional; sector-specific multifunctionality rules and applicable PEFCR take precedence.

claims.text: Different rules do not always produce different numbers. If two frameworks' separate applicability conditions are each independently met, and the substituted quantity, system boundary, and complete substitution inventory happen to coincide, subtracting the same reference from the same joint inventory yields the same residual. Numerical equality neither proves that the two frameworks impose identical evidentiary standards nor implies that both are applicable. Conversely, differing residuals driven by different reference supplies do not automatically mean the two studies made contradictory claims about the same real-world market outcome. Functional comparability establishes whether an alternative can deliver the same service; applicable rules, inventories, and empirical evidence must separately explain why that alternative was chosen and what conclusions follow.
claims.scope: Conditional numerical equivalence across distinct rule sets and comparative interpretation
caveats: Does not construct a real-world case satisfying both frameworks simultaneously or judge which framework predicts markets more accurately.

claims.text: Test three common claims directly against the equations above: (1) "Both sets of shares sum back to the full batch, so both prove that substitution occurred"; (2) "X's negative residual shows that the plant removed gas from the air"; and (3) "In the half-utilization scenario, one simply halves the original substitution credit." Identify the missing link in each statement, then recompute the half-utilization route from explicit activity levels. Finally, set q = 0 while still requiring delivery of the original X and Y services: which supply must be added, and which output must be treated? Writing the positive activity route before computing emissions reveals whether an activity changed or only a label.
claims.scope: Worked-case exercise testing accounting additivity, substitution, negative residuals, and the zero-utilization route

claims.text: Check first whether product shares sum back to the batch, then check which services each route delivers and which activities appear. Additive shares confirm only that the listed burden was fully partitioned; substitution requires service matching and evidence or premises that separate supply withdraws. A negative residual reflects subtraction of a reference supply—J's positive emissions never disappeared. The half-utilization route must be written as 1J + 3S-Y + 3W-Y, giving a net difference of (−35/2, 23/5); the positive make-up term disappears from the simplified residual only because it cancels against the Y reference. At q = 0, the route still requires 1J plus 6S-Y to supply the Y service and 6W-Y to treat unused joint Y, yielding (31, 226/5) and a net difference of (−7, 86/5) relative to the separate route. Applying this construction to real supply requires empirical evidence on yields, service equivalence, waste fates, displaced technologies, supply responses, and boundaries; reporting product shares still requires justifying the chosen partitioning rule.
claims.scope: Exercise solution: reconstructing half- and zero-utilization routes and identifying empirical requirements

claims.text: Reading any joint-production result begins by asking which quantity it delivers and whether its governing rule can be audited. Reporting partitioned shares requires stating the partitioning basis; deducting a reference supply or comparing routes requires aligning services and specifying the reference; claiming decision consequences requires verifying which activities actually change; and citing a named procedure requires checking its exact version and applicability conditions.
claims.scope: Accounting, causal, normative, and versioning checks for reading allocation and substitution rules
caveats: Offered as an analytical reading checklist rather than a claim that methodological debates are settled or empirically validated.

claims.text: Breaking this step down separates three quantities that must be labeled distinctly: product shares answer how a joint burden is partitioned among co-products; a reference residual is what remains after subtracting a reference supply for another function from the joint inventory; and a full route difference compares two complete supply systems delivering identical functions. Returning from a residual to a full comparison requires subtracting the retained function's separate reference inventory. Labeling all three quantities explicitly lets readers see whether a change stems from the partitioning rule, the chosen reference supply, or the underlying question itself.
claims.scope: Three distinct reporting quantities across the worked batch case and cross-framework rule comparison
caveats: Residuals and full differences follow the chapter's fixed-service and fixed-reference algebraic relations and do not certify compliance with any specific external standard.

claims.text: The joint-production case stipulated that separate supply withdrew by a specified quantity, permitting one route to be subtracted from another. In reality, whether such withdrawal occurs must be verified. If demand for a material falls, who cuts production? If output expands, which regional power grid generates more electricity? The average origin of electricity already consumed, the supplier named on a contract, and the process that actually increases or decreases output each require different evidence. This chapter examines how to identify which activities respond and under what conditions those different answers converge.
claims.scope: Transition from stipulated supply responses in joint production to empirical identification of responding activities

claims.text: Weidema, Frees, and Nielsen (1999) define a marginal production technology as one whose activity level changes in response to a small change in demand. While comparing the resulting increases or decreases, their framework holds the rest of society's production constant; interventions large enough to reshape the wider background economy require separate scenarios. Here "marginal" specifies which change is being estimated—whether a technology is modern, high-emitting, or newly built must be determined separately for the affected activity.
claims.scope: Definition of marginal production technology under small demand perturbations in Weidema, Frees, and Nielsen (1999)

claims.text: Determining how supply responds starts with asking what can adjust over the relevant time horizon. Firms can alter utilization of existing equipment, or they can build, replace, or retire capital equipment. Weidema, Frees, and Nielsen (1999) define the long term by whether capital equipment adjusts rather than by a universal number of years across industries. They argue that most life cycle assessment (LCA) decisions affect investment, while noting exceptions such as internal adjustments without commercial exchange, sectors without investment plans, or capacity governed outside market mechanisms. Uncoordinated replacement schedules across firms can also cause aggregate capacity to adjust continuously. Whether long-term capacity adjustment applies depends on the specific decision and on current and expected market trends.
claims.scope: Capacity utilization, capital adjustment, and long-term relevance in Weidema, Frees, and Nielsen (1999, §2(a))

claims.text: The 1999 five-step procedure first establishes the time horizon and then tests whether the change propagates through a market. If evidence shows that the change falls exclusively on a specific process without passing through a market to other producers, the procedure stops and identifies that process as the responding activity. If the change propagates through a market, the analyst sequentially examines the market trend, which technologies are constrained from adjusting, and which unconstrained technology is most likely to respond. The paper's complete decision tree is built for long-term capacity adjustments; analyzing short-term operational dispatch requires separate evidence.
claims.scope: Sequence, stopping condition, and long-term scope of the 1999 five-step identification procedure

claims.text: Naming a supplier on a contract does not settle whether that supplier adjusts its own output. Weidema, Frees, and Nielsen (1999) note that close cooperation, shared ownership, or even a sole-supplier relationship can still transmit demand changes to other firms. On-site self-generation qualifies as a directly affected process only when its output varies with internal demand without altering generation in the general market. Moving from a purchase certificate to an actual change in generation requires a verifiable transmission mechanism.
claims.scope: Conditional distinction between a named contractual supplier and an actually responding process

claims.text: Falling demand does not automatically trigger immediate capacity retirement. If demand declines more slowly than equipment naturally wears out, new capacity additions may still be needed; early retirement becomes the likely adjustment only when demand falls faster than the normal replacement rate. Near that boundary, delayed retirement can alter the outcome, so the authors advise retaining both scenarios. Next, the analyst checks which technologies are constrained by resources, product quality, policy, emission caps, or co-product outlets, and examines how investors or plant operators weigh cost and flexibility—engineering cost alone is only one factor.
claims.scope: Role of capital replacement rates, constraints, and investor preferences in the 1999 procedure

claims.text: The 1999 paper illustrates this reasoning using contemporary European long-term baseload electricity supply. Whether coal-fired power responds depends on market liberalization, transmission capacity, and whether emission targets constrain hard coal; altering emission constraints shifts the Nordic conclusion as well. Hydropower, nuclear power, wind power, and combined heat and power (CHP) each face distinct resource, policy, technical, and heat-market constraints. The example demonstrates how boundary conditions change the inferred supplier; identifying incremental generation in any current region requires checking that region's actual conditions.
claims.scope: Historical fuel and constraint conditions in the 1999 European long-term baseload illustration

claims.text: The same paper also illustrates when average and responding technologies can converge. In its pulp and paper example, transport distances, raw-material availability, and expansion potential at existing mills make the supply response vary by region. Where existing mills within a region use relatively uniform technology, the inferred marginal technology can closely resemble the regional average technology. Convergence is possible under specific conditions, but its extent must still be explained through regional mechanisms.
claims.scope: Conditions for convergence between regional average and marginal technologies in the 1999 pulp and paper example

claims.text: The 1999 critique shifted attention first to where aluminum comes from. Eirik Nordheim of the European Aluminium Association argued that aluminum is a global commodity whose small demand increments can be met simultaneously by expanding existing smelters, reactivating idle capacity, and building new plants rather than by a single new smelter. Hydropower sites may lie far from load centers, constrained by transmission limits. Even when a buyer specifies a particular supplier, the delivered metal may originate from varied regions or recycled streams. Any method must therefore clarify how aluminum delivery links to specific production activities and their electricity supply.
claims.scope: Nordheim's 1999 critique regarding global aluminum supply, capacity adjustments, and transmission limits

claims.text: Nordheim accordingly recommended aggregating data across all potential delivery sources when assessing future supply of a global commodity, citing a stable hydropower share in industry statistics to oppose designating a single power source. Strictly speaking, those statistics show that hydropower's share remained similar over the comparison period. Establishing what would have happened without the extra demand still requires a counterfactual, and attributing an increment to specific sources still requires supply-response evidence. The geographic-boundary critique Nordheim raised and the evidentiary reach of his cited statistics must be evaluated separately.
claims.scope: Nordheim's average-source recommendation and the inferential limits of its supporting statistics
caveats: The original International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) statistics cited in the comment were not independently verified here; figures reported in the comment do not constitute a reconstructed industry sample.

claims.text: In his reply, Weidema (1999) argued that although a single small change may not alter capital stock in the short run, many small increments accumulate to require new capacity. At the same time, he conceded that the original five-step procedure had not specified geographic market boundaries and accepted that affected aluminum production should be identified on the global commodity market rather than the European market assumed in the packaging study under discussion. Once the commodity market is bounded, electricity markets must still be delineated separately: the commodity market may be global, whereas electricity markets remain constrained by regional grid connections.
claims.scope: Weidema's 1999 reply on cumulative increments and his concession on geographic market boundaries

claims.text: When aluminum smelting capacity adjusts across several regions at once, power generation may respond separately in each region. The 1999 paper treated much aluminum-sector hydropower as already fully utilized and therefore constrained, while preserving local exceptions lacking immediate alternative electricity users. Weidema's reply further linked low-cost power sources to new smelter siting: in some cases existing hydropower is diverted from other users, whereas in others new smelters accompany the development of previously untapped power resources. Distinguishing the two mechanisms requires specifying location, grid connectivity, and time horizon.
claims.scope: Conditional link between a global aluminum market and multiple regional electricity responses

claims.text: Weidema's reply also cited an unpublished industry compilation of announced new smelter projects and their planned power sources to show that tracing market responses could still yield a high hydropower share. Because that compilation remained unpublished, whether announced projects materialized requires tracking, and project announcements alone cannot isolate the effect of a particular demand change. The reply shows how Weidema answered the critique, but it does not empirically verify the actual global electricity response of aluminum production.
claims.scope: Evidentiary limits of the unpublished industry capacity projections cited in Weidema's 1999 reply
caveats: The unpublished Aluminium Association (1999) compilation was not retrieved; its sample, weights, project deduplication, and realization rates cannot be reconstructed.

claims.text: When Ekvall and Weidema (2004) synthesized system boundaries and input data for consequential life cycle inventory analysis, they explicitly traced the five-step identification procedure back to the 1999 paper. That citation lineage is verifiable directly in the text. Because the 2004 article cites neither Nordheim's comment nor Weidema's reply, sequential publication and overlapping authorship cannot by themselves establish that all points from the 1999 debate were resolved.
claims.scope: Documented citation lineage from 1999 to Ekvall and Weidema (2004) versus unverified resolution of the 1999 debate

claims.text: Ekvall and Weidema (2004) operationalize the task by identifying the competing market first. Obligatory product properties, geographic boundaries, customer segments, and temporal segments determine which suppliers actually compete; even within the same power grid, peak-load and off-peak periods may require separate analyses. Only within the relevant market segment does the analyst evaluate capacity, utilization, trends, and constraints. Because the resulting response may involve multiple technologies acting together, defining the competitive scope must precede modeling how individual activities change.
claims.scope: Obligatory properties and market segmentation preceding marginal technology identification in Ekvall and Weidema (2004)

claims.text: Ekvall and Weidema (2004) use Nordic aluminum smelting to illustrate constrained hydropower. If total hydropower generation does not expand with demand, additional hydropower consumed by a smelter must be diverted from other electricity users. If those other users maintain their electricity consumption, replacement generation must fill the gap. Constant hydropower generation is what allows hydropower to cancel out of the net change, and unchanged demand among other users is what requires replacement generation. Knowing that installed capacity is fixed does not by itself prove that generation is fixed; short-term dispatch and long-term capacity expansion must still be distinguished.
claims.scope: Diversion and replacement-generation mechanism under constrained hydropower with fixed demand from other users

claims.text: Even asking only where electricity already consumed in a region originated requires explicit rules for imports, exports, and transit flows. Weidema's 1999 reply cites the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) report by Ménard, Dones, and Gantner (1998), which weights supply sources by electricity volume to derive average consumption mixes. Whereas the pulp example examined whether technologies within a region are similar, a consumption mix reports average historical origins; determining which generator increases output for one extra unit of demand remains a separate question.
claims.scope: Distinguishing PSI average consumption mixes from regional technology homogeneity and marginal demand response

claims.text: The PSI report begins by placing all flows in a common electricity unit: domestic generation P, imports I, exports E (recorded as a positive quantity), and domestic consumption plus network losses V. Vectors mP, mI, mE, and mV record the source shares of each flow under a consistent classification, giving the balance equation P × mP + I × mI = V × mV + E × mE. Total electricity volumes balance first, but assigning source shares still requires an accounting rule: can imported electricity be re-exported, and do exports carry the domestic generation mix or a pooled mix? Different rules produce different consumption mixes from the exact same cross-border electricity flows.
claims.scope: Electricity balance equation with consistent source shares and loss-inclusive domestic consumption V in PSI (1998)

claims.text: PSI defines four accounting models, M1 through M4. Model M2 blends domestic generation and imports into a single pool from which both domestic consumption and exports draw; because imports themselves carry foreign mixes, trade loops and indirect trade can require solving simultaneous equations. Model M3 deducts exports from domestic generation and assigns imports to domestic consumption, ruling out simultaneous transit or stripping out known transit flows first. Physical power flows, contractual claims, and accounting allocations each require different evidence; here only the accounting allocation rule changes.
claims.scope: Contrasting attribution rules between PSI pooled model M2 and domestic-net-of-exports model M3

claims.text: Applying M3 to the report's 1995 Swiss data illustrates the denominator discipline required. Domestic generation of 60,277 gigawatt-hours (GWh) plus imports of 18,113 GWh minus exports of 25,143 GWh equals 53,247 GWh. Table A.1 of the report lists final consumption (51,567 GWh) and network losses (1,680 GWh) separately, while the main-text definition of V includes both in the denominator. Dividing loss-inclusive source volumes by final consumption of 51,567 GWh alone would break the requirement that shares sum to one. Reporting a mix at the final-user meter requires specifying how losses are allocated and where electricity is delivered; the calculation below retains the loss-inclusive denominator V.
claims.scope: Loss-inclusive denominator V versus final consumption in the 1995 Swiss M3 calculation

claims.text: First deduct exports from domestic generation: under M3, Swiss generation retained domestically is 60,277 − 25,143 = 35,134 GWh. Adding imports from Germany (7,014 GWh), France (9,116 GWh), Austria (1,973 GWh), and Italy (10 GWh) sums exactly to 53,247 GWh. Dividing each entry by this denominator yields source shares of approximately 65.9831%, 13.1726%, 17.1202%, 3.7054%, and 0.0188%, respectively. These percentages reproduce the exact relationship between the report's integer electricity tables and the M3 rule; they do not imply that incremental electricity demand would be met in those five proportions.
claims.scope: Recomputed source shares from integer electricity volumes under the PSI M3 rule for Switzerland (1995)

claims.text: Once source shares are established, each origin must be paired with its corresponding emission inventory. PSI draws on existing energy-system inventories to compute carbon dioxide (CO₂) and other flows. Converting those totals into emissions per kilowatt-hour requires checking system boundaries, voltage levels, and network losses; likewise, CO₂ mass cannot be extended directly to CO₂-equivalent across all greenhouse gases. Whenever electricity results diverge sharply, analysts must inspect the mix rule, denominator, and emission factors before attributing the gap to underlying generation technologies.
claims.scope: Coupling source shares with underlying inventories, voltage levels, and network-loss delivery boundaries

claims.text: The PSI authors acknowledge that rigorously estimating a demand change calls for modeling supply responses. Because future market and policy scenarios are uncertain, however, they recommend reporting an average consumption mix first—to preserve consistency and comparability—and testing sensitivity with marginal scenarios. In their example, Swiss purchases of French nuclear power might induce additional generation in Italy, yet they attribute that induced burden to Italian electricity users. Footnote 14 records reviewer Frischknecht's dissent: decision-oriented studies should use the marginal mix directly. Both sides address demand-induced supply changes; they divide over which mix should serve as the primary reported baseline.
claims.scope: PSI authors' average-first recommendation, responsibility attribution, and Frischknecht's footnote 14 dissent

claims.text: Now hold an incremental material service constant and compare two hypothetical electricity responses. Under fixed location, period, and grade specifications, an additional 1 kg of material demand is met by a selected plant increasing output by exactly 1 kg, consuming a fixed 10 kilowatt-hours (kWh) per kg. This link from demand to output at that specific plant is stipulated here rather than inferred from plant location or purchase certificates. Both response scenarios deliver the same extra 1 kg of material while all other grid users continue consuming 100 kWh; the baseline excludes the extra 1 kg. Rather than comparing two equal-service substitutes, the baseline and each intervention are used to isolate the net change caused by the same added service.
claims.scope: Stipulated incremental material output and matched additional service across two electricity-response scenarios

claims.text: Fix the electricity subsystem cleanly. Suppose generators H and G supply interchangeable electricity within this market, with no transmission constraints, imports, exports, or network losses; non-electricity inputs, co-products, and demand feedback are omitted. H and G are abstract hypothetical sources rather than empirical hydropower or fossil-fuel factors, with linear CO₂ inventories of 0.02 kg/kWh and 0.8 kg/kWh, respectively. Both scenarios share identical factors and boundaries, varying only which generator actually responds: in Scenario 1, total output of H is capped and G expands; in Scenario 2, H expands while G remains unchanged. Both are static before-and-after comparisons over an abstract period without distinguishing dispatch from capacity expansion. The result measures CO₂ changes within this bounded power subsystem—not a full material footprint, climate impact score, or real-market forecast.
claims.scope: Subsystem boundaries, emission factors, and stipulated supply responses for the hypothetical electricity case

claims.text: Start from the baseline without incremental material production. Other users draw 40 kWh from H and 60 kWh from G, totaling 100 kWh, while the selected plant has zero incremental electricity use. Applying the stipulated factors gives baseline CO₂ emissions of 40 × 0.02 + 60 × 0.8 = 48.8 kg. In each scenario below, all positive generation activities are listed in full before subtracting this baseline, separating electricity assigned to the buyer from generation actually added across the system.
claims.scope: Positive-activity baseline and CO₂ inventory for the hypothetical incremental-demand case

claims.text: Now supply the plant's 10 kWh under Scenario 1, where total output of H is locked at 40 kWh. Once the plant claims 10 kWh of H, other users receive only 30 kWh of H and must draw 70 kWh from G to maintain their 100 kWh service. Post-intervention system generation is therefore 40 kWh of H plus 70 kWh of G, totaling 110 kWh, with CO₂ emissions of 40 × 0.02 + 70 × 0.8 = 56.8 kg. Relative to the baseline, H does not change, G rises by 10 kWh, and CO₂ rises by 8 kg. No negative power plant appears: H delivered to other users falls, while positive generation expands at G.
claims.scope: Constrained-H scenario: G expansion and net CO₂ increase when H is capped and other users' demand stays fixed

claims.text: Next allow H to expand under Scenario 2. Here H increases output by 10 kWh to supply the plant while G stays at 60 kWh. Other users continue drawing 40 kWh of H and 60 kWh of G, and the plant adds 10 kWh of H, bringing total system generation to 50 kWh of H plus 60 kWh of G (110 kWh) and CO₂ emissions to 50 × 0.02 + 60 × 0.8 = 49 kg—an increase of 0.2 kg over the baseline. The added material service, total electricity service, and emission factors are identical to Scenario 1; only which source expands has changed, yet that single condition creates a 7.8 kg difference in net emissions.
claims.scope: Expandable-H scenario: positive generation activities and net CO₂ increase when H expands and G stays fixed

claims.text: Return to the plant's electricity purchase record. Multiplying its purchased 10 kWh of H by H's factor of 0.02 kg/kWh yields 0.2 kg in both scenarios. That product answers an attribution question for the contracted electricity; it matches the system-wide net increase in Scenario 2 (0.2 kg) but diverges sharply from Scenario 1 (8 kg), where claiming H never caused H to generate more electricity. Whether contractual attribution equals the system change depends on physical supply response, not on whether the same generator name appears on the certificate.
claims.scope: Conditional comparison between identical contractual attribution and divergent system-level net changes

claims.text: Applying this logic to a globally traded material begins by identifying which plants adjust output. Let the output change in region r be Δqᵣ (in kg) and its electricity intensity be eᵣ (in kWh/kg). Once linearity and efficiency premises are verified, multiplying Δqᵣ by eᵣ gives the regional change in electricity demand. Each region's power-generation response must then be evaluated according to local time periods, grid connections, and capacity constraints before summing the resulting inventories. The material market provides evidence of producer adjustments, while regional electricity markets provide evidence of generation adjustments; neither identification step can be skipped.
claims.scope: Unit-consistent linkage from regional material output changes to regional electricity demand and generation responses

claims.text: Deciding between competing response hypotheses calls for targeted empirical checks: whether the plant actually expanded output or merely switched delivery channels, whether H increased total generation, how other users met their electricity demand, and whether inter-regional transmission limits bound the grid. Analysts must also distinguish short-term dispatch, reactivation of idle capacity, new construction, and capacity retirement over the study period. Contracts, generation statistics, plant records, and policy documents each support one link in this chain rather than constituting an observed end-to-end market response on their own.
claims.scope: Empirical verification checklist derived from competing market-response models

claims.text: Because observing every capacity, trade, and dispatch response in real markets typically exceeds the reach of a single study, major international handbooks, standards, and background databases each codify operational modeling boundaries. Whether examining the International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) 2010 Handbook, the ecoinvent v3 background system models, the European Union (EU) Product Environmental Footprint (PEF), or the Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Protocol Product Standard, all four confront the same four structural questions introduced above: (1) how large is the supported decision, and does it cross a threshold that alters background capacity additions or retirements; (2) which supply activities are constrained by resources, policy, or joint production from expanding freely; (3) should purchased electricity or bulk materials be accounted for via physical trade balances, contractual tracking with residual mixes, or long-term unconstrained marginal mixes; and (4) should co-products and recycling flows triggered by demand changes be resolved through substitution credits, attributional allocation, or fixed formulas?
claims.scope: Four shared structural market-boundary questions across major international LCA frameworks
caveats: Facing the same structural questions does not mean the four frameworks share a single objective: the first two permit consequential market modeling under defined conditions, whereas the latter two intentionally lock in attributional accounting for comparability and auditability.

claims.text: Across those four questions, the frameworks share three conditional points of convergence. First, all recognize that inventory modeling must serve the study's goal rather than declaring attributional or consequential modeling universally superior: just as Ekvall, Tillman, and Molander (2005) link retrospective and prospective approaches to distinct normative ethics, the ecoinvent v3 guideline recommends consequential modeling for decisions while explicitly reserving attributional models for societal hot-spot screening, fair environmental-tax allocation, and retroactive responsibility or reward. Second, all enforce double-counting prevention in electricity and supply mixes: both PSI's import–export balance and EU PEF's removal of claimed green power to form national residual consumption mixes reject crediting the same low-carbon attribute to both a contractual buyer and the public grid. Third, every framework that permits substitution places the burden of proof on the party claiming the credit: substitution is never subtracting a nominal inventory at will, but requires showing that the displaced supply exists, the market can absorb it, and applicable conditions are met.
claims.scope: Three conditional convergences: goal dependence, double-counting prevention, and substitution burden of proof
caveats: Conditional convergence covers basic accounting discipline and does not harmonize national certificate regimes or evidentiary sufficiency thresholds for marginal identification.

claims.text: Sharp divergence begins with decision-context classification and scale thresholds. ILCD (2010) classifies studies by decision-support role and whether changes induce large-scale structural shifts: Situation A (micro-level decision support) assumes changes stay below capacity thresholds and uses existing supply chains and average consumption mixes as a pragmatic simplification; only when added demand or supply exceeds the normal annual capacity-replacement rate of an affected process—triggering new builds or early retirements—does Situation B (meso/macro-level decision support) apply long-term marginal mixes to "large-change" processes alongside 90% error-range plausible worst- and best-case scenarios. Pure accounting (C1/C2) may not support procurement or policy comparisons, and footnote 15 clarifies that past versus future is not the dividing axis between attributional and consequential modeling. The ecoinvent v3 consequential model directly challenges ILCD's micro-scale simplification: Weidema et al. (2013) argue that individual purchases cumulatively drive investment, adopt a default 30-year capital lifetime (3.33%/year replacement rate) to distinguish old from modern/new marginal suppliers, and represent absolute constraints via conditional exchanges without empirical elasticities. EU PEF and the GHG Protocol Product Standard, by contrast, lock product inventories to attributional boundaries, leaving market-response consequential analysis to policy or mitigation-project evaluations.
claims.scope: Framework divergence on decision-context classification and capacity-replacement scale thresholds
caveats: ILCD Situation B's "large-change" threshold depends on estimating annual replacement capacity for affected processes, while ecoinvent v3's 30-year / 3.33% rule is a uniform database default; both can deviate from actual equipment lifetimes in specific industries.

claims.text: The same divide is starkly visible in electricity-mix accounting rules. The Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) models (M1–M4) build physical trade balances from customs and generation statistics without relying on contractual certificates; even though the four rules yield different average origins from the same 1995 Swiss data, the PSI authors advocate reporting average mixes first with marginal sensitivity checks, whereas Frischknecht (footnote 14) insists decision-oriented studies use marginal mixes directly. EU PEF (Annex I §4.4.2) takes a strict attributional contractual-tracking route, stepping down a four-tier hierarchy: supplier-specific electricity products meeting tracking criteria, supplier total mixes, country residual consumption mixes (with mandatory fallback when untracked shares exceed 95%), and regional residual mixes, while applying consumption grid mixes in the use phase. By contrast, ecoinvent v3's consequential model excludes constrained sources—such as hydropower, waste incineration, and CHP co-product electricity—from marginal supply and weights unconstrained technologies by their positive capacity growth between scenario years. As Treyer and Bauer (2016) and Vandepaer et al. (2019) emphasize, that algorithm models long-term capacity expansion rather than hourly dispatch, and normalizing solely by positive growth breaks down in shrinking markets that respond through delayed retirement.
claims.scope: Divergence across physical trade balances, contractual residual mixes, and long-term marginal electricity models
caveats: PEF's contractual tracking hierarchy prevents attributional double counting on paper but does not test whether certificate purchases trigger additional renewable capacity; ecoinvent v3 long-term marginal electricity likewise cannot substitute for hourly dispatch and load-shifting analyses examined in the next chapter.

claims.text: How a framework diagnoses market constraints also governs its treatment of co-products and recycling flows. In ecoinvent v3's consequential model, joint production retains in principle a single determining reference product; constrained by-products are always substituted by unconstrained marginal routes, or converted into reduced consumption by other users through conditional exchanges when a market is constrained. ILCD Situation A permits substitution with an average market mix when subdivision is infeasible and market-absorption conditions hold, falling back to two-step allocation otherwise; Situation C2 allocates uniformly. EU PEF (Annex I §4.5) raises the bar further, demanding dual proof of a direct market effect and a directly representative inventory before permitting direct substitution, and replaces open-ended consequential modeling at end-of-life with the Circular Footprint Formula—whose fixed parameters A (0.2, 0.5, or 0.8) and default B (0) are policy conventions rather than dynamic elasticities. The GHG Protocol Product Standard (§9.3.2) confines system expansion to an attributional frame: credits are allowed only when a company knows the by-product's fate and applies supplier-specific or average factors (for example, crediting 50 kg for black-liquor electricity against a local grid reduces 1,000 kg to a net 950 kg), while §11.3.2 prohibits deducting market-mediated "avoided emissions" from inventory totals and requires any separate disclosure to report indirect emission increases alongside.
claims.scope: Divergence on co-product substitution, the Circular Footprint Formula, and avoided-emission prohibitions under demand changes
caveats: Detailed mathematical treatments of co-product allocation/substitution and recycling appear in *Joint Production* and *Material Recycling Chains*; this paragraph focuses on how market-constraint identification drives institutional divergence across frameworks.

claims.text: These framework differences are not mere semantic disputes; they can invert option rankings under identical physical facts and purchase contracts. Return to the hypothetical case: given the exact same 10 kWh purchase contract and a fixed total cap on low-carbon source H, EU PEF contractual tracking or GHG Protocol supplier attribution records 0.2 kg of CO₂ for the plant, whereas Weidema and ecoinvent v3 constrained-market logic traces the diverted supply to 10 kWh of extra high-carbon G generation, lifting the net system increase to 8 kg of CO₂—a 40-fold gap (net difference of 7.8 kg). Similarly, in the Swedish Thorskog Castle hotel case (Ekvall et al. 2005), hydropower appears low-carbon under local attribution yet can correspond to fossil-fuel expansion under marginal consequences; likewise, Switzerland's 1995 M3 mix (65.9831% domestic retention and roughly 34.02% imports from four neighbors) cannot be extrapolated as the response share of incremental demand. Whenever an alternative relies on green certificates or hydropower contracts tied to constrained low-carbon generation, switching frameworks can reverse the ranking of electricity-intensive processes; conversely, applying long-term marginal factors to short-term dispatch or shrinking markets can misstate mitigation effects in the opposite direction. Silently mixing system boundaries within a single comparison is therefore untenable.
claims.scope: Conditions under which framework switches invert option rankings and create reverse-distortion risks
caveats: The 40-fold ratio (8 kg versus 0.2 kg) stems from this chapter's fixed-factor teaching example to illustrate directional mechanism rather than to predict an empirical grid multiplier.

claims.text: Comparing all five frameworks leaves three unresolved empirical and governance unknowns that must be stated candidly. First, broad ex-post empirical validation of whether real markets absorb an increment of demand through short-term dispatch, idle-capacity reactivation, delayed retirement, new investment, or price-induced demand reduction remains scarce; theoretical flowcharts and full-elasticity assumptions must not be mistaken for observed facts. Second, ILCD lacks a cross-industry empirical threshold separating Situations A and B, while ecoinvent v3 replaces industry-specific dynamics with a uniform 30-year / 3.33% default, omits empirical elasticities, and has exhibited version-specific implementation errors and high sensitivity to scenario windows (Vandepaer et al. 2019 documented hard-coal omissions, hydropower mapping issues, and concentrating solar power double-counting in v3.4, with an average correction under 3%, subsequently fixed in v3.5). Third, underlying datasets for several historical capacity compilations cited in this chapter were not retrieved, and certain later reviews lie outside open verification scope. Until empirical evidence closes these gaps, cross-framework findings should be presented alongside their governing premises, constraint assumptions, and sensitivity ranges rather than treating any single compliant calculation as the sole truth of market response.
claims.scope: Empirical evidence gaps in real-world market responses, database implementation sensitivity, and verification boundaries
caveats: Empirical gaps do not render modeling useless; rather, they require reporting attributional ledgers and consequential scenarios distinctly while exposing untested market-response assumptions to readers and reviewers.

claims.text: Returning to the chapter's starting point, the Swiss electricity accounts show that average supply origins can be audited once import–export allocation rules are fixed, whereas the two incremental-demand scenarios and cross-framework comparison show that identical electricity purchases can still trigger generation from different power plants—and that scale thresholds, contractual tracking, and physical constraint assumptions can flip option rankings. Interpreting a subtracted credit in joint production as a real-world consequence requires specifying the action taken and the service delivered, then investigating market boundaries, supply constraints, and which activities actually adjust. Building on this foundation, the next chapter, *Electricity Systems*, examines where electricity is delivered, where it is generated, and how supply models estimate the consequences of demand changes.
claims.scope: Distinct evidentiary scopes of average-share recomputation, conditional response calculations, and real-world supply evidence

claims.text: When a factory decides to use one fewer kilowatt-hour (kWh) of electricity, the first question is which kWh is being avoided: where on the grid was it delivered, and during which hours was it consumed? If the goal is simply to allocate the burden of existing supply to users, the calculation can start from realized generation and emissions. If the goal is to determine which generating units reduce output as a result of saving electricity, the analysis must also examine how supply responds. The discussion below traces electricity backward from the equipment delivery point and then compares system responses across different time horizons.
claims.scope: Locating a kilowatt-hour at its delivery point; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Reducing consumption by 1 kWh specifies only an energy quantity. If lighting duration, production output, or charging service also changes, the functional equivalence of the two options must be stated explicitly. In the calculations that follow, the timing and magnitude of the demand reduction are written directly into the model and evaluated using independent grid, generation, and unit-level datasets, making it possible to verify exactly which specified change the calculation answers.
claims.scope: Locating a kilowatt-hour at its delivery point; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Tracing the origin of a unit of electricity requires three coordinates: the voltage level of delivery, the supply region, and the time of use. Voltage determines which network segments the electricity traverses; regional boundaries govern how power plants and interregional exchanges are accounted for; and the clock convention aligns load with the corresponding hourly records. A Norwegian transmission and distribution study illustrates physical delivery chains, U.S. annual and hourly datasets show how generation and consumption are reconciled, and prospective scenarios show how electricity supply shifts when generating capacity can also adjust.
claims.scope: Locating a kilowatt-hour at its delivery point; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Arvesen and colleagues trace electricity delivery in Norway across the main transmission grid, regional transmission networks, and local distribution networks. Local networks typically operate at 11 or 22 kV before stepping down to 230 or 400 V for ordinary end users, whereas both regional and main transmission grids include 132 kV lines and large industrial consumers may connect further upstream. Identifying which grid infrastructure serves a given load therefore requires reading nominal voltage values together with the functional role of each network segment.
claims.scope: How delivery points bring in transmission and distribution activities; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Once the delivery path is established, the inventory must account both for the electricity lost along the way and for the activities required to build and maintain the network. The Norwegian study compiles inventories for lines, conductors, cables, transformers, and switchgear across manufacturing, transport, construction, inspection, and end-of-life, while assuming operational leakage from equipment containing sulfur hexafluoride (SF₆). Asset lifetimes govern how construction burdens are amortized across annual delivered electricity. Network materials and direct emissions should be reported separately from the additional generation required to compensate for line losses.
claims.scope: How delivery points bring in transmission and distribution activities; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Evaluating line losses begins by checking which quantity serves as the denominator. Let E_in denote network input and E_out denote network output. If the loss rate is defined on an input basis as ℓ = (E_in − E_out) / E_in, delivering 1 megawatt-hour (MWh) requires an input of 1 / (1 − ℓ) MWh, and the extra ℓ / (1 − ℓ) MWh represents the energy lost. If a dataset instead defines the loss rate relative to output, the loss per delivered MWh equals that loss rate multiplied by the delivered quantity.
claims.scope: How delivery points bring in transmission and distribution activities; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: The Norwegian study's supporting information confirms this conversion. For 2011 local distribution operated by NTE Nett in Nord-Trøndelag, the input-based loss rate is 6.3%. Converting on that denominator gives approximately 67.24 kWh of compensating losses per delivered MWh, which the original supplement lists as 67 kWh. Applying the same conversion to the 1.6% regional transmission loss rate yields approximately 16.26 kWh, listed as 16 kWh in the supplement. Both pairs match within the published table's rounding precision, and the supplement links these loss inputs to the Norwegian electricity mix. This recalculation verifies only the loss-reference conversion, not the full life cycle result of the network.
claims.scope: How delivery points bring in transmission and distribution activities; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions
caveats: The numerical check does not propagate underlying statistical, parameter, or model-structure uncertainty; displayed decimals reflect tabulated calculation values rather than equivalent measurement or predictive precision.

claims.text: In the Norwegian example, the two "per delivered MWh" figures are each referenced to the output of their respective network segments. Because some customers withdraw power upstream, the total electricity passing through the regional and local grids differs. Stepping backward from a low-voltage delivery point therefore requires linking each upstream segment's output to the next segment's input while explicitly tracking intermediate withdrawals and injections. Sequential multiplication of segment delivery ratios applies only along an unbranched path with no intermediate injections.
claims.scope: How delivery points bring in transmission and distribution activities; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Mapping the same physical delivery chain into a life cycle inventory (LCI) database requires checking the database's own activity classifications. In ecoinvent v3 as documented by Treyer and Bauer, high, medium, and low voltage are defined as above 24 kV, 1–24 kV, and below 1 kV, respectively, with transformation activities linking adjacent voltage markets. Same-voltage transmission, voltage transformation, infrastructure, and losses are modeled separately. Thus, the 11 or 22 kV lines termed local distribution in the Norwegian study do not fall into ecoinvent's low-voltage class; practitioners must verify network role, specific process dataset, and reference voltage together.
claims.scope: How delivery points bring in transmission and distribution activities; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: A geographic label on a database market does not guarantee that voltage-specific losses come from local measurements. The ecoinvent v3 methodology differentiates regions using local total-loss statistics, but when voltage-level breakdowns are unavailable, it borrows Swiss shares to disaggregate total losses across voltage tiers. The resulting tier-specific losses therefore depend on those borrowed shares, and determining actual local losses at each voltage level requires local disaggregated data.
claims.scope: How delivery points bring in transmission and distribution activities; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: With the delivery chain clarified, annual generation accounts can be examined at the power-plant end. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Emissions & Generation Resource Integrated Database (eGRID2023) sums plant-level emissions by region and divides by annual net generation, which already deducts in-plant electricity use. Estimating emissions for electricity delivered to end users still requires accounting for transmission and distribution losses and identifying the consumption mix. A regional output emission rate reflects only the generation and emissions inside that ledger; imports, exports, fuel extraction and transport, and power-plant construction must be addressed separately.
claims.scope: What annual generation accounts include; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: The numerator also requires checking which emission column is used. eGRID retains both unadjusted and adjusted emissions and relies on adjusted emissions for regional summaries: following its edition rules, it removes biomass carbon dioxide (CO₂) and allocates out the portion of combined heat and power (CHP) emissions attributable to useful thermal output. If two tables adopt different attribution rules, differences in their reported figures cannot be interpreted solely as changes in the generating fleet.
claims.scope: What annual generation accounts include; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Recalculating the eGRID2023 Revision 2 workbook for the ERCT subregion (Electric Reliability Council of Texas, ERCOT All) checks this arithmetic directly. The subregion row reports approximately 477,137,386.101 MWh of net generation and 175,076,531.801 U.S. short tons of CO₂. Using 2,000 pounds (lb) per short ton to convert emissions to pounds and dividing by net generation yields approximately 733.8621 lb CO₂/MWh, matching the published value of 733.862 lb CO₂/MWh. This check confirms the annual average and its display precision for the workbook's numerator and denominator, whereas estimating how much CO₂ is avoided by saving electricity in a specific hour requires response data.
claims.scope: What annual generation accounts include; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions
caveats: The numerical check does not propagate underlying statistical, parameter, or model-structure uncertainty; displayed decimals reflect tabulated calculation values rather than equivalent measurement or predictive precision.

claims.text: Workbooks carrying the same 2023 data year can still differ by revision. Revision 2 of eGRID2023 restored negative net generation values that had previously been zeroed out and updated plant matching and aggregation fields, so recalculations must preserve those negative values. The data year identifies when generation and emissions occurred, whereas the revision number specifies how the workbook aggregated them.
claims.scope: What annual generation accounts include; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: eGRID estimates grid gross loss from a separate interconnection-level annual balance with its own denominator. Here, total disposition combines sales, electricity furnished without charge, utility own use, and losses; after deducting net interstate exports, the ERCOT interconnection row equals approximately 477,196,420.049 MWh. Subtracting approximately 33,326,181.969 MWh of direct use that bypasses the grid yields the loss-rate denominator. Dividing estimated losses of approximately 18,707,069.898 MWh by (disposition excluding net exports − direct use) gives 4.2145%, published as 4.2%. Because this denominator is a distinct accounting quantity, it cannot be replaced with the ERCT power-plant net generation figure above.
claims.scope: What annual generation accounts include; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: The published eGRID loss figures also contain a source discrepancy. Both the eGRID2023 Technical Guide and the Revision 2 workbook report 4.2% for ERCOT and 4.1% for the Western interconnection, whereas the cited EPA FAQ webpage reverses those two values. This analysis adopts the values explicitly bound to the Technical Guide and Revision 2 workbook while recording the FAQ discrepancy, as the webpage's update timestamp does not explain the transposition. Even after selecting a loss factor, loss adjustment scales only the required electricity quantity; the origin of imported power still requires separate investigation.
claims.scope: What annual generation accounts include; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Annual totals conceal when a region relies on external supply during the day. In U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) Form EIA-930 balancing-authority records, demand is derived as reported net generation minus total net interchange, where net exports are positive and net imports are negative. Each row reports hourly average power in megawatts (MW) stamped at hour-ending, so multiplying by one hour yields hourly energy in MWh. This ledger covers the bulk wholesale grid visible to the balancing authority, whereas distribution-connected resources and retail end-use meters have separate boundaries.
claims.scope: How hourly balances link generation and demand; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Two hourly records from the EIA-930 balancing authority labeled ERCO contrast net exports with net imports. For the hour ending at 01:00 local time on January 1, 2023, ERCO recorded 36,539 MW of net generation and 710 MW of net exports, giving 35,829 MW of demand. For the hour ending at 09:00 local time on July 1, 2023, it recorded 51,829 MW of net generation and −81 MW of net interchange, giving 51,910 MW of demand. The negative interchange in the second row indicates net imports—making demand exceed local net generation—rather than "negative electricity use."
claims.scope: How hourly balances link generation and demand; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Constructing a full-year hourly balance requires auditing missing reports. Selecting 2023 by local data date for ERCO yields 8,760 non-empty hourly values each for demand and net generation, while total net interchange has 6 missing entries alongside 187 explicit zero reports. Even in hours where all three fields are populated, non-zero balance residuals can appear. Missing interchange can be back-calculated from the other two quantities for the same hour, provided the imputed status is documented, and sums over populated records alone must be kept distinct from complete annual totals.
claims.scope: How hourly balances link generation and demand; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Joining two hourly tables requires a reliable time key. In these records, Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) hours are continuous and unique, whereas local clock timestamps repeat at the end of daylight saving time, and the final local hours of 2023 fall on 2024 UTC dates. Merging tables solely on calendar year and local clock hour risks dropped or duplicated matches; analysts must use time-zone-aware keys and state both the year boundary and whether timestamps mark hour-beginning or hour-ending.
claims.scope: How hourly balances link generation and demand; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Regional alignment must also be verified down to individual power plants. In EPA's AVoided Emissions and geneRation Tool (AVERT), the Texas (TE) region includes the SRO Cogen plant, which eGRID2023 assigns to the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (MISO) balancing authority and the SRMV subregion. Conversely, Tenaska Kiamichi sits in Oklahoma yet is assigned to TE in AVERT and to ERCO and ERCT in eGRID. These two plants alone show that state borders diverge from statistical and modeling boundaries; a region name cannot substitute for verifying the plant lists inside the numerator and denominator.
claims.scope: How hourly balances link generation and demand; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Some hourly grid products also publish CO₂ estimates. EIA documents that it estimates hourly generation emissions from generation and fuel emission factors and then assigns imports and exports using a multi-regional input-output flow-attribution framework. Using hourly consumption-based emissions therefore requires verifying three steps independently: the electricity balance, the generation-emission estimate, and the trade-attribution rule. Complete records at the first step do not validate the assumptions embedded in the other two.
claims.scope: How hourly balances link generation and demand; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: If the analytical question is how much emission burden from realized supply is attributed to a user, dividing the relevant emissions by electricity gives an average rate. If the question is which emissions decline when electricity use falls, the calculation must compare two distinct supply states. Having examined the denominators of average accounts above, we now inspect how different response indicators determine which generating units adjust.
claims.scope: Why average rates and operational responses are different estimands; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: eGRID's non-baseload output emission rate approximates which units respond to dispatch using plant capacity factors—the ratio of actual generation to maximum continuous rated output. Plants with capacity factors below 0.2 receive full weight, those above 0.8 receive zero weight, and those in between follow a linear weight declining from 1 to 0. Weighted emissions are divided by weighted generation, with renewable-fuel generation excluded from the calculation. While this rate can serve as a rough proxy for certain energy-efficiency or renewable interventions displacing fossil generation, identifying which units actually respond in a given hour requires additional evidence, and maintenance outages also shift capacity factors.
claims.scope: Why average rates and operational responses are different estimands; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Siler-Evans and colleagues (2012) paired hour-to-hour changes in fossil gross generation with corresponding changes in emissions, estimating average marginal emission factors from regression slopes. Their dataset drew on 2006–2011 Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems (CEMS) records grouped by North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC) region, without tracking interregional imports or exports and assuming that uncovered non-fossil sources do not respond. Because these estimates capture statistical associations in historical fluctuations, verifying the concrete effect of a specific energy-saving intervention still requires matching engineering and power-system evidence.
claims.scope: Why average rates and operational responses are different estimands; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Graff Zivin, Kotchen, and Mansur shifted the explanatory variable to hourly consumption, regressing interconnection-wide emissions on 2007–2009 Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Form 714 hourly load data. In the Eastern Interconnection, consumption in one region can thus be linked to emission changes across the shared grid without restricting the response to local generators. Their weekday regressions include hour-of-day by sample-month fixed effects, and the authors justify demand exogeneity on the ground that retail customers generally do not face real-time wholesale prices. That causal identification argument must still be evaluated against whether the specific decision problem satisfies the same assumption.
claims.scope: Why average rates and operational responses are different estimands; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: One empirical approach links emission differences to changes in fossil gross generation, whereas the other links emissions to changes in end-use consumption. Siler-Evans and colleagues caution that even narrow statistical confidence intervals may omit data errors, model-specification choices, and transferability risks, while also noting complications from hydroelectric intertemporal shifting and wind curtailment. Changing the explanatory variable in the second study provides a valuable cross-check, yet because both studies rely in part on the same CEMS emission records, their estimation errors can remain correlated.
claims.scope: Why average rates and operational responses are different estimands; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Wholesale market reports also describe a fuel as being "on the margin." The Southwest Power Pool (SPP), for example, reports marginal fuel shares by the fraction of intervals in which each fuel sets the market price, whereas regression studies estimate each fuel's share of incremental energy generation. Knowing how frequently a fuel sets price does not by itself tell us how many MWh it adds or what emissions result; connecting price-setting frequency, incremental energy, and emission changes requires separate evidence for each link.
claims.scope: Why average rates and operational responses are different estimands; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: AVERT organizes historical unit-level operating relationships into an hourly evaluation tool. Here we run the 2023 Texas (TE) regional dataset and native calculation functions from EPA AVERT Web Edition v4.3.0, where TE covers generating units in both Oklahoma and Texas. The data file tabulates unit responses across regional load bins—using one annual set of curves for generation and separate May–September and non-summer curves for pollutants and heat input—and evaluates both baseline and perturbed load profiles to sum the state difference. Because AVERT estimates operational response from existing unit relationships, dispatch under full transmission constraints requires a separate model.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: AVERT's load coordinate is the regional fossil load—in MW—that must be met by fossil generating units covered in the emissions database, multiplied by one hour to obtain hourly energy. Nuclear, hydroelectric, wind, and solar units do not enter these unit-level generation and emission totals directly; instead, energy efficiency or new renewable supply is treated as a request to reduce fossil load. The example below follows this convention without separately modeling non-fossil output or import responses.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: We begin with a uniform hourly reduction: subtracting 1 MWh of end-use electricity in every hour of the 2023 dataset, for a total of 8,760 MWh across the year. No solar, wind, storage, or electric-vehicle profiles are added, and the calculation runs on the full TE region without scaling by state shares. This input is a conditional model test rather than an implemented efficiency project, while a zero-change profile provides a baseline check within the same code.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: To translate end-use reductions into fossil-load requests, the native AVERT client applies the TE loss parameter 0.0457913819880058 via 1 / (1 − ℓ). Each 1 MWh of end-use reduction thus requests approximately 1.047989 MWh of fossil-load reduction, summing over the year to −9,180.3824 MWh (where negative values denote scenario minus baseline). Because this intermediate input already incorporates the program's line-loss adjustment, it must not be treated again as unadjusted end-use electricity once it enters the calculation core.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: The documentation behind that loss formula also warrants scrutiny. The AVERT v4.3 User Manual likewise writes the conversion as division by 1 − ℓ, yet its footnote defines the loss factor as (net generation + net imports − sales) divided by sales. If the denominator were indeed sales, energy balance would require multiplying by 1 + ℓ instead. Here we document the exact transformation executed by the software without resolving how the footnote definition reconciles with the parameter's derivation; its denominator must also be checked separately from eGRID's grid gross loss.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Inside the calculation core, each hourly requested load is located between two adjacent load bin edges L₀ and L₁. If a unit's tabulated outputs at those edges are y₀ and y₁, linear interpolation at load L gives y(L) = y₀ + (y₁ − y₀)(L − L₀) / (L₁ − L₀). Evaluating both baseline and perturbed loads, aggregating each series to monthly totals, and taking the difference means that an identical end-use reduction yields different responses depending on the starting load bin, whether the change crosses a bin boundary, and each unit's curve.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: The native functions return an annual fleet-wide generation change of −9,187.9183 MWh and a direct CO₂ change of −5,672.7223 U.S. short tons. The code aggregates unit results into monthly regional totals, subtracts baseline from scenario for each month, and sums the monthly differences. The modeled generation change differs from the requested fossil-load change by approximately −7.5359 MWh because unit-level interpolation does not constrain the sum of individual unit responses in each bin to equal the requested load; this residual must not be interpreted as an additional line loss.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: That single emission change can be normalized by two different electricity denominators. Converting at 1 U.S. short ton = 907.18474 kg gives a modeled CO₂ reduction of approximately 5,146,207.11 kg. Dividing by the specified 8,760 MWh end-use reduction yields approximately 587.47 kg/MWh, whereas dividing by the magnitude of the modeled generation reduction yields approximately 560.11 kg/MWh. The first rate is per MWh saved at the end user, and the second is per MWh avoided at the modeled generators; the gap reflects only the choice of denominator.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions
caveats: The numerical check does not propagate underlying statistical, parameter, or model-structure uncertainty; displayed decimals reflect tabulated calculation values rather than equivalent measurement or predictive precision.

claims.text: Passing a zero-change profile into the code tests whether identical baseline and scenario states produce any spurious non-zero difference, while checking whether every hour stays inside the interpolable load-bin range flags skipped or unevaluable records. These checks establish internal numerical consistency, not real-world accuracy. The model can also predict emission increases at a few individual units even when total load drops; confirming whether a real intervention triggers that operating mechanism still requires empirical observation.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions
caveats: This check verifies interpolable bounds against the fixed Regional Data File's load_bin_edges rather than treating the Texas annual observed extremes in Table 7 of the User Manual as code bin edges. None of the scenarios hit out-of-range values or upper endpoints; this does not validate real-world intervention outcomes.

claims.text: Next, two separate single-hour tests each reduce end-use electricity by 100 MWh in a single hour—labeled July 1 at 03:00 and July 1 at 16:00 in the Regional Data File (RDF)—while leaving all other hours unchanged. On AVERT's fossil-load coordinate, those two hours sit at 34,246 MW and 45,576 MW, respectively. Although both runs request the exact same fossil-load reduction, modeled CO₂ changes are −60.2830 and −56.6234 short tons, or approximately 546.88 and 513.68 kg per specified MWh of end-use reduction. Entering the model with the same energy reduction at two different operating points produces different responses.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Looking at criteria pollutants reverses the ranking between the two hours. In the same 03:00 and 16:00 tests, modeled sulfur dioxide (SO₂) changes are approximately −34.55 and −56.28 lb, and nitrogen oxides (NOₓ) changes are approximately −18.74 and −105.91 lb—so the 16:00 reduction avoids larger masses of both pollutants. Masses of different pollutants cannot be added directly, nor do these mass changes alone constitute a particulate-matter exposure, human-health, or multi-category life cycle impact assessment.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: These two single-hour profiles were evaluated directly through AVERT v4.3.0's native numerical functions; the web interface described in the v4.3 User Manual does not accept arbitrary user-supplied hourly load-change series. Before using such results to compare conservation options, one must verify that both 100 MWh reductions deliver the same final service and can feasibly be executed in the target hours. Linking the results to EIA records also requires aligning the RDF clock with UTC hours. Only after those conditions are verified does comparing the resulting CO₂ rates become meaningful.
claims.scope: Feeding a demand change into the native model; scope bounded to named historical datasets, native models, and explicit assumptions

claims.text: Load shifting requires placing both the decrease and the increase inside one complete schedule. When a service can be deferred, the intervention combines reduced consumption in the original window with added consumption in another window, and the comparison quantity is the emission difference between the complete shifted schedule and the baseline schedule. The two single-hour reduction runs above each answer only what happens when load drops in that hour; one cannot simply flip the sign of one reduction and treat it as a load increase without verification. Both schedules must deliver the same service within the allowed deadline, while equipment efficiency changes the electricity required and grid or storage losses change the generation required—each tracked at its own delivery point.
claims.scope: Moving from two separate single-hour reductions to a two-sided demand shift delivering the same service

claims.text: Steinsultz and colleagues constructed an empirical benchmark from ERCOT operating records, using 2020–2022 data for system-wide comparisons. They summed hourly CO₂ emissions across units covered by EPA's Clean Air Markets Program Data (CAMPD) and modeled hourly emission changes as a controlled function of changes in wind High Sustained Limit (HSL) across node groups. HSL is a reported measure of available wind output typically set from short-term forecasts, whereas actual generation is also affected by dispatch and curtailment; the study treats a drop in available wind as a proxy for a net-load increase, interpreting the two with opposite signs. Although grounded in operating records, applying this benchmark to a specific user's load change still requires verifying that the response matches at the same node and system state.
claims.scope: Observed object of the ERCOT wind-potential benchmark and conditions for transferring it to load shifting
caveats: HSL is generally declared from short-term forecasts rather than representing manipulated customer load or physically deliverable energy at every instant.

The authors are affiliated with providers of the evaluated statistical and dispatch signals, the benchmark and statistical model share CAMPD data, and node groups were formed using the dispatch signal; methodological differences do not imply independence of authors, data, or holdout samples.

claims.text: Using each signal's own 10th percentile as a cutoff, the study compared fitted benchmark responses in the lowest decile against the remaining hours. Within the sample, locational marginal prices and heat-rate signals also identified a low-decile group with lower benchmark emissions. Yet usefulness for screening does not mean a signal's numerical value equals the CO₂ change per added MWh: prices are still denominated in currency per MWh, and heat-rate methods still require checking whether their implied emission rates match the benchmark magnitude. In the largest node group, moreover, neither heat-rate nor price signals varied monotonically with the benchmark across quantiles.
