claims.scope: Conditional correspondence between EF 3.1 net-calorific-value MJ midpoints and ReCiPe 2016 higher-heating-value FFP midpoints.
caveats: Embedded short descriptions in the EF 3.1 method and elementary-flow XML files retain legacy "Radioactivity" text; inspecting the flow-property definition file for UUID 93a60a56-a3c8-11da-a746-0800200c9a66 is necessary to verify that the property is net calorific value (MJ).

claims.text: Category boundaries diverge just as sharply: should natural uranium mined for nuclear power be classified as a mineral element or an energy carrier? Documentation from the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) explains that while the original ADP model assigned uranium a mass-based (kg) factor, the ILCD elementary flow list places uranium under non-renewable underground energy resources measured in MJ; EF therefore assigns uranium 1 MJ/MJ inside "Resource use, fossils." Inspection of the official EF 3.1 method file confirms that this category contains six flows—brown coal, crude oil, hard coal, natural gas, peat, and uranium—while "Resource use, minerals and metals" excludes uranium. Conversely, a table note in Van Oers et al. (2020) explicitly opposes the EU Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) decision to group uranium with fossil or energy carriers, emphasizing that uranium also has non-energy uses; their workbook keeps uranium in elemental depletion (cumulative ADP ≈ 0.007823 kg Sb-eq/kg, rounded to 7.8 × 10⁻³ in the main table). ReCiPe 2016 likewise keeps uranium in its mineral SOP table and omits it from fossil FFP (Table 1). When comparing nuclear power against coal or natural gas electricity across LCIA systems, this single flow-unit and classification choice shifts the uranium resource burden between "fossil" and "mineral" indicators.
claims.scope: Classification divergence for natural uranium across EF 3.1, Van Oers et al. (2020) elemental ADP, and ReCiPe 2016 mineral SOP.
caveats: The EF 3.1 dataset retains the literal title "Resource use, fossils" even though it includes nuclear fuel uranium; interpreting a "fossil resource" score requires checking which elementary flows are included.

claims.text: Once a midpoint or endpoint position is chosen, a study must still decide how far into the future to look and what level of effect evidence to accept. The ReCiPe 2016 methodology paper and RIVM Report 2016-0104 organize those choices into three cultural perspectives: Individualist (short-term, such as a 20-year horizon or economic reserves), Hierarchist (default baseline, such as a 100-year horizon), and Egalitarian (long-term precautionary, such as an infinite or 100,000-year horizon), while simultaneously varying the evidentiary threshold required to include an effect. Even the longest perspective is constrained by underlying model data and does not integrate every category to infinity. Differences between two perspectives can therefore reflect both time horizon and effect inclusion simultaneously, rather than a single physical parameter change; selecting the perspective that fits a study's goal requires an explicit justification.
claims.scope: Scenario and cultural-perspective analysis in Section 2.3 of the ReCiPe 2016 methodology paper.
caveats: Section 4.1 of the paper notes that time and evidence choices remain unquantified for several categories; the three perspectives do not represent a complete probability distribution of all uncertainties.
Evidentiary acceptance levels cited by the 2016/2017 authors should not be rewritten as current normative standards.

claims.text: Beyond time horizon, where an emission occurs also determines what consequences a model can represent. "Global scale" does not mean that every location has been characterized in spatial detail. The ReCiPe 2016 paper provides regionalization options for categories such as particulate matter, ozone formation, acidification, freshwater eutrophication, and water use, while noting substantial spatial-resolution needs in other categories. Likewise, aggregated local species loss cannot be interpreted directly as global extinction risk. If a study asks how a specific receiving ecosystem changes, it must first check whether that system lies within the spatial scope of the model and its input data; a table of global-scale factors will not automatically supply site-specific ecological conditions.
claims.scope: Discussion of regionalization, ecosystem indicators, and omitted pathways in the ReCiPe 2016 methodology paper.
caveats: Methodological discussion of regionalization does not substitute for site-specific impact measurements; regionalized applicability depends on the underlying factors and validation evidence.
The paper's list of omitted pathways reflects that version and does not represent every subsequent release.

claims.text: In stratospheric ozone depletion, how far ahead one looks directly reverses midpoint rankings across gases (Table 2). EF 3.1 publishes only infinite-horizon steady-state ODP values (beyond 100 years), whereas RIVM Report 2016-0104 Tables 3.1 and 3.2 scale each substance by its removal rate relative to CFC-11 (atmospheric lifetime ≈ 45 years) to provide Individualist (20-year), Hierarchist (100-year), and Egalitarian (infinite) midpoints. Shorter-lived brominated or chlorinated gases concentrate their ozone destruction in the first few decades: for equal 1 kg emissions, Halon-1211 (lifetime ≈ 16 years) and Halon-1301 (lifetime ≈ 65 years) score 15.053 versus 11.841 kg CFC-11-eq over 20 years (Halon-1211 roughly 27% higher), but reverse at 100 years and infinity so that Halon-1301 is higher. The fumigant methyl bromide (lifetime under 1 year) exceeds the reference substance CFC-11 over 20 years, whereas CFC-115 (lifetime over 1,000 years) climbs steadily as the horizon lengthens.
claims.scope: Controlled ranking reversals in stratospheric ozone depletion across 20-year, 100-year, and infinite time horizons.
caveats: Controlled emission pairs test the algebraic ordering of characterization tables and do not represent full life cycle inventories of agricultural or refrigeration product systems; N₂O ODP values are explicitly marked preliminary in RIVM Report 2016-0104.

claims.text: Which substances enter the ozone depletion category—and which WMO assessment edition supplies the factors—can likewise invert option rankings. ILCD 2011 adopted WMO 1999, EF 3.0 and EF 3.1 upgraded to WMO 2014 steady-state values with supplementary additions, and ReCiPe 2016 used WMO 2011, all in kg CFC-11-eq. However, RIVM Report 2016-0104 (predating the 2017 methodology paper) Table 3.2 additionally includes the non-halocarbon nitrous oxide (N₂O), flagged with an asterisk as preliminary at 0.007, 0.011, and 0.017 kg CFC-11-eq/kg across the three perspectives, whereas the official EF 3.1 ozone depletion dataset omits N₂O entirely (while the same package's climate change method assigns 273.0 kg CO₂-eq/kg to that N₂O air flow). Compare agricultural or chemical Option A emitting 1 kg N₂O against refrigeration Option B leaking 0.2 kg hydrochlorofluorocarbon-22 (HCFC-22): EF 3.1 gives 0 versus 0.0068 kg CFC-11-eq, and ReCiPe 2016's 20-year perspective also ranks A below B (0.007 vs. 0.017 kg CFC-11-eq), yet both the 100-year (0.011 vs. 0.009) and infinite (0.017 vs. 0.008) perspectives reverse to rank A higher. Even holding the horizon fixed at infinite steady state, updating the WMO edition flips 1 kg Halon-1301 versus 1 kg Halon-2402 from 15.900 > 13.000 in ReCiPe 2016 Egalitarian (WMO 2011) to 15.2 < 15.7 in EF 3.1 (WMO 2014) (Table 2).
claims.scope: Divergent N₂O inclusion, WMO edition updates, and controlled ranking reversals in stratospheric ozone depletion.
caveats: Option A (1 kg N₂O) and Option B (0.2 kg HCFC-22) form a controlled emission pair to test factor-table ordering rather than full agricultural or refrigeration inventories; N₂O ODP values are explicitly flagged as preliminary in RIVM Report 2016-0104.

claims.text: In ionizing radiation, the reference radionuclide and emission compartment alter both numerical scale and comparability. The official EF 3.1 dataset retains human exposure efficiency relative to uranium-235 (kBq U-235-eq/kBq), whereas RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table 4.2 references the collective dose of 1 kBq cobalt-60 (Co-60) emitted to air (kBq Co-60 to air-eq/kBq). For radionuclides where both systems share the same Frischknecht et al. (2000) 100,000-year collective dose without recalculated fate and exposure, the U-235 to Co-60 (air) ratio is 14:11; multiplying an EF 3.1 factor by 14/11 (≈ 1.273) therefore matches ReCiPe 2016 Egalitarian (for instance, U-235 to air 1.0 vs. 1.27, Co-60 to air 0.786 vs. 1.0, as well as short-lived entries such as Co-60 to freshwater, cesium-134 to air, and radon-222 to air). Once the integration horizon changes or De Schryver et al. (2011) fate-and-exposure revisions apply (as for cesium-137, carbon-14, and iodine-129), that fixed ratio no longer holds. Compartment differences span orders of magnitude: in EF 3.1, 1 kBq cesium-137 scores 7.86 in freshwater, 0.636 in air, and only 0.00371 kBq U-235-eq in marine water (a freshwater-to-marine ratio exceeding 2,000, and over 1,700 in ReCiPe 2016); carbon-14, which enters global photosynthesis as gaseous CO₂, scores 10.0 kBq U-235-eq/kBq in air versus only 0.0557 in freshwater or marine water. Comparing results requires aligning both reference nuclide and emission compartment first.
claims.scope: The 14:11 U-235 vs. Co-60 collective-dose reference ratio in ionizing radiation and order-of-magnitude compartment differences across air, freshwater, and marine releases.
caveats: The 14/11 ratio holds only where both systems share the same Frischknecht et al. (2000) integration horizon and unrevised dose model; changing the horizon, nuclide coverage, or adopting De Schryver et al. (2011) updates breaks the ratio.

Short-lived nuclide 14/11 pairs (EF 3.1 vs. ReCiPe 2016 Egalitarian): Co-60 freshwater 2.07 vs. 2.64, Cs-134 air 0.564 vs. 0.718, Rn-222 air 0.00114 vs. 0.00145. In ReCiPe 2016 Hierarchist and Egalitarian, Cs-137 is 10.0 (freshwater), 1.64 (air), and 0.00582 (marine) kBq Co-60 to air-eq/kBq (> 1,700× freshwater-to-marine ratio).

claims.text: Ionizing radiation stretches collective-dose integration to 100,000 years, not only flipping rankings but also determining whether key radionuclides are scored at all (Table 3). Although the EF 3.1 method file tags its time field as "time independent," its factors for globally dispersed long-lived nuclides such as carbon-14 and iodine-129 still come from Frischknecht et al.'s 100,000-year integration; RIVM Report 2016-0104 Tables 4.1 and 4.2 explicitly separate 20-year, 100-year, and 100,000-year columns. Comparing 1 kBq carbon-14 (half-life ≈ 5,730 years) with 1 kBq cesium-137 (half-life ≈ 30 years) emitted to air, carbon-14 is roughly 15.7 times cesium-137 in EF 3.1 and 7.87 times in ReCiPe 2016 Egalitarian (100,000 years); truncating to 100 or 20 years pushes most of carbon-14's future dose outside the window and immediately reverses the order so cesium-137 ranks higher. For iodine-129 (half-life > 10 million years), moving from 100 to 100,000 years in ReCiPe 2016 raises the air factor from 10.5 to 207 and the freshwater factor from 0.287 to 155 (roughly 540-fold), diverging sharply from EF 3.1 values converted by 14/11 (56.4 air, 5.99 freshwater kBq Co-60 to air-eq/kBq) because De Schryver et al. (2011) recalculated its fate and exposure. Equally critical is a coverage gap in RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table 4.2 and footnote a: characteristic uranium-mining and tailings nuclides—uranium-234, uranium-235, uranium-238, and thorium-230 (converted from Frischknecht et al. 2000 alongside alpha-plutonium and alpha-curium per footnote a), together with radium-226 and plutonium-238—are populated only in the Egalitarian (100,000-year) column and left blank in Individualist and default Hierarchist. Even EF 3.1's reference nuclide U-235 has no factor in ReCiPe's default 100-year table, whereas EF 3.1 assigns nonzero values to all five air emissions (U-234, U-235, U-238, Th-230, Ra-226). Conversely, technetium-99 and airborne strontium-90 appear in ReCiPe 2016 but are absent from EF 3.1 (which includes only waterborne Sr-90 at 1.93 × 10⁻⁴). Applying the default 100-year perspective without auditing nuclide coverage silently zeroes out long-lived alpha emitters from tailings.
claims.scope: C-14 vs. Cs-137 rank reversals, I-129 jumps across 20/100/100,000-year horizons, and blank uranium-series and transuranic coverage in ReCiPe 2016 I/H perspectives.
caveats: Even the 100,000-year Egalitarian horizon is noted in RIVM Report 2016-0104 as short relative to ultra-long-lived nuclides such as U-235 (half-life 7.1 × 10⁸ years) and should not be misread as an infinite integral over complete decay chains.

claims.text: When moving from midpoint to human health endpoints, disease-evidence thresholds and low-dose extrapolation assumptions are bundled into each perspective's conversion constant. Within a single perspective, ReCiPe 2016 multiplies each pathway by a fixed positive scalar. For ozone depletion (RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table 3.3), Individualist, Hierarchist, and Egalitarian multiply by 2.37 × 10⁻⁴, 5.31 × 10⁻⁴, and 1.34 × 10⁻³ DALY/kg CFC-11-eq (replacing the ReCiPe 2008 design of separate damage factors for six substance subgroups criticized in ILCD 2011 §3.2.7); the first two perspectives count only three skin cancers (malignant melanoma, basal cell carcinoma, and squamous cell carcinoma), whereas only Egalitarian adds cataracts, whose UV-exposure evidence remains more contested. For ionizing radiation (Tables 4.1 and 4.3), the multipliers are 6.8 × 10⁻⁹, 8.5 × 10⁻⁹, and 1.4 × 10⁻⁸ DALY/kBq Co-60 to air-eq: the model divides the 0.05 fatal cancers and 0.12 non-fatal cancers per man·Sv derived from Hiroshima, Nagasaki, and occupational moderate-to-high-dose studies by a dose and dose-rate effectiveness factor (DDREF) of 10, 6, and 2, respectively; expands included cancer sites from 4 (thyroid, bone marrow, lung, breast) to 11 and then to 13 (adding bone surface and remaining cancers); and adds 0.01 severe hereditary diseases per man·Sv (valued at 57 DALY/case in RIVM under 50% immediate mortality and 0.4 disability weight, compared with 61 DALY/case without age weighting cited in ILCD 2011).
claims.scope: Disease scope, DDREF, and hereditary-disease DALY choices bundled into ReCiPe 2016 ozone depletion and ionizing radiation endpoint conversion factors.
caveats: The difference between 57 and 61 DALY/case reflects differing disability-weight or life-table assumptions, illustrating why ILCD 2011 declined to formally recommend an ionizing radiation health endpoint given high hereditary-effect DALY uncertainty.

claims.text: Within any single ReCiPe 2016 perspective, multiplying by a positive constant preserves that perspective's midpoint substance ranking. Across perspectives, however, time horizon, radionuclide coverage, disease scope, and DDREF change together, so endpoint differences cannot be attributed to a single physical parameter. Spatial resolution is equally constrained: whether estimating UV health effects from Hayashi et al.'s 10-degree latitudinal bands and indigenous skin-color distributions (ignoring modern migration) or extrapolating French nuclear facilities globally under Dreicer and Frischknecht's assumption of a constant 10 billion world population for 100,000 years, the result is a spatially undifferentiated global default potential. It cannot substitute for site-specific radiation dose-limit compliance around a nuclear facility or local UV public-health assessment.
claims.scope: Cross-perspective co-variation and global-default spatial limits in ozone depletion and ionizing radiation health endpoints.

claims.text: Nor do cultural perspectives imply that every category has separate time horizons: RIVM Report 2016-0104 does not quantify value choices for land-use factors. The LC-IMPACT land-stress technical chapter provides an explicit horizon contrast instead. Starting from local habitat change, it applies regional species–area relationships, vulnerability scores, and taxonomic aggregation to build a global species-loss indicator; the 2020 LC-IMPACT paper interprets global potentially disappeared fraction of species multiplied by years (PDF·yr) as a time-integrated global extinction-risk indicator—neither a count of observed extinctions nor a prediction that extinct species reappear—making it a different estimand from ReCiPe's species-loss metric that cannot be converted directly by area and years. Equation 11.18 of the LC-IMPACT land chapter calculates the "core" contribution over the first 100 years after abandonment, while adjacent text explains that core plus tail equals the full recovery contribution. Those 100 years begin when land use ceases—not when occupation starts—and do not truncate the preceding occupation inventory; if modeled recovery finishes within 100 years, the core captures all of it, and if recovery lasts longer, the curve beyond 100 years is not forced to zero. Choosing a 100-year horizon therefore does not assume ecosystems recover by year 100; it is a mathematical time-truncation rule in the formula, not an empirical observation of site recovery speed.
claims.scope: Core 100-year horizon in LC-IMPACT Chapter 11 Eq. 11.18 and its relationship to full-recovery tails.
caveats: A parenthetical note under "Level of robustness" on the same page of the technical chapter abbreviates core as t_reg ≤ 100; this analysis follows the explicit t_reg > 100 branch in Eq. 11.18 and the adjacent "Time horizon" text rather than excluding slow-recovering strata. No official erratum has been verified to resolve that internal discrepancy.

claims.text: Examining a single unweighted regional stratum in the LC-IMPACT land chapter—fixing land-use type, ecoregion, taxon, and factor basis prior to vulnerability and taxonomic weighting—clarifies what time truncation does. Let the occupation factor be c ≥ 0 (regional species loss/m²) and the recovery duration be T > 0; at s years after abandonment, the modeled linear recovery gap is c(1 − s/T), reaching zero at T (a mathematical representation in the source formula, not a field-measured recovery trajectory). Integrating only over the first H ≥ 0 years with u = min(H, T) yields an area under the gap curve of c[u − u²/(2T)], compared with the full recovery area cT/2 (both in regional species loss·yr/m²), which is then multiplied by transformed land area to obtain the stratum's recovery contribution (the time-integral area is distinct from inventory land area, and the chapter's core horizon is 100 years rather than a release of official factors for arbitrary H). Checking T = 2H shows the difference clearly: half the gap remains at H, so the first H years account for 3cH/4, whereas mistakenly accelerating recovery to finish at H or multiplying the full area by H/T yields only cH/2. Counting fewer years is not the same as making the ecological deficit disappear faster; when T ≤ H both integrals coincide, and when c = 0 a 0/0 retention ratio is undefined.
claims.scope: Analytical integral reproducing the LC-IMPACT time-truncation branches within a fixed unweighted regional stratum.

claims.text: Such truncation generally cannot be approximated by a single universal ratio. Because strata have different recovery durations, each retains a different fraction within the first 100 years; each stratum must be evaluated using its own recovery time before aggregating with consistent scope and weights, whereas averaging recovery durations first performs a different calculation. Likewise, the fraction retained in recovery alone is not the retention fraction of total land impact including occupation. Relaxing c ≥ 0 changes the ordering as well: while non-negative c keeps the core contribution between zero and the full-period contribution, negative c reverses those inequalities. Negative lower quantiles in LC-IMPACT Table 11.1 do not establish net ecological gain for a parcel, nor can separate core and full-period quantiles determine the corresponding tail quantiles without the joint distribution pairing them. ReCiPe's fixed multiplier k cannot specify which years LC-IMPACT excludes, much less serve as a rule for restoring the tail.
claims.scope: Distinct roles of stratum-level time truncation, aggregation, sign convention, and quantile pairing.

claims.text: For mineral SOP, "how far ahead" is operationalized as how much resource is included in the future extraction cap. In RIVM Report 2016-0104, the Individualist (short-term) perspective uses economically mineable reserves under prevailing prices and technology, whereas Hierarchist and Egalitarian use ultimate recoverable resources—set by cited assumption to 0.01% of total elemental mass in the upper 3 km of Earth's crust. This cap is an assumed upper bound on future extraction, not a deterministic exhaustion year and not the geological stock used in ADP. Averaging the grade curve over different caps can shift individual factors, while copper itself always equals 1 in each perspective's normalized column. Mineral scenario differences therefore cannot be mapped directly onto the 100-year time window of the land-recovery example.
claims.scope: Meaning of future extraction caps and copper normalization across perspectives in mineral SOP.
caveats: Here "short-term" refers to the relative framing of the Individualist perspective in RIVM Report 2016-0104 rather than a fixed number of years. Changing the absolute extraction cap does not guarantee every copper-normalized factor changes; copper equals 1 in both columns.

claims.text: Endpoint scenario choices for fossil resources work differently again. Chapter 13 of RIVM Report 2016-0104 assumes lowest-cost fossil reserves are extracted first—moving from conventional crude oil to enhanced oil recovery or Arctic fields—and averages the undiscounted future surplus extraction cost over expected total future production to define surplus cost potential (SCP) in constant 2013 US dollars (USD2013). Section 13.2 explicitly states that fossil resources have no perspective differences at either midpoint or endpoint: crude oil, hard coal, and natural gas use maximum future production estimates from the 2013 International Energy Agency (IEA) report and share identical endpoint factors across all three perspectives. Turning to Table 13.2, however, brown coal and peat are left blank in Individualist and Hierarchist due to missing production and cost data, while Egalitarian borrows the hard coal factor (0.034 USD2013/kg) on a precautionary basis. Even when horizons and reserve caps stay fixed, missing-data proxy rules can still alter category coverage across perspective columns.
claims.scope: Fossil endpoint SCP assumptions, three-perspective identity, and Egalitarian brown-coal/peat proxies in RIVM Report 2016-0104 Chapter 13.
caveats: Blank Individualist and Hierarchist cells for brown coal and peat in Table 13.2 mean endpoint factors were not explicitly computed due to missing data; they must not be interpreted as evidence of zero future extraction cost increase.

claims.text: The same method name can refer either to a mathematical model or to the source of its input data. ReCiPe 2016's toxicity characterization builds on USES-LCA 2.0 while drawing substance data from USEtox; the authors explicitly caution that this does not constitute an implementation of the USEtox model. A model defines the equations linking emission, fate, exposure, and effect; input data parameterize those equations; and a factor release package stores numerical outputs computed under one specific set of conditions. Sharing input data does not make equations or scenarios identical, and citing the same method name still requires checking which factor release was actually loaded. Interpreting any LCIA result requires stating both what consequence the model estimates and which equations and data produced the numbers.
claims.scope: Distinction between toxicity model implementation, input data, and factor release artifacts in the ReCiPe 2016 methodology paper.
caveats: A methodology paper does not substitute for independent verification of factor tables, databases, or software implementations; the 2017 paper, the 2016 RIVM report, and the 2017 v1.1 update remain distinct versions.
This historical implementation choice does not imply that later USEtox versions lacked any capability.

claims.text: For fossil resources, no constant midpoint-to-endpoint conversion factor exists in the first place. By RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table 13.1, extracting 1 kg of crude oil, roughly 1.190 Nm³ of natural gas (1/0.84), or roughly 2.381 kg of hard coal (1/0.42) yields the exact same midpoint score of 1 kg oil-eq. Multiplying by the fuel-specific endpoint factors in Table 13.2—0.457 USD2013/kg for crude oil, 0.301 USD2013/Nm³ for natural gas, and 0.034 USD2013/kg for hard coal—produces endpoint surplus costs of approximately 0.457, 0.358, and 0.081 USD2013, making crude oil about 5.6 times hard coal (using unrounded appendix higher heating value ratios of 45.8/38.3 and 45.8/19.1 still yields approximately 0.360 and 0.0815 USD2013 for natural gas and hard coal). The divergence is not a rounding artifact; the model has changed its question. The midpoint compares fuel energy content, whereas the endpoint estimates extraction difficulty from each fuel's own reserve scale and cost–cumulative production curve—two relationships that do not move in lockstep, so no single positive multiplier can map identical kg oil-eq scores onto those endpoint costs.
claims.scope: Verification of endpoint SCP divergence across crude oil, natural gas, and hard coal at an identical 1 kg oil-eq midpoint in ReCiPe 2016.
caveats: The 1/0.84 Nm³ and 1/0.42 kg quantities are controlled inputs constructed to fix the midpoint at 1 kg oil-eq and do not imply that 1 MJ of different fuels delivers equal electricity or heat efficiency in power plants or boilers.

claims.text: Missing-data proxies alter equal-energy rankings even further. At 0.22 kg oil-eq/kg in RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table 13.1, matching the same 1 kg oil-eq midpoint requires extracting roughly 4.545 kg (1/0.22) of brown coal or peat. Under Individualist and Hierarchist, that midpoint burden receives no fossil endpoint score because endpoint factors are absent. Under Egalitarian, however, Table 13.2 copies hard coal's 0.034 USD2013/kg directly onto brown coal and peat on a per-kilogram mass basis without adjusting for their lower heating value (9.9 vs. 19.1 MJ-eq/kg); consequently, 1 kg oil-eq of brown coal or peat jumps to roughly 0.155 USD2013 (0.034/0.22) at the endpoint—about 1.9 times equal-energy hard coal (≈ 0.081 USD2013). Here too, dollars represent a modeled proxy for future surplus extraction cost, excluding combustion greenhouse gases (examined in Climate Equivalence), power-plant conversion losses, and current coal purchase prices.
claims.scope: Quantitative effect of blank I/H entries versus mass-basis Egalitarian hard-coal proxy for brown coal and peat at 1 kg oil-eq, and cross-chapter boundaries.
caveats: The 0.155 USD2013 score exceeding hard coal's 0.081 USD2013 arises purely from borrowing a mass-based hard-coal proxy while normalizing by heating value; it must not be read as empirical evidence that brown coal has a steeper future cost curve than hard coal.

claims.text: Unlike fossil resources, where a single conversion factor is rejected, RIVM Report 2016-0104 links mineral midpoints and endpoints through one common multiplier. Under the ultimate recoverable resources scenario, all minerals share 0.23 USD2013/kg Cu-eq; multiplying the reported SOP values yields future surplus cost factors of 0.23, ≈ 0.665, and ≈ 0.0189 USD2013/kg of extracted element for copper, nickel, and manganese (or USD2013 for 1 kg of each). As noted earlier, multiplying by a common positive scalar preserves the midpoint ranking identically. USD2013 denotes a fixed currency base year rather than an expenditure incurred in 2013; the report bridges ore demand and cost via a regression relating prices, ore demand, and extraction costs, so expressing the unit in dollars does not automatically add metal-specific cost mechanisms.
claims.scope: Uniform copper cost-conversion rate under Hierarchist/Egalitarian in RIVM Report 2016-0104 and multiplication from displayed table values.
caveats: Displayed table products are 1 × 0.23 = 0.23, 2.89 × 0.23 = 0.6647, and 0.0823 × 0.23 = 0.018929, with the latter two rounded in the text; this does not claim inspection of an official endpoint workbook or software execution.

Original Table 12.3 abbreviates the denominator as kg Cu, whereas §12.4 defines the conversion per kg Cu-eq. USD2013 is a currency base year, not an expenditure date or spot purchase price; these are future cost indicators, not actual mine outlays.

claims.text: Fitting cost curves separately for each metal produces a different ranking. Using mine operating costs already allocated across co-products by revenue, Vieira et al. (2016) rank mines by operating cost per kilogram of target metal, fit separate cost–tonnage curves for each metal, and average over the assumed future extraction interval to define an indicator interpreted as future surplus extraction cost per kilogram extracted today. Under their ultimate recoverable resources scenario, copper, nickel, and manganese score 0.744, 5.62, and 4.42 USD2013/kg: nickel still exceeds copper, but manganese flips from below copper to well above it. Because no single positive scalar can reproduce both copper–manganese orderings, uniform cost scaling of an ore-based midpoint is not equivalent to metal-specific cost modeling. Because underlying data, curves, and estimators all differ simultaneously, the gap cannot be attributed solely to metal-by-metal fitting, nor does it prove that the metal-specific model accurately predicts actual future costs.
claims.scope: Bounded vector comparison between metal-specific SCP and ReCiPe's uniform mineral cost proxy.
caveats: Eq. (2) in Vieira et al. (2016) integrates and averages C over the future extraction interval, whereas ReCiPe's supporting material writes ΔC for cost increase; this chapter reports each author's stated interpretation without equating the formulas term by term or reconstructing causal cost differences.

The model relies on historical cross-mine cost fits (Supplementary Table S1 lists 9 mines for manganese); because curves, samples, and estimators change together, the entire discrepancy cannot be attributed causally to metal-specific fitting alone.
The paper converts annual operating costs to 2013 USD and weights them by mine production per kg of target metal before ranking mines; the ranking is not an unallocated total mine-cost sequence.

claims.text: Unexplained numerical discrepancies also remain between the two primary documents. RIVM Report 2016-0104 sets the copper conversion factor to 0.23 USD2013/kg Cu-eq—giving 0.23 USD2013/kg for copper itself (SOP = 1)—whereas the cited Vieira et al. (2016) paper reports 0.744 USD2013/kg; the two sources also list different copper ultimate recoverable resources, so they cannot be treated as using identical inputs. Even in the economic reserves scenario (Individualist), where both sources display matching reserves and starting cumulative extraction for copper and manganese, the copper–manganese cost ranking still reverses: uniform scaling gives 0.16 USD2013/kg for copper and ≈ 0.00602 USD2013/kg for manganese, whereas the metal-specific model gives 0.521 and 1.39 USD2013/kg. Even recalibrating the uniform multiplier to the paper's copper figure would leave manganese below copper because its SOP is below 1; changing the copper reference value alone cannot remove the divergence.
claims.scope: Copper calibration discrepancy and bounded counterexample under matching displayed reserves and cumulative extraction inputs.
caveats: RIVM Table S8.1 and Vieira et al. Supplementary Table S2 list copper URR as 4.36 × 10¹² and 4.63 × 10¹² kg, respectively. Under economic reserves, both display R = 6.90 × 10¹¹ kg and CME = 5.92 × 10¹¹ kg for copper, and R = 5.70 × 10¹¹ kg and CME = 5.80 × 10¹¹ kg for manganese (CME requires cross-reading RIVM Table S8.1 with main-paper Table 1 rather than Table S2 alone).

Under economic reserves, multiplying displayed values gives 0.0376 × 0.16 = 0.006016 vs. SCP values of 1.39 (manganese) and 0.521 (copper). Matching R and CME does not make underlying curves, samples, integral notation, or estimators identical; the examined sources neither explain the 0.23 vs. 0.744 discrepancy nor issue an erratum.

RIVM §12.4's stated slope range does not fully match the 0.92/0.95 cost exponents printed in Fig. S8.2, and Fig. 12.3 labels its axis USD2013 while its caption states USD1998; Vieira et al. Eq. (2) writes C while RIVM writes ΔC. Each artifact's wording is preserved without guessing a "true" coefficient.

claims.text: Model-internal extraction order must also be kept distinct from real-world mining sequences. Extracting high-grade deposits first and low-cost mines first are assumptions built into the derivations above. In reality, prices, exploration, processing technology, and economic cutoff grades continually reshape what is mineable, and the 0.01% / 3 km ultimate recoverable resource assumption has itself been criticized for lacking empirical support. In a 2019 commentary, Ericsson et al. cite reported Boliden data for the Aitik copper mine showing that reported reserves can increase even as cumulative extraction grows, while processing improvements can render lower-grade ore economical. That counterexample does not mean mining leaves underground natural stocks unchanged, but it does show that declining head grades alone cannot prove worsening economic availability. Likewise, curves fitted to a historical cost window cannot separate how much cost variation stems from physical depletion versus price cycles or technological shifts.
claims.scope: Evidentiary limits on mineable-set dynamics and historical cost-curve extrapolation.
caveats: The Aitik figure is drawn from Boliden data as relayed by the commentary authors without independent re-verification of mine time series; a single mine does not prove long-term trends for all minerals. In-situ grade, economic cutoff grade, and processed head grade have distinct meanings.
Cross-sectional historical model fits differ from causal effects of marginal extraction; broad market-coverage percentages cited in the commentary are not adopted as conclusions here.

claims.text: Printed equations, input tables, and released characterization factors do not always agree—and RIVM Report 2016-0104 contains locatable internal discrepancies across three pathways. First, in land-use Appendix Table S7.3, the recovery endpoint factors for grassland/pasture and annual crops disagree with the main-text formula and midpoint table; recalculating from the main-text occupation factors, mean recovery times, and conversion constant shows the two rows are swapped to reported precision. Second, on page 36, the finite-horizon ozone depletion scaling text states that the constant 3 represents a 3-year troposphere-to-stratosphere transport lag, which physically implies an active removal time of t − 3 years (17 and 97 years for 20- and 100-year horizons); yet the printed equation reads F_t = 1 − e^{(−t−3)·k} (equivalent to 23 and 103 years). Recalculating Table 3.2 with WMO 2011 lifetimes matches every halocarbon's 20- and 100-year entry to three decimal places (for instance, methyl bromide's 20-year value is 1.649 rather than the 2.098 implied by a physical lag), confirming that the printed expression was not a mere typo but the actual spreadsheet formula generating the table. Third, fossil-resource page 96 and Appendix Table S9.2 report cumulative extraction in kg or Nm³, yet substituting crude oil's 1.61 × 10¹⁴ kg into the printed log-linear cost equation yields a denominator of roughly −105.6 and no positive cost, while Figure 13.2 labels its horizontal axis in "billion barrels of oil." Without access to unpublished working sheets and underlying IEA curves, one can test midpoint–endpoint relationships only from published Tables 13.1 and 13.2—not invent unit conversions to claim independent recalculation. Locating such discrepancies is not equivalent to finding an official erratum; citations must preserve published table values, keep original reports, updates, and electronic releases distinct, and verify formulas separately from tabulated numbers.
claims.scope: Verification of the (−t−3)·k lag-sign formula against Table 3.2 in RIVM Report 2016-0104, plus locatable land, fossil, and textual/unit discrepancies across RIVM 2016-0104 and the 2017 methodology paper.
caveats: The check 40.0 − 4.45·ln(1.61 × 10¹⁴) ≈ −105.6 demonstrates only that the printed formula does not close directly under Table S9.2's kg unit; it does not invalidate Figure 13.2's original fit in billion barrels.

Demonstrating that (−t−3)·k runs opposite to the physical lag text documents how published Table 3.2 values were generated and does not authorize users to alter official ReCiPe 2016 table values when citing them.

Additional RIVM 2016-0104 ozone/radiation details: k is inverse atmospheric lifetime (distinct from the land conversion factor k), and F_t is the fraction of potential released within horizon t; halocarbons matching (−t−3)·k to three decimals include CFC-12 (0.421/0.587; physical-lag 20 yr = 0.407), Halon-1301 (11.841/14.066), Halon-1211 (15.053/8.777; physical-lag 20 yr = 16.432), and methyl bromide (1.649/0.734). The 2017 paper §3.1.2 mentions only infinite-horizon ODP (WMO 2011), omitting Table 3.2's 20- and 100-year columns; RIVM p. 38 defines 10-degree "latitudinal zones" then later prints "longitudinal zone"; summary Table 1.5 rounds Table 3.3 to 2.4 × 10⁻⁴, 5.3 × 10⁻⁴, and 1.3 × 10⁻³ and prints "yr//kBq Co-60 to air"; pp. 44–45 print mass units ("Co-60 to air eq/kg", "DALY/kg Co-60 to air eq.") and miscite Table 4.3 as "Table 3.3".

Additional RIVM 2016-0104 fossil-chapter citations and units: p. 96 miscites the higher-heating-value appendix as Table S9.2 (actually S9.1), miscites the crude-oil cost curve as Fig. 11.2 (actually Fig. 13.2), attributes C_x = 1/(a_x + b_x·ln CFE_x) to the mineral SOP paper (Vieira et al. 2016b), and cites endpoint factors as an unpublished "in preparation" manuscript; Table S9.2 lists crude oil a = 40.0, b = −4.45, CFE = 1.61 × 10¹⁴ kg, prints hard-coal cumulative extraction as n.a., and labels current costs USD2008 while the main endpoint table uses USD2013.

claims.text: Similar misalignments appear between EU Environmental Footprint technical reports and the machine-readable Extensible Markup Language (XML) files in the official EF 3.1 reference package—and even within the reports themselves. For ozone depletion, Tables 1 and 2 of the 2018 methods report (JRC109369) and the description field of the official EF 3.1 method XML still state "based on WMO 1999" with 23 items, yet §4.2, Annex 1, Table 1 of the 2023 update report (JRC130796), and the actual XML (25 substance names, 124 factors) implement WMO 2014 steady-state values plus supplementary additions; furthermore, carbon tetrachloride and methyl bromide added under synonym-flow rules lack Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) numbers in their flow XML, and methyl bromide has only 4 air sub-compartments (omitting "lower stratosphere + upper troposphere" compared with 5 for carbon tetrachloride). For ionizing radiation, Table 2 of the 2018 report mislabels the flow property as mass, and §4.5 claims that lower stratosphere/upper troposphere and most non-freshwater aquatic sub-compartments were excluded while marking freshwater "estimated"; yet the actual EF 3.1 ionizing radiation XML (header stating 30 items, actually containing 29 radionuclide prefixes and 189 factors) correctly binds the radioactivity flow property, retains those atmospheric and aquatic sub-compartments, and marks freshwater "Calculated," while elementary-flow XML synonym fields for Cs-137, I-129, and Rn-222 erroneously include names of other isotopes. Because software results follow the loaded method XML and universally unique identifier (UUID) flow mappings, auditing requires checking both reports and XML files rather than relying on summary tables alone.
claims.scope: Measured conflicts between JRC109369/JRC130796 report text and official EF 3.1 XML datasets (b5c629d6 and b5c632be) regarding WMO edition, Annex 1 counts, flow properties, sub-compartments, estimation status, and synonyms.
caveats: Where official XML datasets diverge from technical report prose, LCA software computes from the loaded method XML and flow UUID mappings; audits must inspect both rather than summary tables alone.

EF 3.1 package and report details: ozone depletion XML UUID prefix b5c629d6; JRC109369 §4.2 and Annex 1 list 23 substances across 113 rows (omitting upper-atmosphere rows for CFC-113 and HCFC-142b, and listing chloromethane as R-40); added carbon tetrachloride matches CFC-10 at 0.72 (5 air sub-compartments) and methyl bromide matches Halon-1001 at 0.57 (4 sub-compartments); removing duplicate flow Bromomethane from the normalization inventory shifted the per-capita reference from 5.36 × 10⁻² to 5.23 × 10⁻² kg CFC-11-eq/person, while ionizing radiation remained 4.22 × 10³ kBq U-235-eq/person. Ionizing radiation XML UUID prefix b5c632be; both reports' Table 1 omit "eq" (printing kBq U235), 2018 Table 2 prints "Mass U235-equivalents (kg)", and flow XML cross-isotope synonym errors include Cs-137 → "Cs-131", I-129 → "Iodine, isotope of mass 125", and Rn-222 → "219rn".

claims.text: Mineral resource modeling also remains the subject of genuine methodological disagreement. Berger et al. (2020) tentatively accepted a subsequent SOP release for evaluating consequences of declining mineral quality, while questioning both uniform copper-based cost conversion and metal-specific cost estimates shaped by high-demand boom periods; Ericsson et al. (2019), more broadly, argued against using "future efforts" models in LCIA at all. Neither a tentative recommendation nor a broad critique settles physical truth for the reader. What is clear is that primary stock depletion, future ore demand, and future extraction cost estimate different quantities, equal elemental extractions can rank differently across them, and fixed multipliers cannot substitute for resource-specific models. Using such indicators to select materials still requires restoring functionally equivalent product inventories and choosing a justified model with explicit applicability boundaries for the resource consequence of interest.
claims.scope: Conditional model comparison and genuine methodological disagreement over mineral resource LCIA.
caveats: Berger et al.'s tentative recommendation refers to the Vieira 2017/2018 SOP_URR lineage (75 mineral factors), not the original 2016 table rows examined here; their ADP recommendation at the time also does not automatically cover the 2020 cumulative update.

Shared authorship, reused datasets, and citation chains are not independent empirical replication; this section compares published method documents, reviews, and official release packages rather than conducting independent geological or mining-engineering investigations.

claims.text: Bringing all four inventory starting points together, reading any midpoint or endpoint result requires four checks. First, verify the midpoint estimand and category boundary: whether a resource midpoint tracks geological stock, future ore demand, or energy content; whether heating value is net or higher; whether natural uranium is classified as an energy carrier or a mineral (otherwise cross-method power or heating comparisons misread boundary shifts as fuel changes); and whether nitrous oxide is included in stratospheric ozone depletion (otherwise systems with nitrogen fertilizer or combustion N₂O face a structural break between EF 3.1 and ReCiPe 2016). Second, verify reference and horizon settings: which WMO steady-state edition applies, whether finite-horizon scaling is used, whether ionizing radiation references U-235 or Co-60 to air, whether integration stops at 100 or 100,000 years, which compartment receives the release, whether minerals use economic reserves or ultimate recoverable resources, how many years of land recovery are counted, and whether any entries are blank under the chosen perspective. Third, check the machine-readable factors actually executed—verifying method XML by flow UUID, substance or nuclide identity, and CAS number rather than trusting outdated header years, missing update tags, or uncleaned synonyms. Fourth, check what the endpoint adds—a fixed multiplier, new disease and low-dose extrapolation models, or fuel-specific cost curves and missing-data proxies. The resulting DALY, species·yr, and USD2013 figures remain model-conditioned global default indicators, never substitutes for nuclear site radiation safety licensing, local UV epidemiology, or commodity market prices. The next chapter turns to the relationship between greenhouse gas emissions and climate response.
claims.scope: Cross-system verification boundaries and interpretation limits across all four midpoint/endpoint inventory starting points.
caveats: These four checks ensure transparency and comparability within LCIA characterization only; they do not substitute for probabilistic reactor safety analysis, deep geological repository safety cases, or geophysical ozone-recovery modeling.

This summary states conditions supported by examined method texts and release tables; it does not replace energy-security assessments, power-dispatch simulations, or mine/oilfield financial appraisals.

Multi-pathway gases such as chloromethane are scored separately across stratospheric ozone depletion, climate change, and photochemical ozone formation, as discussed further in Acidification and Nutrient Enrichment.

claims.text: When two activities both report one metric ton of carbon dioxide (CO₂) equivalents, do they cause the same climate change? Answering that question requires knowing how equivalence was computed. Analysts first model the climate response to each gas emission and then compare it with a prescribed CO₂ reference response; emission dates, metric choice, and factor edition all shape the result. Under global warming potential (GWP), if two calculations use the same factor edition, model assumptions, time horizon, and CO₂ reference, equal CO₂-equivalent scores mean that modeled cumulative radiative forcing is comparable within reporting precision. Switching to temperature change at a chosen point in time changes what is being compared.
claims.scope: Compared physical quantity, reference basis, and timing conditions underlying physical climate metrics.

claims.text: In a life cycle inventory, kg methane (CH₄) records the mass of methane released to the environment, whereas kg CO₂-eq is an accounting quantity obtained by scaling a specified climate effect of that release against a chosen CO₂ reference effect. CO₂ equivalents are not physical mass of CO₂ emitted. Emitted gas mass, radiative forcing, global mean temperature change, and human health or ecosystem damage occupy distinct positions along the causal chain; grouping them under one "greenhouse effect" heading does not make them the same physical quantity.
claims.scope: Distinction between inventory emission mass, relative CO₂-equivalent scores, and physical quantities along the climate causal chain.

claims.text: To trace that chain, emissions are first idealized as a pulse: releasing one unit mass of gas at t = 0 into a specified background state and comparing the perturbed system against the unperturbed baseline. Unit-pulse responses provide the building blocks for emissions distributed across multiple dates. Summing multiple pulse responses, however, relies on the chosen background state and a linear approximation; expressing a factor "per kilogram" does not guarantee that linearity holds for arbitrarily large emissions.
claims.scope: Unit-mass emission pulses under a fixed background state and linear superposition.
caveats: Pulse superposition in this chapter is restricted to the stated linear impulse responses and background state; it is not a full nonlinear Earth-system model.

claims.text: The CO₂ reference response itself must be modeled. Added carbon exchanges among atmospheric, oceanic, and terrestrial reservoirs across multiple timescales, so no single atmospheric chemical lifetime summarizes its removal. Impulse response functions typically fit this composite behavior with several exponential decay terms plus a very slow residual term; an individual fitted time constant cannot be labeled as the lifetime of one isolated ocean or ecological process.
claims.scope: Interpretation of CO₂ reservoir exchange and multi-exponential impulse response fits in Joos et al. (2013).

claims.text: The two curves in the figure answer two distinct questions: the top panel shows the fraction of an emission pulse still remaining in the atmosphere at each point in time, while the bottom panel shows the cumulative area accumulated under that fraction curve from emission up to each time point. The shaded area in the top panel equals the value on the bottom curve at that time; the remaining fraction is dimensionless, whereas the time integral carries units of time. Reconstructed from the published Joos et al. fit, the figure illustrates this distinction within a bounded finite range; its constant term does not prove that a fixed share of carbon remains permanently in the real atmosphere. Reading the figure requires separating the remaining fraction at an instant from the cumulative integral up to that instant; the appendix lists the fitted parameters and term-by-term integrals.
claims.scope: Conceptual interpretation of the reconstructed Joos et al. impulse response figure without adding new numerical claims, permanent-carbon assertions, or empirical validation.
caveats: The figure is an author reconstruction from the published fit, not the original multi-model trajectories, a full Earth-system replay, or an independent validation for a new product.

claims.text: Reference curves are not context-free constants. Propagating CO₂ and temperature impulse responses from different modeling experiments into emission metrics, Olivié and Peters found that experiment duration, background state, and parameter identifiability all affect metric values. Because their J13 ensemble draws directly on the Joos et al. data, it cannot be treated as an independent set of observations. Joos et al. applied observational constraints to parts of their model ensemble, yet constraining models with observations, intercomparing models, and validating a new application against independent evidence each answer a different question.
claims.scope: Distinct evidentiary roles of model ensembles, experimental design, observational constraints, and independent validation.

claims.text: Converting atmospheric burden into radiative forcing requires radiative efficiency. Under a small-perturbation, fixed-background approximation, multiplying radiative efficiency per unit atmospheric burden A by the impulse response R(t) gives the radiative forcing trajectory F(t) per unit emission. Background concentration alters that conversion; even when another gas's emission is unchanged, revisions to the CO₂ reference response or CO₂ radiative efficiency shift relative metrics through the denominator.
claims.scope: Radiative forcing scaling under small-perturbation, fixed-background assumptions and denominator sensitivity to the CO₂ reference.

claims.text: To compare radiative forcing accumulated over a time interval after emission, F(t) is integrated from 0 to H to obtain the absolute global warming potential, AGWP(H). Expressed per kilogram emitted, AGWP(H) has units of W m⁻² yr kg⁻¹; dividing by the AGWP(H) of 1 kg CO₂ over the same horizon yields the relative global warming potential, GWP(H). The "100" in GWP100 specifies the post-pulse integration window—it means neither that the gas remains in the atmosphere for exactly 100 years nor that the product must last 100 years.
claims.scope: Radiative forcing integral of a unit-mass pulse and relative GWP over a matched integration horizon.

claims.text: Absolute global temperature change potential (AGTP) asks for the temperature response at year H, so radiative forcing must also pass through the climate system's thermal response. Denoting the temperature impulse response to a unit forcing pulse as R_T, AGTP(H) = ∫₀ᴴ F(u) R_T(H − u) du: forcing at each moment u experiences a different elapsed thermal response time H − u before summing at the target year H. Here the forcing pulse is normalized to a time integral of 1 W m⁻² yr, so R_T carries units of K/(W m⁻² yr)—not the response to a sustained 1 W m⁻² step—and AGTP has units of K kg⁻¹. Relative global temperature change potential (GTP) then divides by CO₂'s corresponding endpoint temperature response, preserving an end-of-horizon temperature comparison rather than GWP's cumulative forcing area.
claims.scope: Convolution of radiative forcing with the unit forcing-pulse thermal kernel for AGTP and GTP at a common target year.

claims.text: In GTP, "endpoint" refers first to the time of observation. The result still sits at global mean temperature change and has not yet modeled human mortality, ecological damage, or monetary loss. A climate metric's temporal endpoint therefore cannot be equated with a life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) damage-level endpoint; translating temperature change into damages requires additional models, parameters, and explicit applicability conditions.
claims.scope: Distinction between the temporal endpoint of a physical climate metric and damage-level endpoints in LCIA.

claims.text: Precisely because a temporal endpoint is not a damage endpoint, major LCIA frameworks have diverged into three architectures for where climate assessment stops (Table 1). First, stopping at the 100-year midpoint with no endpoint: the 2011 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook awarded Level I recommendation to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) 2007 GWP100, and the European Union Environmental Footprint (EF 2.0 through 3.1) retains this boundary (carrying the highest single-score weight at 21.06% and a global per-capita normalization reference of 7,553.08 kg CO₂-eq/person). Second, multiplying three-horizon midpoints by constant endpoint factors: ReCiPe 2016 from the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) derives gas-independent constants from the integrated CO₂ temperature response across Individualist (I, 20 years), Hierarchist (H, 100 years), and Egalitarian (E, 1,000 years) perspectives to convert to disability-adjusted life years (DALY) and species·yr—preserving rank order strictly within each perspective while omitting thermal-inertia differences across gas lifetimes. Third, dispensing with midpoints to model damage directly: LC-IMPACT outputs global human health and ecosystem damages across "certain" and "all" evidence tiers.
claims.scope: Structural divergence across ILCD 2011, EF 2.0–3.1, ReCiPe 2016, and LC-IMPACT regarding climate midpoint truncation, constant integrated-temperature scaling, and evidence-tiered direct damage modeling.
caveats: ReCiPe 2016's constant midpoint-to-endpoint multipliers preserve relative gas ratios only within a single fixed cultural perspective (one time horizon); switching perspectives or using explicit time convolution breaks proportionality.

ReCiPe 2016 (RIVM Report 2016-0104 Chapter 2) midpoint-to-endpoint constants (I/H/E): integrated CO₂ temperature response (IAGTP) = 9.03 × 10⁻¹⁵, 4.76 × 10⁻¹⁴, 4.23 × 10⁻¹³ °C·yr/kg CO₂; human health (malnutrition, malaria, diarrhea, flooding) = 8.12 × 10⁻⁸, 9.28 × 10⁻⁷, 1.25 × 10⁻⁵ DALY/kg CO₂-eq; terrestrial ecosystems (Urban 2015 slope 0.037 PDF/°C × 1.08 × 10¹⁴ m² × 1.48 × 10⁻⁸ species/m²) = 5.32 × 10⁻¹⁰, 2.80 × 10⁻⁹, 2.50 × 10⁻⁸ species·yr/kg CO₂-eq; freshwater ecosystems (Hanafiah et al. 2011 × 7.89 × 10⁻¹⁰ species/m³) = 1.45 × 10⁻¹⁴, 7.65 × 10⁻¹⁴, 6.82 × 10⁻¹³ species·yr/kg CO₂-eq. LC-IMPACT (Verones et al. 2020) Table 3 distinguishes 100-year and 1,000-year horizons (labeled infinite in Fig. 4): "certain impacts" cover diarrhea, malaria, and coastal flooding with freshwater ecosystems blank, whereas "all impacts" add malnutrition, cardiovascular disease, inland flooding, and freshwater fish within 42° N/S; in its three-fuel automotive case, total health damage varied by up to a factor of 4.

claims.text: Once the denominator is fixed, the numerator must be checked for matching physical boundaries. Warming induced by a non-CO₂ gas alters land and ocean CO₂ uptake and release, creating a climate–carbon feedback. Gasser et al. showed that including this feedback in the CO₂ reference denominator while omitting it from the non-CO₂ numerator produces an inconsistent ratio. Non-CO₂ metrics tabulated in the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6) include the corresponding feedback; that contribution must be distinguished from the gas's direct radiative forcing.
claims.scope: Numerator–denominator consistency for climate–carbon feedbacks in relative emission metrics.

claims.text: Feedback involves more than initial carbon release. Gasser et al.'s simplified impulse response also represents carbon re-uptake by reservoirs after a temperature pulse subsides, whereas Sterner and Johansson compared internal redistribution among carbon reservoirs against treating induced carbon as an external emission, showing that the two formulations leave different long-term tails. This is a structural difference in model formulation rather than a unit convention; both studies remain subject to calibration, omitted processes, and background conditions, and a model recovery curve does not prove that real ecological processes are fully reversible.
claims.scope: Handling of induced carbon release, reservoir redistribution, and recovery in two simplified climate–carbon feedback models.

claims.text: Numerator–denominator asymmetry in climate–carbon feedbacks is not merely theoretical—it is built into a widely used LCIA method (Table 2). In ReCiPe 2016 (RIVM Report 2016-0104 Tables 2.1–2.2, covering 207 gases), the CO₂ reference denominator includes carbon-cycle feedback across all three perspectives, yet non-CO₂ climate–carbon feedbacks are switched on only in Hierarchist (100 years: non-fossil methane 34, fossil methane 36, nitrous oxide [N₂O] 298 kg CO₂-eq/kg) and switched off in both Individualist (20 years) and Egalitarian (1,000 years). Two consequences follow immediately. First, N₂O traces a non-monotonic path of 264 (20 years) → 298 (100 years) → 78.8 (1,000 years): the 100-year factor exceeds the 20-year factor not because direct forcing grows stronger, but because warming-induced carbon release is added only in the 100-year column. Second, comparing 3.5 kg of non-fossil methane against 1 kg of N₂O ranks methane higher under Individualist (294 vs. 264) but flips to N₂O higher under both Hierarchist (119 vs. 298) and Egalitarian (16.8 vs. 78.8)—and ReCiPe's perspective-constant multipliers transmit that reversal intact to all three endpoints.
claims.scope: Asymmetric non-CO₂ climate–carbon feedback toggles across the three ReCiPe 2016 perspectives, causing non-monotonic N₂O behavior and CH₄/N₂O rank reversals.
caveats: The 3.5 kg non-fossil CH₄ versus 1 kg N₂O pair is a controlled emission contrast isolating horizon and feedback-asymmetry effects, not a measured emission ratio for a specific agricultural or energy process.

Lacking published 1,000-year feedback tables, ReCiPe 2016 Egalitarian (1,000 years) integrates each gas's radiative efficiency, concentration conversion factor, and atmospheric lifetime exponentially without feedback, then divides by the Joos et al. (2013) 1,000-year CO₂ AGWP of 5.48 × 10⁻¹³ W m⁻² yr kg⁻¹ (which still includes carbon-cycle feedback), yielding 4.8 (non-fossil CH₄), 4.9 (fossil CH₄), and 78.8 (N₂O) kg CO₂-eq/kg.

claims.text: Methane also alters climate agents such as ozone and stratospheric water vapor through atmospheric chemistry. Distinct timescales govern how rapidly a methane burden perturbation decays versus how methane oxidizes to CO₂ via hydroxyl (OH) radicals. Seeing a "radiative efficiency" column header therefore requires checking whether indirect chemical effects are included; multiplying a single tabulated efficiency by one decay curve does not suffice to claim reconstruction of a complete methane metric.
claims.scope: Distinct roles of indirect atmospheric chemistry, perturbation lifetime, and oxidation timescale in methane metrics.

claims.text: Oxidation also converts methane's own carbon atom into CO₂. Fossil methane draws that carbon from a fossil reservoir, whereas biogenic methane is tied to prior atmospheric carbon uptake, and part of emitted methane or its intermediates can be removed through other sinks. AR6 accounts for these pathways and oxidation delay separately while warning against double-counting: if the same carbon is already booked elsewhere in the inventory, embedding its oxidation again inside the characterization factor shifts the accounting boundary. This tracks methane's own carbon, whereas warming-induced carbon feedbacks reflect changes in terrestrial and oceanic carbon reservoirs.
claims.scope: Methane carbon origin, delayed oxidation to CO₂, and prevention of double-counting relative to inventory boundaries.

claims.text: Because methane's own carbon can be accounted for in different ways, factor tables list multiple methane rows. In the October 7, 2025 AR6 errata replacement main table, central GWP100 values are 28.1 for fossil methane and 25.3 for non-fossil methane; the replacement supplementary table provides a generic row of 26.2 that leaves the origin and fate of methane's own carbon to the user's carbon budget. That generic row still includes warming-induced carbon feedbacks and is not an alias for non-fossil methane. The comparisons here use central values; fossil methane also carries an uncertainty range of ±10.4, which fixed-factor checks do not propagate as a probability distribution.
claims.scope: Three methane carbon-accounting rows in the October 2025 AR6 errata main and supplementary replacement tables.

claims.text: Labeling carbon "biogenic" does not by itself establish zero climate impact. Comparing bio-based or land-use pathways still requires specifying the reference baseline for carbon uptake, when uptake occurs, where carbon is stored, when and as which gas it is released, and what the inventory versus characterization factors have already counted. Zieger et al.'s dynamic framework records associated CO₂ uptake explicitly as negative inventory flows and models delayed methane oxidation—one explicit carbon-budgeting choice, not a universal rule setting all biogenic gases to zero.
claims.scope: Timing of biogenic carbon uptake and release and explicit inventory accounting choices.
caveats: Complete land-use transitions, reference carbon pools, and ecological recovery pathways require dedicated evidence; this paragraph does not establish climate neutrality for real biomass products.

claims.text: In the EU Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) framework (Commission Recommendation [EU] 2021/2279 and the official EF 3.1 package), carbon-origin boundaries are codified into four machine-readable Extensible Markup Language (XML) method files (Table 3): total Climate change (1,099 factors) equals the exact non-overlapping union of Fossil (1,074), Biogenic (13), and Land use and land-use change (12). Any sub-indicator exceeding 5% of total absolute climate impact must be reported separately, yet none of the three sub-indicators has independent normalization or weighting factors. Three routing rules create critical boundaries. First, the Biogenic sub-indicator sets both biogenic CO₂ uptake and emission to 0.0, scoring only the 6 atmospheric sub-compartments of biogenic methane at 27.0 kg CO₂-eq/kg (the official AR6 table value). Second, the Land use and land-use change sub-indicator assigns −1.0 to CO₂ uptake and +1.0 to CO₂ emission, scores land-use methane at 29.8 (matching fossil methane), and counts native-forest timber and soil carbon releases at +1.0 while excluding photosynthetic uptake. Third, the Fossil sub-indicator includes peat, limestone calcination, and all 6 nitrous oxide flows (273.0)—routing N₂O from agricultural fertilizers and biomass boilers entirely into "Climate change – Fossil."
claims.scope: Non-overlapping partition of the four EF 3.1 climate XML methods (1,099 = 1,074 + 13 + 12), native-forest and agricultural N₂O routing rules, and absence of independent sub-indicator normalization/weighting.
caveats: Routing all nitrous oxide into "Climate change – Fossil" in EF 3.1 reflects current elementary-flow naming granularity; analysts interpreting the "Fossil" sub-indicator for agricultural or bio-based products must not assume it originates solely from fossil-fuel combustion.

EF 3.1 climate XML UUID prefixes and factor counts: total Climate change (6209b35f, 1,099) = Fossil (7fce5b3a, 1,074, including 2 fossil CO₂ air-capture resource flows set to 0.0) + Biogenic (706261af, 13: 1 uptake and 6 emission CO₂ flows at 0.0, plus 6 CH₄ flows at 27.0) + Land use and land-use change (14af9ca7, 12: 1 CO₂ uptake at −1.0, 5 CO₂ emissions at +1.0, plus 6 CH₄ flows at 29.8). Studies of fully mineralized products such as food may use a simplified approach modeling only biogenic methane.

claims.text: When is setting managed biogenic CO₂ to "0 uptake, 0 emission" (the 0/0 convention) equivalent to booking growth uptake as −1 and end-of-life oxidation as +1 (the −1/+1 convention), and when does it break? Consider a sustainably harvested wood product leaving the factory gate with 1 kg of biogenic carbon stored (44/12 ≈ 3.67 kg biogenic CO₂), 0.5 kg of upstream fossil CO₂ from processing, and complete end-of-life incineration releasing all biogenic CO₂ (with no methane). Over a closed cradle-to-grave life cycle using consistent conventions upstream and downstream, 0/0 (0.5 + 0 = 0.5) and −1/+1 (0.5 − 3.67 + 3.67 = 0.5) are strictly identical. At a cradle-to-gate intermediate boundary, however, the two ledgers differ by the full 3.67 kg CO₂-eq (+0.5 vs. −3.17). If a downstream analyst plugs a −1/+1 upstream wood dataset (−3.17) into an EF 0/0 background incineration module (multiplying biogenic CO₂ by 0), the full life cycle drops artificially from the true +0.5 to −3.17 (fabricating roughly −3.67 kg of phantom negative carbon per kilogram of biogenic carbon); the reverse mismatch double-counts to +4.17. That is precisely why EU 2021/2279 §4.4.10.2 pairs 0/0 characterization factors with mandatory separate reporting of physical biogenic carbon content at the cradle-to-gate boundary.
claims.scope: Quantitative comparison of PEF 0/0 versus explicit −1/+1 biogenic CO₂ accounting under closed cradle-to-grave equivalence and cradle-to-gate cross-module mismatch.
caveats: Even when upstream and downstream conventions match consistently under either −1/+1 or 0/0, anaerobic landfilling that converts part of biogenic carbon into biogenic methane (factor 27.0 rather than 0) eliminates climate neutrality.

claims.text: Even with identical gases and carbon-budget rules, metric values change across editions. Official IPCC AR6 Working Group I (WGI) Chapter 7 Table 7.15 retains its originally published figures, while the October 7, 2025 errata issue replacement tables and simultaneously catalog Final Government Distribution (FGD) revisions already incorporated prior to publication. Citations must distinguish those two correction classes and specify table name, carrier edition, errata status, substance row, and metric column together; only then can one determine whether a numerical difference stems purely from edition.
claims.scope: Document identity distinguishing published AR6 Table 7.15, October 2025 replacement tables, and pre-publication FGD revisions.

claims.text: A later publication date does not guarantee newer characterization factors. The supplementary material to Zieger et al.'s November 2025 paper still tabulates pre-errata radiative efficiencies and factors, listing a CO₂ reference AGWP100 of 0.0895 pW m⁻² yr kg⁻¹ compared with 0.093 in the October 2025 replacement table. The paper remains useful for understanding its dynamic model and case study, but identifying which AR6 parameter baseline it uses requires inspecting the numerical values in its supplement.
claims.scope: Identification of the pre-errata AR6 parameter baseline used in Zieger et al. (2025).

claims.text: Test what "equal" means using two same-day pulses at year 0: emitting 28.1 kg of CO₂ versus 1 kg of fossil CH₄. Under the corrected AR6 GWP100, both score 28.100 kg CO₂-eq. Keeping the same fossil-methane row but switching to corrected GWP20 yields 28.100 versus 77.400. Keeping the 100-year horizon but switching to corrected GTP100 gives 28.100 versus 7.100 kg CO₂-eq—equivalent to the year-100 temperature response of those CO₂ pulse masses, with units still in reference mass rather than kelvin. Neither emitted mass changed; only the climate effect or observation horizon changed. These two masses are chosen purely to diagnose metric behavior and do not represent equivalent product services.
claims.scope: Same-day diagnostic emission pulses illustrating metric shifts under the corrected AR6 main-table fossil methane row.
caveats: These two emission masses are diagnostic pulses constructed to test metric definitions and do not establish equivalent product service.
Numerical magnitudes across different metrics cannot be compared directly to infer which gas has a larger "overall impact."

claims.text: To compare alternatives delivering identical service, take one fixed illustrative inventory from the wall-coating example. For a smooth substrate and shared electricity intensity θ = 0.3 kg fossil CO₂/kWh, Option A emits 26 kg CO₂ and 0.07 kg fossil CH₄, while Option B emits 27 kg CO₂ and 0.09 kg fossil CH₄—both delivering the specified 100 m², 10-year wall service. Holding this inventory and its performance, activity, and cutoff assumptions fixed isolates the effect of swapping characterization factors.
claims.scope: Fixed service and gas inventory vector for the smooth-substrate, θ = 0.3 wall-coating comparison.
caveats: The original teaching inventory's cutoff, performance, shared-parameter, and service assumptions remain in force; no real paint data or time-resolved emission calendar is implied.

claims.text: Under corrected AR6 GWP100, Options A and B score 27.967 and 29.529 kg CO₂-eq, giving a difference B − A of 1.562 kg CO₂-eq. Replacing the methane factor with the originally published AR6 table value of 29.8 changes the difference to 1.596; switching to corrected GWP20 widens it to 2.548. The magnitude shifts across editions and horizons, yet remains positive throughout because Option B emits more of both gases and every characterization factor is positive. Changing factors alters comparison scale without necessarily reversing rank order.
claims.scope: Edition and horizon recalculations on the fixed illustrative wall-coating inventory.

claims.text: Beyond rank order, a comparison requires explicit decision criteria. The tolerance defined for the original wall-coating example belongs to that stated question and cannot carry over silently to GTP or another time horizon. Similarly, coefficients embedded in a historical electricity model explain that edition's reported output; swapping factor tables afterward does not turn it into a new model run. When recalculating for a new question, analysts should report original outputs and recalculated values separately, stating gas origins, calculation purpose, and comparison criteria.
claims.scope: Why existing comparison tolerances and historical model outputs cannot be silently overwritten by new climate metrics.

claims.text: In the wall-coating example containing only CO₂ and methane, updating editions merely rescaled the margin; in real industrial inventories containing carbon monoxide (CO), updating editions can flip rankings outright. EF 2.0 and 3.0 set fossil and land-use methane to 36.75 (34 plus 2.75 for complete oxidation, rounded to 36.8 in JRC130796) and assigned fossil and land-use CO roughly 1.57 kg CO₂-eq/kg (with biogenic CO at 0). Upgrading to EF 3.1, the European Commission's Joint Research Centre (JRC) updated fossil/land-use methane, biogenic methane, and N₂O to official AR6 values of 29.8, 27.0, and 273.0, and zeroed CO completely because AR6 no longer publishes GWP values for short-lived CO. Zeroing global fossil CO alone (previously ≈ 141.5 kg CO₂-eq/person) combined with lower methane factors reduced the global per-capita normalization reference by 6.7% (from 8.10 × 10³ to 7.55 × 10³ kg CO₂-eq/person); across 2,752 official EF datasets, climate scores fell by 2.9% on average while specific waste-incineration processes swung from −58% to +302%. If Furnace A emits 20 kg more fossil CO (dropping from 31.4 to 0) while Furnace B emits 25 kg more fossil CO₂, their preference order reverses completely between EF 3.0 and EF 3.1.
claims.scope: Impact of the EF 3.0-to-EF 3.1 methane oxidation update and CO factor removal on the global normalization reference (−6.7%) and 2,752 official datasets.
caveats: Zeroing CO in EF 3.1 climate characterization does not mean CO no longer oxidizes to CO₂ or lacks atmospheric effects; it reflects AR6's boundary assigning short-lived reactive species to coupled chemistry–climate modeling.

Relative to EF 3.0, EF 3.1 removed 32 legacy AR5 substances and added roughly 43 AR6 substances (23 unmapped due to missing elementary flows); 2010 global fossil CO emissions totaled 6.216 × 10¹¹ kg; only 6% of the 2,752 official datasets rose, with extremes in Spanish treated wood waste incineration (−58%) and Danish polyurethane waste incineration (+302%, reflecting sign effects from energy-recovery credits). CO retains precursor factors under photochemical ozone formation in Acidification and Nutrient Enrichment.

claims.text: Auditing the official EF 3.1 archive against technical reports also reveals tangible traces of coexisting drafts, published tables, and errata. First, while the EF 3.1 climate XML files and JRC130796 use the official AR6 biogenic methane value of 27.0 (25.3 after the 2025 errata), the package's official normalization workbook retains the AR6 Final Government Distribution value of 27.2, inflating the global normalization total by 2.61 × 10¹⁰ kg CO₂-eq (+3.79 kg/person), alongside draft trailing digits for chlorofluorocarbon-11 (CFC-11) and hydrofluorocarbon-134a (HFC-134a). Second, despite upgrading to IPCC 2021, metadata in all four climate XML files still cite "IPCC 2013" and the bundled reference PDF remains the 2019 draft guidance. Third, the Land use and land-use change sub-indicator includes only 5 atmospheric CO₂ flows, omitting the "lower stratosphere + upper troposphere" sub-compartment (whereas methane and other CO₂ flows each have 6), and EU 2021/2279 text still lags behind by referencing CO. Fourth, print errata remain in ILCD 2011 and RIVM Report 2016-0104 (detailed in the caveats). Auditing software calculations and normalization references requires documenting these discrepancies faithfully rather than silently altering published figures.
claims.scope: Documented discrepancies across the official EF 3.1 normalization workbook, XML metadata, LULUC upper-atmosphere coverage, EU 2021/2279 prose, and ILCD/RIVM printed reports.
caveats: Using 27.2 instead of 27.0 for biogenic methane in the normalization workbook alters the global per-capita climate reference (7,553.08 kg CO₂-eq/person) by only about +0.05%, leaving orders of magnitude unchanged, yet reproducing the official normalization sum requires preserving the workbook's cached value.

Detailed source discrepancies: (1) the EF 3.1 normalization workbook multiplies 1.306 × 10¹¹ kg biogenic CH₄ by the pre-publication FGD value 27.2 (FGD 80.8/27.2/7.3), enters 6226 for CFC-11 (XML 6230.0) and 1526 for HFC-134a (XML 1530.0), and includes a UUID-less halon 1301/2402 geometric mean entry of 3952.72; (2) the November 2022 data-guide addendum switched to IPCC 2021 and EU 2021/2279, yet all four method XMLs and the converter copy still cite IPCC 2013 Table 8SM15 and bundle the 248-page 2019 JRC draft PDF; (3) ILCD 2011 §3.1.6 (p. 18) inverted the N₂O 500-year vs. 100-year comparison—roughly half in AR4 (falling from 298 to 153)—into "about twice as high"; RIVM Report 2016-0104 p. 25 Table 2.2 misprints the 1,000-year CFC-13 factor as "1,2684.1".

claims.text: An emission inventory can preserve not only which gases and total masses are released, but also the dates when they enter the environment. Starting from the loss of temporal detail when emissions are summed into a single total, Levasseur et al. (2010) linked year-by-year inventories to dynamic characterization factors. That step first changes how the inventory itself is written; whether one fuel or product outperforms another still depends on the specific case comparison.
claims.scope: Interpretation of Levasseur et al. (2010) via the author's 2011 thesis Annex 1 rather than the journal PDF.
caveats: This discussion relies on the author's thesis Annex 1 reprint and does not substitute for the ACS journal PDF, supplementary files, or original case-study inputs.

claims.text: Once emissions carry dates, an evaluation time must also be specified. If an emission occurs in year j and is evaluated at time t, its climate response depends on the elapsed interval t − j. Equal masses of the same gas—one newly emitted and another released years earlier—sit at different stages of decay at time t. Because the response model requires those elapsed intervals for every pulse, aggregated mass totals alone cannot supply them.
claims.scope: Conceptual explanation of discrete-year elapsed-time characterization in Levasseur et al. (2010), not a runnable indexing convention or software specification.
caveats: This conceptual relation does not replace explicit step-size, endpoint, and zero-lag implementation rules or numerical testing.

claims.text: "Observing for the same duration after every emission" and "evaluating all emissions at one shared calendar date" are therefore two distinct setups. The first shifts the observation endpoint forward with each emission date; the second gives later emissions shorter elapsed response times. Using a building life cycle timeline, Levasseur et al. argued that comparisons must use commensurate time boundaries. Fixed-horizon GWP answers the first question; using it to stand in for a common-calendar-endpoint comparison requires separate justification.
claims.scope: Time-horizon framing around a common calendar endpoint in Levasseur et al. (2010); not a blanket rejection of all GWP uses.
caveats: The original building timeline is an illustrative example and does not evaluate the environmental performance of a real building.

claims.text: Dynamic characterization multiplies each year's gas emissions by the characterization factor corresponding to its elapsed time, then sums across years and gases. Levasseur et al. applied this convolution to radiative forcing; even what they call an "instantaneous" annual factor is defined by integrating over a one-year step.
