Retaining emission years makes temporal structure visible, but it does not by itself deliver full temperature projections or climate damage forecasts.
claims.scope: Time-resolved inventory and radiative-forcing characterization in Annex 1 §2.1, not a general definition of all dynamic LCIA methods.
caveats: Describing this framework does not make its historical gas-response parameters or characterization factors current defaults.

claims.text: For a dated inventory, the calculation can be written explicitly: let pulse k have mass m_k, gas i_k, and emission date t_k. Under linear impulse-response kernels, cumulative radiative forcing up to a common calendar endpoint T is Σ m_k AGWP_{i_k}(T − t_k), and endpoint temperature response at T is Σ m_k AGTP_{i_k}(T − t_k), summed over all pulses with t_k ≤ T. Each pulse uses its true elapsed duration. If a relative CO₂ equivalent is needed, analysts first sum the absolute responses and then divide by one explicit common reference—such as 1 kg CO₂ emitted at year 0 evaluated at the same T. Dividing each pulse instead by its own 100-year post-emission CO₂ reference defines a different equivalence metric, even though the two algorithms can occasionally yield the same number under particular emission schedules.
claims.scope: Linear-kernel summation of dated mass pulses to a common calendar endpoint.
caveats: Zieger et al.'s main text shares certain symbols across emission profiles and cumulative/instantaneous forcing, requiring explicit input conventions; this paragraph writes an explicit sum of mass pulses without inferring software errors from printed notation.

claims.text: To isolate how emission timing affects results, compare 1 kg of CO₂ emitted at year 0 against 1 kg emitted at year 80, both evaluated at year 100. Holding the historical AR6 author-code kernel fixed—initial unit-mass forcing of roughly 1.709 × 10⁻¹⁵ W m⁻² kg⁻¹ and a two-timescale (fast plus slow) thermal response kernel, with no other emissions, storage credits, or technology changes—the two pulses experience 100 years and 20 years of elapsed time, respectively. This is a standalone timing schedule: its forcing calibration differs from the 1.77 × 10⁻¹⁵ W m⁻² kg⁻¹ noted in Joos et al., and it is not a recalculation of the 2025 errata table.
claims.scope: Controlled early versus late 1 kg CO₂ pulses evaluated with central parameters of the historical AR6 author code.

claims.text: Under that fixed kernel, cumulative radiative forcing to year 100 is 8.947 × 10⁻¹⁴ W m⁻² yr for the early emission versus 2.434 × 10⁻¹⁴ W m⁻² yr for the late emission. Endpoint temperature response at year 100, however, is 3.946 × 10⁻¹⁶ K for the early emission versus 4.954 × 10⁻¹⁶ K for the late emission—making the later emission higher. Cumulative forcing monotonically adds positive area under the forcing curve, whereas endpoint temperature balances decaying gas forcing against thermal inertia from earlier forcing; because the modeled CO₂ pulse temperature response declines between year 20 and year 100 under these parameters, the two indicators point in opposite directions. Observing each pulse for 100 years after release makes both responses identical, but their calendar endpoints are no longer shared—they sit at year 100 and year 180.
claims.scope: Comparison of 20-year and 100-year responses of the historical CO₂ kernel under fixed central parameters.
caveats: Results use a fixed historical kernel and central parameters rather than re-running evolving future climate backgrounds or propagating physical parameter uncertainty.

claims.text: Building insulation illustrates how uptake and release spread across a calendar. Comparing polystyrene and straw insulation delivering the same 50-year thermal-resistance service, Zieger et al. place initial biogenic uptake, manufacturing emissions, and end-of-life releases on their respective calendar dates, showing that cumulative forcing, peak temperature, and time to peak each capture different aspects of performance. The case demonstrates why retaining gas identity and timing matters; yet temporarily negative cumulative forcing in the authors' scenario does not prove one material is superior across all horizons, scenarios, and uncertainty ranges.
claims.scope: Reported results and dynamic indicator proposals from the Zieger et al. (2025) insulation case study.
caveats: This text cites the authors' reported scenario outputs without re-executing their software; the main figure and supplementary table differ by 50 versus 51 years for polystyrene end-of-life timing and cannot be assumed identical.
Parameter baseline, sampling scope, and omitted feedback uncertainties still limit comparisons, and product-specific post-peak times do not constitute a shared calendar endpoint.

claims.text: Even when equations handle dated emissions cleanly, analysts must still choose the cutoff year at which evaluation stops. Contributions beyond that endpoint drop out of the score, and adding time discounting further alters temporal weighting. Levasseur et al. link both choices to policy and value judgments, noting explicitly that discounting is independent of their dynamic characterization method. Temporal settings therefore require justification matched to the study's question rather than reporting a bare horizon year.
claims.scope: Treatment of analytical time horizons and discounting in Levasseur et al. (2010), plus reporting obligations.
caveats: Policy commentary in Levasseur et al. (2010) is not cited as binding legal text or a formal standard requirement.

claims.text: Recording emissions year by year still leaves the underlying response model's assumptions intact. Levasseur et al. rely on specified atmospheric load responses under fixed background concentrations while noting that real backgrounds evolve and that radiative forcing does not map simply onto climate damages. Extending dynamic characterization to other impact categories requires dedicated dynamic models as well. "Dynamic" therefore preserves one specific set of temporal relationships; it does not mean a model captures every form of real-world change.
claims.scope: Explicitly stated limitations of the 2010 dynamic LCA framework, not a survey of all subsequent dynamic methods.
caveats: Historical response parameters from 2010 do not automatically carry over to later climate models or current assessments.

claims.text: While dynamic characterization restores emissions and removals to their calendar dates, institutional EU PEF rules compress the timeline to enforce cross-study comparability. The 2018 pilot Product Environmental Footprint Category Rules (PEFCR v6.3) guidance and EF 2.0/3.0 previously allowed biogenic carbon sequestered for over 100 years to claim a −1 kg CO₂-eq/kg credit via a dedicated flow. Formal Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279 and EF 3.1 deleted that flow completely (factor count 0), prohibiting credits for temporary or permanent carbon storage and delayed emissions and requiring all emissions and removals to be modeled as occurring "now" without time discounting. Simultaneously, the rule adopts British Publicly Available Specification (PAS 2050:2011) by amortizing direct land-use change (dLUC) over the 20 years prior to assessment (or one longer rotation period), setting conversions older than 20 years to zero, and excluding indirect land-use change (iLUC) from mandatory totals. In the dynamic notation above, modeling emissions as occurring "now" forces every emission date j to zero—erasing interim negative forcing from long-lived bio-based materials that absorb carbon early and release it 50 years later—while the 20-year lookback is an institutional accounting window for historical deforestation responsibility, not a physical carbon-pool relaxation constant.
claims.scope: Shift from PEF pilot 100-year storage credits to the EU 2021/2279 ban on storage/delayed-emission credits and 20-year PAS 2050 dLUC amortization window contrasted with dynamic LCA calendar integration.
caveats: The EU 2021/2279 ban on carbon-storage and delayed-emission credits is an institutional comparability rule for product compliance claims, not a denial of physical residence effects in long-lived wood products or soil carbon; long-term storage or soil-carbon gains may only be disclosed as additional environmental or technical information.

The deleted atmospheric resource flow in EU 2021/2279 Annex I §4.4.10 was originally named "carbon dioxide (biogenic-100yr)"; for crops of unknown origin, §4.4.10.3 permits computing dLUC as a weighted average across source countries covering at least 90% of import mass.

claims.text: Assigning a date to every emission leaves one fundamental question unanswered by response equations: where do those future emissions come from? Given an emission profile, response kernels can evaluate it, but they do not generate future technology trajectories, equipment lifetimes, energy-system transitions, or market scenarios. Estimating when future emissions will occur depends on assumed technologies and production activities; analysts must explain how those process, energy, and market conditions are constructed—a topic examined in a later chapter on future technology and context.
claims.scope: Analytical distinction between temporal impact characterization and prospective technology scenario modeling.
caveats: The label "dynamic" is not treated here as having a single uniform meaning across the LCA literature.

claims.text: Estimating the temperature response to sustained emissions requires tracking emission rates and how long they persist. Even after methane's atmospheric burden approaches steady state, ongoing emissions sustain elevated radiative forcing while the climate system continues to adjust. Under the same linear response, raising the emission rate by a constant step ΔE (kg yr⁻¹) from year 0 through year H produces a year-H temperature change equal to ΔE multiplied by the integral of unit-mass AGTP from 0 to H (K yr kg⁻¹ × kg yr⁻¹ = K). Rate-based metrics use current and historical emission rates to approximate temperature change and cannot be applied directly as static per-product characterization factors.
claims.scope: Relationship between a sustained step in emission rate and the integral of unit-mass pulse AGTP.

claims.text: Cain et al. (2019) compute an annual rate of CO₂ warming-equivalent emissions (CO₂-we)—the revised GWP* formulation—from current and earlier methane emission rates: E_W(t) = GWP_H [r (H/Δt)(E(t) − E(t − Δt)) + s E(t)], where E is the annual methane emission rate, H is the GWP horizon, and Δt is the lookback interval. Using H = 100 years, Δt = 20 years, r = 0.75, s = 0.25, and historical GWP100 = 28 simplifies the expression to 112 E(t) − 105 E(t − 20). The output remains an annual accounting rate that must be multiplied by time and summed to obtain cumulative warming-equivalent emissions. Because it is constructed differently from conventional GWP CO₂ equivalents, the two cannot be substituted term for term or summed without explicit justification.
claims.scope: Annual CO₂-we rate expression under the specific Cain et al. (2019) GWP* parameterization, not a generic label for later variants.
caveats: This text preserves the 2019 parameterization and historical GWP100 = 28; mechanically substituting corrected AR6 factors does not preserve the same fit, nor is this a universal definition for later GWP* variants.

The footnote to IPCC AR6 WGI Chapter 7 Figure 7.22 uses a subsequent formulation with coefficients 4.24 on E(t) − E(t − 20) and 0.28 on E(t); this paragraph retains Cain et al.'s 3.75 and 0.25 combination without silently swapping editions across adjacent citations.

claims.text: The weights r and s arise from model fitting rather than unit conversion. Driving the Finite Amplitude Impulse Response (FaIR) model with historical and three Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) methane forcing trajectories, Cain et al. fitted cumulative metrics to modeled temperature trajectories and averaged the resulting weights. The slow term s represents ongoing climate adjustment to past forcing changes, not permanent atmospheric accumulation of methane like CO₂. Because historical trajectories, future pathways, and the response model jointly bound those coefficients, transferring them to another short-lived climate pollutant requires separate justification.
claims.scope: Origin of Cain et al. (2019) weights across three RCP scenarios and physical meaning of the slow adjustment term.
caveats: These weights reflect model-internal fits across scenarios rather than validation against independent methane-only observed temperature series.

claims.text: Why can identical current emission rates produce different scores? Consider three hypothetical fixed-boundary sources A, B, and C emitting 80, 100, and 120 t CH₄/yr respectively throughout 2001–2020, then all emitting 100 t CH₄/yr throughout 2021–2070 (with complete annual records and no missing history padded with zeros). In 2040, conventional historical GWP100 scores all three identically at 2,800 t CO₂-eq/yr, whereas the 2019 rate-based formula yields 2,800, 700, and −1,400 t CO₂-we/yr. Because the rate formula retains differences in prior emission rates, identical current methane emissions produce diverging annual scores.
claims.scope: Three controlled hypothetical annual emission histories for the same gas under fixed boundaries.
caveats: These are illustrative hypothetical emission rates, not measured inventories for actual companies or nations.

claims.text: By 2041, the 20-year lookback window moves forward to 2021, where all three sources already emitted 100 t CH₄/yr, so their annual rates converge to 700 t CO₂-we/yr. Yet earlier differences persist in cumulative totals: over 2021–2040, cumulative totals are 56,000, 14,000, and −28,000 t CO₂-we; cumulated through 2070, they stand at 77,000, 35,000, and −7,000 t CO₂-we. Interpreting either annual rates or cumulative warming-equivalent totals therefore requires specifying exactly where the evaluation window begins and ends.
claims.scope: 20-year and 50-year cumulative totals and lookback-window shift for the three controlled emission histories.

claims.text: Under a shared boundary, total emissions across the three sources remain constant at 300 t CH₄/yr in both past and future periods, yielding an aggregate rate of 2,100 t CO₂-we/yr—exactly the sum of A, B, and C by linearity of the formula. Source C's negative score indicates a decline relative to its higher past emission rate; it does not mean CO₂ was removed from the atmosphere in that year, nor that global temperature fell below a world without those emissions, since other gases and prior emissions can still drive net warming upward.
claims.scope: Linear aggregation under a shared historical boundary and interpretation of negative CO₂-we increments.

claims.text: Once history-dependent metrics are proposed for burden sharing or emissions offsetting, a separate question arises: how should past emissions shape future obligations? Rogelj and Schleussner's 2019 critique evaluated Allen et al.'s (2018) pure rate form (equivalent to r = 1, s = 0), whereas Cain et al.'s 2021 comment stressed how the revised formulation distinguishes differing historical warming trajectories. In their formal reply, Rogelj and Schleussner acknowledged the improved physical approximation yet demonstrated with comparable examples under the revised formula that how existing emission histories enter future accounting still alters allocation outcomes across actors. Improving temperature approximation and allocating responsibility are therefore distinct questions; solving the first does not automatically resolve the second.
claims.scope: Formulas and equity-allocation arguments across the 2019 critique, 2021 comment, and formal reply.
caveats: This paragraph summarizes the published exchange between named papers without recalculating national inventories, judging legal regimes, or prescribing allocation rules.

claims.text: In practice, comparing "kg CO₂-eq" or climate-damage datasets from different sources reduces to five diagnostic checks. First, check causal-chain level and feedback pairing—whether a method stops at a 100-year midpoint, scales three horizons by constant multipliers, or models direct damage, and whether asymmetric feedback toggles such as ReCiPe's 100-year-only non-CO₂ switch distort trends. Second, check sub-indicator routing—verifying that EF 3.1 assigns native forests to land use, routes all N₂O to Fossil, and provides no independent sub-indicator normalization or weighting. Third, audit the cradle-to-gate biogenic carbon ledger—preventing −1/+1 and 0/0 mismatches that fabricate negative carbon, and verifying physical biogenic carbon content. Fourth, separate static institutional windows from dynamic calendar integration—distinguishing EU 2021/2279's zero storage credit and 20-year historical dLUC window from dynamic kernels preserving true elapsed time t − j. Fifth, audit package and print discrepancies—including CO zeroing, the 27.2 normalization-workbook cache, and missing upper-atmosphere sub-compartments. Isolating these five layers makes the exact validity conditions of every climate comparison transparent.
claims.scope: Five-step practical diagnostic protocol for auditing "kg CO₂-eq" and climate-damage scores across standards, databases, and LCIA packages.
caveats: Completing these five alignment checks guarantees internal consistency within climate metrics only; it does not replace prospective energy and technology scenario modeling, nor does it settle intergenerational responsibility allocation.

claims.text: Climate equivalence allows explicitly specified gas emissions to be compared against a chosen reference effect. Holding the wall-coating service and inventory fixed shows how swapping factor editions shifts comparison margins; dated inventories compare responses at a shared calendar endpoint; and annual emission-rate histories preserve trajectory changes invisible to single-year totals. When edition, carbon budget, and research question align, each tool supports its stated comparison and clarifies where differences originate. Equal CO₂-equivalent units alone, however, cannot establish that two emissions cause identical overall climate impacts or decide how mitigation responsibility should be shared.
claims.scope: Synthesis supported jointly by the calculations, source comparisons, and methodological debates in this chapter.

claims.text: How does one kilogram of ammonia in a life cycle inventory become an acidification or eutrophication indicator? The answer starts with where the substance is released. Airborne ammonia undergoes atmospheric transport and chemical transformation before depositing onto soil or water; applying nitrogen to soil or discharging it directly to a river establishes a different starting point. Sharing a chemical element neither guarantees that two emissions follow the same environmental pathway nor justifies applying a single characterization factor to both. Tracing what happens after release clarifies whether a model estimates substance fate, environmental state, or ecological response.
claims.scope: Explaining the link from inventory to indicator through the acidification and aquatic eutrophication pathways in Chapter 3 of UNEP 2019.

claims.text: Following an air emission onto land, sulfur oxides, nitrogen oxides, and ammonia react in the atmosphere, deposit onto ground surfaces or vegetation, and enter the soil. These reactions can increase hydrogen-ion supply or deplete the buffering capacity of base cations. What happens next depends on the receiving soil: differences in baseline soil chemistry and geology produce different buffering capacities, so identical emission masses do not necessarily cause identical changes in acidity. Resulting shifts in soil chemistry can in turn alter nutrient availability, plant survival, and community composition.
claims.scope: The air-emission, deposition, terrestrial soil, and plant pathway in UNEP 2019.

claims.text: The terrestrial acidification model described in the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) 2019 Global Guidance on Environmental Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators (GLAM) represents these processes through deposition, soil sensitivity, and plant response. An atmospheric transport and deposition model links emission and receiving locations, a soil model captures receiving-soil sensitivity to changes in deposition, and an effect relationship links soil change to vascular-plant species response. The midpoint acidification potential is expressed in sulfur dioxide equivalents (SO₂-eq), measuring relative potential within the chosen model rather than field soil pH or actual sulfur dioxide mass emitted. Extending to the ecological endpoint links the Potentially Disappeared Fraction (PDF) of species to area and time, yielding PDF·m²·yr; even at the endpoint, results remain conditional on the receiving ecosystem and response model.
claims.scope: Midpoint indicator, soil sensitivity, and vascular-plant endpoint of the terrestrial acidification model in UNEP 2019.
caveats: At the time of publication, this endpoint used the model developers' average effect factors under the conditions detailed later in this chapter; it cannot be interpreted as a marginal response around current local conditions.

claims.text: Even two indicators both labeled "acidification midpoint" can measure different quantities. The Accumulated Exceedance (AE) method recommended for European assessments in the 2011 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook links atmospheric transport and deposition to critical loads in receiving areas, covering both terrestrial ecosystems and selected inland waters. Critical loads define the threshold above which the model registers exceedance, and AE tracks both where that threshold is exceeded and by how much. Accordingly, AE equals neither total deposited mass nor counted plant losses. Comparing AE with the terrestrial acidification potential introduced above requires aligning their receiving systems and modeled consequences rather than treating both as interchangeable midpoints.
claims.scope: ILCD 2011 European recommendation for the acidification midpoint and its covered receiving systems.
caveats: The receiving-system coverage reflects the 2011 model specification and does not establish actual acidification or ecological damage in any individual region.

claims.text: This distinction appears clearly within a single receiving area. Holding critical loads and all other model conditions fixed, suppose deposition declines while remaining above the critical load across the previously exceeded zone. The area exceeding the critical load may stay unchanged even as the magnitude of exceedance falls. An indicator that counts only unprotected area can therefore signal a different change than AE, which retains the degree of exceedance. This illustration explains how two indicators respond to a shift in load rather than declaring ecosystem recovery; critical loads, deposition patterns, and model background must still fit the specific study.
claims.scope: Comparing an area-only indicator and AE within a single receiving region under fixed model conditions.
caveats: The change conditions in this example are fixed by the author to contrast exceeded area with exceedance magnitude; no published characterization factor or ecological recovery is estimated.

claims.text: UNEP's 2019 Global Guidance on Environmental Life Cycle Impact Assessment Indicators (GLAM) places atmospheric transport, receiving-soil change, and vascular-plant response along a single terrestrial acidification pathway, reporting its recommended midpoint as terrestrial acidification potential referenced to SO₂. Both GLAM and AE account for emission location and receiving conditions, yet one centers explicitly on critical-load exceedance while the other centers on the selected terrestrial acidification model and an SO₂ reference. Converting mol H⁺ eq into kg SO₂ eq therefore requires showing first that the two methods truly re-encode the same modeled quantity, receiving scope, and reference relation; the word "equivalent" in a unit does not establish that equivalence automatically. Available documentation provides no country-by-country matched factor set linking the two methods, so no fixed conversion constant can be derived from their unit labels alone.
claims.scope: Comparing the indicator structure and unit conditions of European ILCD AE and the UNEP 2019 terrestrial acidification midpoint.
caveats: Pure unit rescaling requires an identical measured quantity and an explicit reference relationship; no matched dataset or numerical conversion between EF and GLAM is established here.

claims.text: This comparison must also preserve an internal tension in the recommendation text. The overview in the 2019 guidance describes the endpoint as adding soil sensitivity and effects after the midpoint, attributing the midpoint to Roy et al. (2012b) on atmospheric fate; yet the pathway description in the same volume groups soil sensitivity within a broader fate step, and the subsequent GLAM Phase 3 scoping review explicitly states that the 2019 midpoint includes soil sensitivity. The underlying model papers separate atmospheric, soil, and plant components, but those summaries alone cannot verify which exact factors were combined, how they were assembled, or how references were set in an uninspected release workbook. Accordingly, the recommendation is neither reduced here to "deposition only" nor treated as verified against the 2019 release values via the later scoping review; comparable model structure and unverified numerical implementation must be recorded separately.
claims.scope: Verifiable propositions across the UNEP 2019 text, the component structure of the Roy et al. papers, and the GLAM Phase 3 scoping review.
caveats: A tension remains between the stepwise wording in UNEP 2019 Section 3.4 and the later GLAM Phase 3 attribution of midpoint composition; neither the 2019 release workbook nor a formal erratum was inspected.
Only the publicly available author abstracts of the three Roy et al. papers were reviewed.

claims.text: Published release entries allow a direct test of another oversimplification. The acidification method in the European Union (EU) Environmental Footprint (EF) 3.1 reference package adopts AE; for the exact same versioned SO₂ emission-to-air flow, output direction, non-urban/high-stack subcompartment, and per-kilogram mass basis, the characterization factor is 2.12 mol H⁺ eq/kg for Czechia (CZ) and 0.032 mol H⁺ eq/kg for Albania (AL). Applying these two entries to a 1 kg SO₂ emission record yields 2.12 and 0.032 mol H⁺ eq, respectively. Here the location field identifies the country of emission; it neither implies that all deposition and impact occur inside that country nor specifies a single receiving soil. This comparison reads fixed reference-package entries directly without rerunning atmospheric models in software or measuring field damage in either country.
claims.scope: Characterizing a hypothetical 1 kg matching SO₂ air output using two original factors from EF 3.1 Acidification 01.04.000.
caveats: The 1 kg emission is a conditional illustration with identical input; no software rerun, receptor disaggregation, or field damage measurement is performed.

claims.text: If SO₂'s chemical formula and a 1 kg mass alone determined the outcome, both countries would yield the same number, making it impossible to reconstruct these two published factors. Within this method dataset, changing the emitting country requires checking a different factor row; the two rows themselves neither attribute the gap to a specific transport or soil mechanism nor represent a ratio of observed real-world damages. This does not invalidate legitimate chemical scaling: the Joint Research Centre (JRC) release report derives factors for NO and SO₃ from existing NO₂ and SO₂ factors using charge and molar-mass ratios. That is a bounded proxy for specific inputs under explicit premises, not a substitute for country-specific factors derived from molecular formulas alone. Nor does this EF-internal check prove that no conditional correspondence could exist between EF and GLAM.
claims.scope: Counterexample from selected EF 3.1 SO₂ rows against single-variable chemical reconstruction, alongside the bounded JRC proxy.
caveats: The two rows neither decompose contributing processes nor predict field damage, and they do not rule out other conditional cross-method correspondences.

claims.text: Eutrophication asks a different question: how does an added nutrient supply alter ecosystems? Excess limiting nutrients can stimulate primary production, shift algal, plant, and food-web structure, and—through organic-matter decomposition and respiration—deplete dissolved oxygen in water. Any concrete model represents only part of this chain. The freshwater model selected in the 2019 UNEP guidance first simulates phosphorus transport and retention across river networks and then links total phosphorus concentration to species occurrence. River transport, water abstraction, biomass uptake, and sorption to suspended solids followed by sedimentation all alter phosphorus residence and distribution, yet the chosen model neither explicitly models full phosphorus-speciation exposure nor simulates every ecological process listed above.
claims.scope: Distinguishing general aquatic eutrophication mechanisms from the selected freshwater phosphorus model in UNEP 2019.

claims.text: The coastal marine model examines how nitrogen inputs drive bottom-water hypoxia. Nitrogen enters coastal waters via soils, river networks, or atmospheric deposition and stimulates primary production under the assumed nutrient-limited conditions; the resulting organic matter is consumed, degraded, and respired, depleting oxygen in bottom waters. This model therefore adds an explicit exposure step: it first translates nitrogen input into oxygen depletion and then estimates ecological effects from taxon-specific sensitivities to low oxygen. These two steps separately estimate bottom-water oxygen loss and species response to hypoxia.
claims.scope: The watershed-to-coastal-marine nitrogen, bottom-water oxygen depletion, and hypoxia-response model in UNEP 2019.
caveats: Model capability statements apply strictly to the version documented in the 2019 guidance; oxygen replenishment is omitted, and its unmodeled magnitude is not estimated here.

claims.text: The selected freshwater model tracks phosphorus and the coastal marine model tracks nitrogen, whereas nutrient limitation in real water bodies varies with local conditions. The 2019 guidance explicitly retains the possibility of nitrogen–phosphorus co-limitation and limitation by other nutrients. Moreover, the coastal model depends on watershed transport, nitrogen retention and removal, and bottom-water oxygen consumption, while omitting oxygen replenishment that could offset depletion. Phosphorus or nitrogen equivalents express impact potential under these premises; determining whether a specific water body actually becomes hypoxic requires site-specific data.
claims.scope: Nutrient-limitation assumptions and omitted oxygen replenishment in the selected UNEP 2019 freshwater and marine models, without extrapolating to later versions.

claims.text: Nutrient enrichment also occurs on land. Nitrogenous emissions travel through the atmosphere and deposit onto soils, where added nutrient supply alters plant growth and community composition without passing through aquatic oxygen depletion. Two country-differentiated European terrestrial eutrophication methods described in the 2011 ILCD Handbook—AE and Environmental Design of Industrial Products 2003 (EDIP 2003)—both link atmospheric deposition to critical loads in sensitive receiving areas. Accumulated Exceedance tracks the extent of critical-load exceedance, whereas EDIP 2003 expresses the midpoint as unprotected ecosystem area exceeding the nitrogen critical load. Here square meters (m²) record exposed area rather than counted species losses or aquatic nutrient equivalents.
claims.scope: European country-scale AE and EDIP 2003 methods in ILCD 2011 and terrestrial nutrient mechanisms, without constituting global or current universal recommendations.
caveats: The AE and EDIP 2003 methods discussed here are 2011 European country-scale approaches whose ready-made factors should not be extrapolated globally; exact SI factor units for AE are not specified here.

claims.text: Indicator units help identify what environmental change a model actually estimates. In the 2019 UNEP guidance, the midpoints for terrestrial acidification, freshwater eutrophication, and marine eutrophication use kg SO₂-eq, kg P-eq, and kg N-eq, reflecting distinct reference substances and environmental fates. Ecological endpoints further retain terrestrial area or aquatic volume alongside time, written as PDF·m²·yr or PDF·m³·yr. Although both endpoint units contain PDF, one describes terrestrial ecological impact and the other aquatic ecological impact; area and volume have different physical dimensions and cannot be summed directly into a physically meaningful total.
claims.scope: Midpoint and endpoint dimensions across the three UNEP 2019 categories, excluding cross-category normalization or weighting.

claims.text: Even sharing the name Accumulated Exceedance does not produce the same environmental equivalent. In EF 3.1, the acidification method reports results in mol H⁺ equivalents, whereas the terrestrial eutrophication method reports results in mol N equivalents, even though both method datasets reference the same flow property named "Moles". That shared property indicates only a mole-based quantity; it does not specify which environmental problem is being equivalized. Analysts must still inspect each method's indicator definition, receiving system, and reference. Treating the two as the same quantity erases the distinction between acidification and nutrient supply and mistakes a shared data-format structure for identical scientific meaning.
claims.scope: Two EF 3.1 AE method datasets sharing the Moles flow property while declaring distinct equivalents.
caveats: The Moles flow property points to version 03.00.000 of the mole unit group, whereas the same-UUID member inside the package declares version 03.00.003; this analysis relies on each method's declared equivalent and shared Moles property without asserting explicit unit-group version matching or software parsing behavior.

claims.text: Ammonia entries in the same reference package provide a concrete test. For the same versioned, identically directed, identical air-subcompartment per-kilogram NH₃ flow, the acidification factors for Czechia and Albania are 3.655 and 0.021 mol H⁺ eq/kg, whereas the corresponding terrestrial eutrophication factors are 10.328 and 7.192 mol N eq/kg. If a single fixed multiplier converted the first category into the second, 10.328 ÷ 3.655 and 7.192 ÷ 0.021 would have to be equal, yet the two ratios differ sharply. Both scores can be computed separately from one emission record, but sharing AE and the Moles property does not allow multiplying one score by a constant to obtain the other. This test rules out a fixed multiplier across these entries; it neither ranks the ecological importance of the two problems nor sets cross-category weights.
claims.scope: Testing whether a fixed cross-category multiplier links acidification and terrestrial eutrophication for the same EF 3.1 NH₃ elementary flow in CZ and AL.
caveats: The non-existence of a fixed multiplier applies to the selected flow and two locations in this package; it does not establish numerical links between EF and GLAM, category weights, or relative environmental importance.

claims.text: A single ecological response curve can also answer different questions about change. In the 2019 UNEP guidance, a marginal effect factor takes the tangent slope at the current working point, capturing the response to a small stress perturbation nearby; an average effect factor selects a target state and divides the response difference between the working point and target by the corresponding stress difference. A pristine state without human intervention, a policy target, or the curve minimum can each serve as a target for different reasons. When current-state data are unavailable, the guidance recommends using PDF = 0.2 as a proxy working point, noting that this reflects expert judgment harmonized with ecotoxicity assessment. That convention allows calculation to proceed, but it does not prove that any real receiving area actually sits at that state.
claims.scope: Marginal versus average response factors and the conditional PDF = 0.2 proxy working point in UNEP 2019 Section 3.5.4.

claims.text: While the guidance defines multiple calculation approaches, which endpoint factors could actually be released depended on data availability at the time. The 2019 guidance states that the required spatial effect data existed only for freshwater eutrophication, so endpoint variants based on current conditions were supplied for that category alone. By contrast, the terrestrial acidification and marine eutrophication factors released in the 2019 guidance used the developers' average effect factors and do not reflect local current conditions. Consequently, two results both called endpoints may represent a response near the working point in one category and an average response relative to a target in another. Explaining differences requires inspecting the actual supplied factors rather than reading methodological recommendations alone.
claims.scope: Actually supplied effect factors and endpoint variants documented on page 68 of UNEP 2019.
caveats: This describes the factors supplied in the 2019 guidance and does not represent the capabilities of subsequent releases.

claims.text: Why cannot the target state simply be omitted? Adding nutrients to a nutrient-poor system or applying modest acid inputs to alkaline soils can raise recorded species richness, yet higher richness alone does not prove that ecological function, vulnerability, or conservation goals have improved. For cases where current stress lies below the target, the guidance therefore recommends setting the effect factor to zero. That zero records how the framework aligns response modeling with protection goals; it does not mean the real ecosystem experiences no change.
claims.scope: Non-monotonic species-richness responses and the zero-effect-factor recommendation in UNEP 2019 Section 3.5.4.

claims.text: The meaning of PDF itself depends on the underlying ecological data. Terrestrial acidification and freshwater eutrophication rely on species-occurrence data expressed as the Potentially Not Occurring Fraction (PNOF), whereas marine hypoxia data use the Potentially Affected Fraction (PAF). Interpreting either metric as PDF in the guidance requires that the sampled systems represent the predicted receiving ecosystems. The resulting indicator represents a local, potential, and reversible ecological shift—not a count of globally extinct species. Whether a specific application holds depends on whether the species pool, background state, spatial scale, and effect relationship cover the ecosystem under study.
claims.scope: Conditional interpretation of PNOF and PAF as PDF in UNEP 2019 acidification and aquatic eutrophication models.

claims.text: Before agricultural fertilizer application can be characterized, analysts must estimate how much phosphorus reaches freshwater. Suppose a background agricultural dataset reports only 2 kg of total phosphorus applied to soil, an input chosen by the author as a worked example. Under the Tier 1 conditions of the 2019 UNEP guidance, a default 10% loss fraction may be applied to total phosphorus applied in background agriculture, yielding an estimated net freshwater emission of 2 kg P × 0.10 = 0.2 kg P. This step estimates an emission rather than a freshwater eutrophication indicator. For foreground agriculture or cases with finer data, the guidance specifies higher-tier loss estimation methods; 10% is not an empirical law for every field.
claims.scope: Author-defined 2 kg total P background-agriculture worked example conditionally applying the UNEP 2019 Tier 1 default 10% loss fraction.

claims.text: Next, let c_FW (in kg P-eq/kg P) denote the regional characterization factor matching that freshwater phosphorus emission; the midpoint indicator is then written as 0.2 kg P × c_FW, with units of kg P-eq. No numerical value is assigned here to c_FW: it must match the emission compartment, location, and chosen model, and switching to a factor defined per kilogram of phosphate requires adjusting for the mass-basis difference. Conversely, if the inventory already reports 0.2 kg P as a net emission to freshwater, characterization starts directly from that record without multiplying by a soil-loss fraction a second time. Applied load is the example's input; from it comes net emission, and only from net emission comes the category indicator.
claims.scope: Constructing a midpoint indicator from the worked example's net freshwater P emission and a compatible symbolic factor without adopting a numerical characterization factor.
caveats: c_FW is purely symbolic; no numerical value from any native characterization-factor package is adopted or verified here.

claims.text: Replacing the abstract symbol c_FW with real impact assessment frameworks immediately confronts a four-way divergence in eutrophication category architecture rather than mere differences in factor magnitude (Table 1). The 2011 ILCD Handbook and EU Environmental Footprint (EF 2.0 through EF 3.1, including Commission Recommendation (EU) 2021/2279) establish three separate midpoints—terrestrial, freshwater, and marine—without formally recommending endpoints (together accounting for 9.47% of the EF 3.1 single-score weighting). The 2019 UNEP guidance establishes only two aquatic categories (freshwater and coastal marine) with local reversible endpoints. ReCiPe 2016 retains only freshwater eutrophication (zero marine categories) because it lacks a global marine endpoint model, multiplying the midpoint by the same constant 6.1×10⁻⁷ species·yr/kg P eq across all three cultural perspectives. LC-IMPACT omits midpoints altogether and models freshwater and marine global irreversible extinction-risk endpoints (PDF·yr) directly. Consequently, switching the same nitrogen-bearing inventory to ReCiPe 2016 yields zero eutrophication score for aquatic nitrogen emissions—a methodological coverage gap that must never be misread as zero coastal hypoxia risk.
claims.scope: Four-way divergence across ILCD 2011, EF 2.0–3.1, UNEP GLAM 2019, ReCiPe 2016, and LC-IMPACT in eutrophication category count, receiving-system coverage, and midpoint-to-endpoint structure.
caveats: ReCiPe 2016's omission of marine eutrophication is a methodological coverage gap rather than a finding of zero impact; LC-IMPACT's freshwater endpoint covers fish species richness only and does not capture direct effects of cyanobacterial blooms on primary producers or drinking-water supplies.

Detailed parameters across the four frameworks: EF 3.1 terrestrial uses Accumulated Exceedance (normalization reference 176.75 mol N eq/person, weight 3.71%), while freshwater and marine use EUTREND (Struijs et al. 2009; normalization references 1.61 kg P eq/person and 19.55 kg N eq/person, weights 2.80% and 2.96%); ReCiPe 2016 freshwater computes a global mean phosphorus residence time of 85 days (0.23 years) on a 0.5°×0.5° hydrological grid combined with a freshwater species density of 7.89×10⁻¹⁰ species/m³ and response curves for autotrophic algae, heterotrophic fish, and invertebrates; LC-IMPACT freshwater spans 449 ecoregions (15,000 freshwater fish species only), and marine spans 5,772 watershed–Large Marine Ecosystem (LME) pairs and 66 coastal LMEs (57 animal species across 6 taxonomic groups).

claims.text: Returning to the 2 kg cropland total-phosphorus example shows how responsibility splits at the inventory–characterization interface create order-of-magnitude discrepancies (Table 2). Section 4.4.1.5 of Annex I to EU 2021/2279 specifies that when field-level phosphorus runoff is known, the net phosphorus leaving the field must be recorded in the water compartment (where EF 3.1 assigns 1.0 kg P eq/kg to freshwater total phosphorus and 0 to seawater); only when runoff is unknown may applied phosphorus be recorded directly to soil for reduction by the method's built-in transfer fraction. Yet those built-in transfer fractions disagree: EF 3.1 inherits EUTREND's 0.05 kg P eq/kg (5%), whereas ReCiPe 2016 Table 8.1 cites Bouwman et al. (2009) for 0.10 (10%), matching the UNEP 2019 Tier 1 inventory default. For the same 2 kg of applied phosphorus, reducing by 10% in the inventory and then mistakenly mapping to a soil flow multiplies the transfer fraction twice, understating the score 10–20×; conversely, mapping the unreduced 2 kg directly to a freshwater flow overstates it 10–20×. Chapter 8 of LC-IMPACT goes further on a 5-arcminute grid, separating direct freshwater discharge, applied-phosphorus leaching, and topsoil erosion (generic crop factor 0.3), requiring inventories to distinguish loss pathways beforehand.
claims.scope: Soil–water interface alignment for the 2 kg cropland total-phosphorus example across UNEP GLAM 2019, EF 3.1, ReCiPe 2016, and LC-IMPACT, contrasting the 2× model difference with 10–20× mapping errors.
caveats: The 2 kg total phosphorus input is a pedagogical example; both EF's 5% and ReCiPe/UNEP's 10% are coarse background default transfer fractions and cannot replace measured phosphorus loss rates for specific sloped croplands or irrigated districts.

Built-in soil phosphorus compound factors: EF 3.1 assigns 0.016 kg P eq/kg to both soil phosphate and phosphoric acid (the freshwater method XML contains 29 locationless factors); ReCiPe 2016 assigns 0.033 kg P eq/kg to soil phosphate and 0 to marine phosphorus.

claims.text: Even seemingly straightforward stoichiometric mass conversions contain factor-of-two errors in authoritative printed reports. In both EF 3.1 and ReCiPe 2016, freshwater emissions of phosphate (PO₄³⁻) and phosphoric acid (H₃PO₄) carry identical factors of 0.33 and 0.32 kg P eq/kg, matching the mass fraction of a single phosphorus atom in each molecule. However, Section 8.3 of the Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment (RIVM) Report 2016-0104 (printed p. 62) prints the freshwater midpoint factor for phosphorus pentoxide (P₂O₅) as 0.22 kg P eq/kg: because each P₂O₅ molecule contains two phosphorus atoms, its true phosphorus mass fraction is roughly 0.44 (2 × 30.974 / 141.943 ≈ 0.436), meaning the printed table omitted the subscript 2 and halved the factor; JRC109369 Table 7 instead creates no standalone elementary flow for reactive P₂O₅ and requires stoichiometric conversion to total phosphorus beforehand. Similarly, Table S4.2 of RIVM 2016-0104 (printed p. 149) labels the ecological half-effect parameter α as "[PDF·L/mg]", whereas Section 8.4 writes "log m³/kg", and checking the linear slopes in adjacent Table S4.1 confirms it is actually defined as log₁₀(mg/L). Recording these intra-source discrepancies prevents blind reproduction of printed typos during recalculation.
claims.scope: Stoichiometric conversion rules for phosphorus compounds, the omitted subscript 2 for P₂O₅ in RIVM 2016-0104 Chapter 8, and the unit-scale discrepancy in Table S4.2.
caveats: Documenting the P₂O₅ = 0.22 entry and the Table S4.2 header discrepancy in RIVM 2016-0104 is intended to prevent miscalculation, not to issue an unofficial revision on behalf of the method developers; software implementations must be checked package by package for independent fixes.

Stoichiometric and effect-slope verification details: approximate molar masses are 94.97 g/mol for PO₄³⁻, 98.00 g/mol for H₃PO₄, 30.974 g/mol for P, and 141.943 g/mol for P₂O₅ (single-P miscalculation: 30.974 / 141.943 ≈ 0.218); in RIVM 2016-0104 Table S4.2, heterotrophs in tropical/subtropical lakes have α = −1.430, and 0.5 / 10^(−1.430 − 3) ≈ 13,458 reproduces the 13,458 PDF·m³/kg printed in Table S4.1.

claims.text: A more subtle interface trap arises because agricultural nitrogen and phosphorus follow opposite compartment rules in the EU Environmental Footprint. Section 4.4.1.5 of Annex I to EU 2021/2279 explicitly specifies that marine eutrophication begins once nitrogen leaves the field and prohibits recording agricultural nitrogen as an emission to soil (both EF 3.1 marine, with 590 factors, and EF 3.1 terrestrial, with 575 factors, contain zero soil-nitrogen entries). Instead, each kilogram of applied nitrogen must be partitioned in the inventory according to Table 3 of that section into airborne nitrous oxide (0.022 kg N₂O/kg N), volatilized ammonia (0.12 kg NH₃/kg N for synthetic fertilizers; 0.24 kg NH₃/kg N for manure), and leached nitrate to water (1.33 kg NO₃⁻/kg N). For 10 kg of synthetic nitrogen fertilizer, compliant partitioning yields roughly 3.12 kg N eq of marine eutrophication and 16.16 mol N eq of terrestrial eutrophication; copying the phosphorus habit and entering soil nitrogen instead triggers no software error while silently zeroing out EF 3.1 eutrophication and acidification. By contrast, Chapter 9 Table 9.3 of LC-IMPACT folds field leaching into the impact model, assigning a global mean of 2.07×10⁻¹⁶ PDF·yr/kg N (3.751×10⁻¹⁶ in Europe) to soil-applied nitrogen. Reusing agricultural inventories across databases therefore requires verifying whether the target method package assigns factors to soil nitrogen.
claims.scope: Asymmetric prohibition of soil-nitrogen flows in EU 2021/2279 and EF 3.1, inventory air/water partitioning ledger, silent zeroing risk, and contrast with LC-IMPACT soil-nitrogen factors.
caveats: EU 2021/2279 Table 3 explicitly restricts its Tier 1 fixed emission factors from being used to compare different synthetic nitrogen fertilizer types; comparing urea against ammonium nitrate requires a finer field nitrogen-balance or empirical model.

Annex I Table 4 of EU 2021/2279 provides an alternative nitrogen-balance testing option: baseline aquatic nitrate loss of 0.44 kg NO₃⁻/kg N, ammonia volatilization of 0.18, 0.12, and 0.024 kg NH₃/kg N for urea, ammonium nitrate, and other synthetic fertilizers respectively, and denitrification of 0.09 kg N₂/kg N. Compliant partitioning check for 10 kg synthetic nitrogen fertilizer: 13.3 kg NO₃⁻ × 0.226 + 1.2 kg NH₃ × 0.092 ≈ 3.12 kg N eq, and 1.2 kg NH₃ × 13.47 ≈ 16.16 mol N eq.

claims.text: Once nitrogen enters waterways or the atmosphere, modeling choices over inland river denitrification and atmospheric deposition generate two-way rank reversals. EF 3.1 marine eutrophication assigns identical stoichiometric factors to freshwater and seawater emissions of the same nitrogen species (such as 1.0 kg N eq/kg for total nitrogen and 0.226 for nitrate), effectively assuming 100% lossless delivery from rivers and lakes to the sea. Accounting for river-network retention in Chapter 9 Table 9.3 of LC-IMPACT reduces the global river-emission factor (9.16×10⁻¹⁶ PDF·yr/kg N) to about 47.0% of direct coastal discharge (1.95×10⁻¹⁵). Comparing 1.5 kg of total nitrogen discharged to an inland river against 1.0 kg discharged directly to coastal waters, EF 3.1 ranks the inland release worse (1.5 vs 1.0), LC-IMPACT reverses the ranking to make coastal discharge worse (1.374×10⁻¹⁵ vs 1.95×10⁻¹⁵), and ReCiPe 2016 scores both at zero. Comparing 3 kg of airborne NOx against 1 kg of freshwater NO₃⁻ produces a second reversal: EF 3.1 assigns 0.389 to airborne NOx and rates the air emission more than five times higher (1.167 vs 0.226), whereas LC-IMPACT's marine pathway excludes airborne nitrogen entirely (0 entries), scoring air at 0 and freshwater at roughly 2.07×10⁻¹⁶.
claims.scope: Two-way rank reversals among inland nitrogen discharge, coastal discharge, and combustion NOx driven by EF 3.1's 1:1 river-to-sea stoichiometry versus LC-IMPACT's watershed retention and omission of atmospheric nitrogen deposition.
caveats: Global and continental averages in LC-IMPACT Table 9.3 are aggregated using nitrogen-fertilizer application or coastline-length weights; in regional assessments, whether inland discharge outperforms coastal discharge depends on the specific watershed's hydraulic residence time and the receiving LME's hypoxia sensitivity.

EF 3.1 marine eutrophication's 50 locationless generic factors cover the 7 nitrogen-bearing groups in JRC109369 Table 7 (excluding chemical oxygen demand, COD, and biochemical oxygen demand, BOD, which have 0 entries): freshwater and marine compartments share 1.0 for total nitrogen (excluding N₂), 0.824 for ammonia, 0.778 for ammonium, 0.304 for nitrite, and 0.226 kg N eq/kg for nitrate. European averages in LC-IMPACT Table 9.3 are 1.962×10⁻¹⁵ for river emissions versus 3.869×10⁻¹⁵ PDF·yr/kg N for coastal emissions (about 50.7%).

claims.text: Inspecting location codes in the EF 3.1 nitrogen eutrophication XML files reveals two opposite spatial structures. First, "country-tagged yet undifferentiated": marine eutrophication includes 540 location-tagged rows across 36 European codes for nitrogen oxides, nitrogen dioxide, and ammonia, yet every single value duplicates the locationless generic row (0.389 for NOx and NO₂; 0.092 kg N eq/kg for NH₃), giving landlocked Switzerland and Austria the exact same factors as coastal states solely so country-tagged air flows do not go unmatched. Second, "default exceeding every listed country": in terrestrial eutrophication, which uses country-specific AE, airborne ammonia spans roughly a 19.5-fold range across the 36 countries from Ireland (1.085) to Switzerland (21.2 mol N eq/kg, generic 13.47); yet the locationless generic NOx and NO₂ factor (4.26 mol N eq/kg) sits about 20.1% above the highest individual country, Luxembourg (3.547, with high-stack NO₂ at 3.55; lowest Greece at 0.3), and is used directly in the EF 3.1 global normalization workbook. Because the generic row retains an earlier European reference scenario, omitting a European country code in EF 3.1 terrestrial eutrophication does not yield an average—it imposes an upper-bound penalty more than 20% above every listed country.
claims.scope: Machine-readable structural analysis of EF 3.1 marine eutrophication's 540 constant location-matching rows and terrestrial eutrophication's locationless NOx factor (4.26) exceeding all 36 European country codes (maximum 3.547).
caveats: In the EF 3.1 terrestrial eutrophication XML, generic NOx = 4.26 originates from an earlier European reference scenario whereas the 36 country rows come from later Posch et al. (2008) recalculations; the generic row cannot be back-calculated as an arithmetic or emission-weighted mean of the 36 countries.

Other locationless airborne generic rows: EF 3.1 marine eutrophication includes nitric oxide (0.596), ammonium (0.087), and nitrate (0.028 kg N eq/kg); terrestrial eutrophication includes locationless nitric oxide at 6.532 mol N eq/kg (35 generic rows plus 540 country rows in total).

claims.text: Checking the official EF 3.1 global normalization workbook (2010 reference population ≈ 6.896 billion) against the agricultural mutual-exclusivity rules exposes double counting inside the normalization denominator itself. For freshwater eutrophication (official per-capita reference ≈ 1.61 kg P eq/person; exact value 1.6069), the calculation sheet first multiplies global synthetic fertilizer and manure phosphorus applications from Bouwman et al. (2013) by the 0.05 soil factor and then immediately adds global agricultural total phosphorus entering freshwater from Scherer and Pfister (2015) multiplied by the 1.0 water factor into the same denominator, inflating the per-capita reference by about +0.2509 kg P eq/person (15.6% of the official value). Marine eutrophication (19.55 kg N eq/person) similarly stacks global aquatic nitrate alongside agricultural total nitrogen entering freshwater. In addition, the three EF 3.1 eutrophication XML files and the 2023 update report retain five intra-source anomalies—including a duplicate elemental-phosphorus Universally Unique Identifier (UUID), misreported inventory-item counts, naming/formatting quirks, and a duplicated fifth-rank column in Table 13 (detailed in the caveats). Compliant Product Environmental Footprint (PEF) studies must retain the official normalization constants, yet analysts interpreting agricultural shares or auditing method packages should disclose these defects explicitly.
claims.scope: Agricultural double counting in the EF 3.1 official normalization workbook for freshwater phosphorus and marine nitrogen, plus five intra-source anomalies across the three eutrophication XML files and JRC130796 Table 13.
caveats: Compliant PEF studies must continue using the official fixed normalization factor (NF) constants when calculating normalized and weighted scores, while noting that the freshwater phosphorus denominator embeds a 15.6% soil-plus-water double-counted component when interpreting agricultural shares across methods.

EF 3.1 normalization workbook (2010 global reference population 6,895,889,018) calculation-row details: freshwater rows 1406–1407 count 1.58×10¹⁰ kg fertilizer P and 1.88×10¹⁰ kg manure P (×0.05 = 1.73×10⁹ kg P eq), row 1408 stacks 5.821×10⁹ kg agricultural total P to freshwater (×1.0), and row 1409 adds 3.529×10⁹ kg from wastewater treatment plants; marine row 1283 counts 7.50×10¹⁰ kg aquatic nitrate from Oita et al. (2016) (×0.226 = 1.695×10¹⁰ kg N eq), row 1288 stacks 5.92×10¹⁰ kg agricultural total N to freshwater from Bouwman et al. (2013) (×1.0), and row 1289 adds 9.691×10⁹ kg from wastewater treatment plants.

Five intra-source anomalies in EF 3.1 eutrophication XMLs and the 2023 update report: (1) the freshwater method contains two freshwater elemental-phosphorus UUIDs with the same name and Chemical Abstracts Service (CAS) number (one carrying a European Community, EC, number and one blank, both with factor 1.0); (2) the three files list inventoryItems as 3, 7, and 6—far below their actual 29, 590, and 575 factor rows—and freshwater and marine reuse the generic Mass flow property underneath; (3) the marine method name omits a comma ("Eutrophication marine"), and both freshwater and marine cite Struijs et al. 2008 as the external source while report text cites 2009; (4) the terrestrial indicator name has a trailing space, its 35 generic rows split into 27 empty location tags and 8 omitted location tags, and airborne ammonium (12.72166667 vs 12.7217) and nitrate (3.160645161 vs 3.16065) exhibit rounding splits across subcompartments; (5) Table 13 of the 2023 update report (printed p. 30) misprints the entire fifth-rank column as identical to the fourth-rank column (152/152, 8/8, and 201/201 across the three eutrophication categories).

claims.text: Stepping beyond deposition pathways, the same airborne precursor also enters atmospheric photochemistry before returning to the surface. Emitted nitrogen oxides react under sunlight with non-methane volatile organic compounds (NMVOC), carbon monoxide, and methane in nonlinear photochemical cycles to form ground-level (tropospheric) ozone. Although ozone itself is not an elementary inventory emission from industrial processes, it irritates human airways, elevates chronic respiratory mortality risk, and damages plant leaf stomata during the growing season, suppressing forest and grassland growth. Constructing characterization factors for such a secondary pollutant requires specifying the perturbed precursor, the background atmospheric ratio of nitrogen oxides to organics, and whether the modeled endpoint counts human respiratory intake or vegetation exposure.
claims.scope: Transition from single-pathway net-emission examples and atmospheric deposition to secondary tropospheric photochemical ozone formation mechanisms and receptor premises.
caveats: This discussion addresses secondary ground-level tropospheric ozone (summer photochemical smog), distinct from the ultraviolet-radiation pathway of stratospheric ozone depletion.

claims.text: Mainstream midpoint indicators for tropospheric ozone have evolved from pure chemical reactivity to a single-receptor model and finally to dual-receptor separation (Table 3). Early CML 2002 used Photochemical Ozone Creation Potential (POCP) referenced to ethylene, comparing only individual organic compounds' ozone-forming reactivity without assigning factors to nitrogen oxides or accounting for downwind population or vegetation distribution. The 2011 ILCD Handbook and EU Environmental Footprint (EF 3.0 and EF 3.1) adopted the European regional transport model LOTOS-EUROS with a single human-health midpoint (kg NMVOC eq), assigning 1.0 to both generic NMVOC and NOx and 0.235 to generic volatile organic compounds (VOC) weighted by 2004 European emissions. Because NMVOC is a chemical mixture, ReCiPe 2016 switched the reference to NOx expressed on an NO₂ mass basis (kg NOx eq), using the global source–receptor model TM5-FASST to split Human Health Ozone Formation Potential (HOFP) from Terrestrial Ecosystem Ozone Formation Potential (EOFP, defined by accumulated daytime exposure above 40 parts per billion over the forest and grassland growing season, AOT40), with fixed constants converting each to disability-adjusted life years (DALY) and species·yr endpoints.
claims.scope: Structural and reference-substance differences among CML 2002 POCP, the ILCD/EF LOTOS-EUROS single midpoint, and ReCiPe 2016 dual HOFP/EOFP midpoints.
caveats: Using the report's printed weights (14.0 × 1.0 + 47.8 × 0.0101) / 61.8 gives an exact quotient of about 0.23435 (0.234 to three significant figures), whereas the official EF 3.1 method XML publishes 0.235 (higher by 0.001 in the last digit); NO remains 1.0 in EF 3.1 photochemical ozone, whereas EF 3.1 acidification and eutrophication and ReCiPe 2016 ozone all rescale NO by molar mass.

Detailed midpoint and endpoint values across frameworks: in EF 3.1 unspecified air, NMVOC, NOx, NO₂, and NO are all 1.0, ethylene is 1.69, methane is 0.0101, and generic VOC is 0.235 (exact weighted quotient ≈ 0.23435 from 14.0 Mt NMVOC and 47.8 Mt methane); in ReCiPe 2016, NO, NO₂, and NO₃ are converted to NO₂ mass on an equimolar-nitrogen basis with factors 1.53, 1, and 0.74; HOFP multiplies by 9.1×10⁻⁷ DALY/kg NOx eq (respiratory mortality aged 30+) and EOFP multiplies by 1.29×10⁻⁷ species·yr/kg NOx eq.

claims.text: Changing the reference from NMVOC to NOx and separating the two receptors involves far more than multiplying by a constant conversion factor. In EF 3.1, generic NMVOC and NOx carry a 1:1 equal weight; in the ReCiPe 2016 global mean table, however, 1 kg of NMVOC equals only 0.18 kg NOx eq under HOFP and 0.29 kg NOx eq under EOFP—giving NOx roughly 5.56 times the weight of NMVOC for human health and 3.45 times for ecosystems. Comparing Option A (1 kg NOx) against Option B (2 kg NMVOC), EF 3.1 scores Option A at half of Option B (1.0 vs 2.0), whereas ReCiPe 2016 reverses the ranking to make Option A higher under both HOFP (1.0 vs 0.36) and EOFP (1.0 vs 0.58). Even within ReCiPe 2016 alone, comparing Option C (0.25 kg NOx) against Option D (1 kg NMVOC) yields a higher score for Option C under HOFP (0.25 vs 0.18) but a lower score under EOFP (0.25 vs 0.29). Because densely populated areas and growing-season vegetation weight the two precursors differently, no single positive constant can bridge either the two frameworks or the two receptors.
claims.scope: Precursor substitution-ratio differences and proof of cross-framework and cross-receptor rank reversals between EF 3.1 photochemical ozone formation and ReCiPe 2016 global HOFP/EOFP.
caveats: Options A through D are controlled precursor comparisons designed to demonstrate the algebraic behavior of published characterization factors, not complete co-emission inventories of a specific combustion-control retrofit.

claims.text: Moving to regionalized factor tables, photochemical nonlinearity can even flip the sign of the same kilogram of NOx between negative and positive across the two receptors (Table 3). In Table S2.1 of RIVM 2016-0104, the combined Benelux region assigns NOx a negative human-health factor of HOFP = −0.48 kg NOx eq/kg (United Kingdom and Ireland: −0.20), while assigning the exact same region a positive terrestrial ecosystem factor of EOFP = +0.16 (United Kingdom and Ireland: +0.44); in those same regions, NMVOC factors rise to +0.69 and +1.10 for Benelux (+0.60 and +1.15 for the United Kingdom and Ireland). In densely urbanized regions with already elevated background NOx, additional nitric oxide titrates ground-level ozone near the source (NO + O₃ → NO₂ + O₂), locally scavenging ozone and reducing nearby human inhalation, whereas the resulting NO₂ is transported downwind and still elevates threshold-exceeding exposure over forests and grasslands. A negative sign therefore reflects only a local marginal direction around year-2000 reference emissions—neither a general rule nor a reduction in ecosystem damage.
claims.scope: Opposite signs for NOx between human HOFP and ecosystem EOFP in Benelux and the UK & Ireland in ReCiPe 2016 Table S2.1, together with chemical and spatial boundary conditions.
caveats: The negative values in Table S2.1 reflect marginal sensitivities computed by TM5-FASST around year-2000 reference emissions; deep regional NOx reductions that cross photochemical regime boundaries alter both the marginal slope and its sign.

claims.text: Contrasting that genuine source–receptor spatial differentiation with release-package inspection shows why analysts must check whether country-tagged entries represent regional modeling or constant copies designed to prevent unmatched flows. Of the 1,401 factor rows in the EF 3.1 photochemical ozone XML, 720 carry one of 36 European country or territory codes, yet every single country assigns 1.0 to NOx and NO₂ and 0.0811 kg NMVOC eq/kg to SOx and SO₂—identical to the locationless generic row. In the same reference package, by contrast, the exact same airborne NOx flow receives distinct country-specific values in acidification and terrestrial eutrophication for Belgium, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom (acidification: 0.837, 0.892, and 0.729 mol H⁺ eq/kg; terrestrial eutrophication: 2.72, 2.109, and 1.084 mol N eq/kg). Once an inventory attaches emitting-country tags for deposition categories, photochemical ozone and marine eutrophication must duplicate matching rows—so seeing a location field never proves country-level ozone modeling.
claims.scope: Distinguishing the 720 constant location-matching rows in EF 3.1 photochemical ozone XML from genuinely country-differentiated factors in acidification and terrestrial eutrophication.
caveats: This documents the numerical structure of location entries in the published EF 3.1 XML and does not deny that underlying LOTOS-EUROS runs used gridded atmospheric transport to derive European averages.

claims.text: Placing atmospheric and deposition categories side by side clarifies why a single precursor must be characterized at full mass across multiple pathways. In EF 3.1, 1 kg of nitrogen oxides emitted to unspecified air (via the same elementary-flow UUID) simultaneously contributes 1.0 kg NMVOC eq to photochemical ozone, 0.74 mol H⁺ eq to acidification, 4.26 mol N eq to terrestrial eutrophication, 0.389 kg N eq to marine eutrophication, and 1.6×10⁻⁶ disease incidence to particulate matter health damage; 1 kg of fossil methane simultaneously contributes 29.8 kg CO₂ eq to climate change (retaining the pre-erratum Sixth Assessment Report, AR6, value) and 0.0101 kg NMVOC eq to photochemical ozone; and 1 kg of methyl chloride simultaneously contributes 0.015 to stratospheric ozone depletion, 5.54 to climate change, and 0.00845 to photochemical ozone. Because molecules participate sequentially in atmospheric oxidation, aerosol formation, and surface deposition—and each midpoint tracks a distinct serial mechanism or receptor—splitting 1 kg across pathways would understate every consequence. This also explains why a negative Benelux ozone factor never implies that emitting more NOx is beneficial. The real risks to guard against are summing midpoints with incompatible units or aggregating ozone and fine-particulate health endpoints (such as DALY) without checking for epidemiological co-adjustment.
claims.scope: Physical basis for full-mass multi-category characterization of a single air precursor, safeguarding against misreading a single negative indicator, and true boundaries for cross-category summation and health-endpoint aggregation.
caveats: Full-mass characterization across midpoints holds when each category reports its own pathway indicator; aggregating into a common health-endpoint unit or combining into a policy- or value-weighted single score still requires verifying epidemiological independence and rules for overlapping policy targets.

claims.text: In practical audits, these photochemical ozone factors face two further boundaries. First, model scale: both EF 3.1 and ReCiPe 2016 publish gridded annual-mean or growing-season marginal factors that cannot substitute for local hourly peak-episode air-quality compliance modeling. Second, package and report discrepancies: auditing EF 3.1 cross-category mappings shows that photochemical ozone assigns 0.0152 kg NMVOC eq/kg to both HCFC-140 (labeled CAS 71-55-6) and its synonym methyl chloroform, whereas stratospheric ozone depletion omits both UUIDs and instead lists "1,1,1-trichloroethane" (0.14 kg CFC-11 eq/kg) with its CAS field mistakenly filled with 79-00-5 (the isomer 1,1,2-trichloroethane). Cross-category audits must therefore track elementary-flow UUIDs rather than relying on chemical synonyms or unverified CAS metadata; remaining table-numbering, asterisk, and indicator-name discrepancies are recorded in the caveats.
claims.scope: Spatial and temporal scale limits of source–receptor photochemical ozone factors, plus retained intra-source discrepancies across JRC109369, JRC130796, EF 3.1 flow tables, and RIVM 2016-0104 Chapter 6.
caveats: Intra-source table-numbering, asterisk, and flow-table CAS metadata discrepancies do not alter the verified precursor rank reversals or full-mass multi-category accounting principles established here, but they show that automated mapping must verify UUIDs and source-table context.

Additional intra-source discrepancies in photochemical ozone reports and packages: (1) the 2023 EF 3.1 update report lists photochemical ozone as an updated category in its abstract, text, and Table 2 (adding 0.0152 for methyl chloroform and 0.115 kg NMVOC eq/kg for methylene chloride), yet omits the update asterisk in summary Table 1 on printed p. 6; (2) the 2018 EF supporting report prints the indicator as POCP, whereas the 2023 update report Table 1 and method XML record "Tropospheric ozone concentration increase"; (3) Chapter 6 of RIVM 2016-0104 jumps from Table 6.2 directly to Tables 6.5 and 6.6 (omitting 6.3 and 6.4) and mis-cites Table 6.6 as "Table 5.6" on printed p. 56.

claims.text: Looking back at the opening kilogram of ammonia, cropland phosphorus, and atmospheric nitrogen oxides, a single inventory flow routinely feeds multiple environmental pathways and need not be partitioned arbitrarily when characterized separately. Before using such results for product comparisons or supply-chain diagnostics, analysts should pass through five checks: first, inspect category coverage (three categories, two aquatic categories, or freshwater phosphorus alone—never mistaking an unmodeled pathway for zero load); second, audit the cropland phosphorus interface and stoichiometry (preventing double reduction, tenfold overstatement, and the printed P₂O₅ error); third, verify agricultural nitrogen partitioning rules (avoiding silent omission from zero-factor soil nitrogen in EF); fourth, test true spatial resolution (separating 1:1 river-to-sea assumptions, roughly 47% inland retention attenuation, constant location copies, and the locationless NOx upper-bound penalty); and fifth, account for normalization-denominator bias and local validity limits (noting the 15.6% double counting in freshwater phosphorus and remembering that regional potentials never replace site-level water-quality or acute-episode compliance modeling). The next chapter continues from airborne emissions to examine population inhalation and human health damage from fine particulate matter.
claims.scope: Category-specific interpretation of acidification and nutrient pathways without treating multi-category characterization as inventory mass partitioning.
caveats: This five-step checklist ensures methodological consistency between life cycle inventories and impact assessment methods for nutrient enrichment; it cannot substitute for watershed water-quality monitoring, ecotoxicological assessment, or local environmental permitting.

claims.text: One kilogram of emission recorded in a life cycle inventory is neither one kilogram of particles inhaled by people nor a realized health loss. Estimating health damage from emitted mass requires separating directly emitted particles from secondary particles formed via gaseous precursors, estimating population intake, and linking exposure to disease and health damage using epidemiological evidence. The sections below first demonstrate a pair of compatible historical methods step by step, then examine what data each step requires and under what conditions it holds.
claims.scope: Historical two-step calculation framework linking particulate emission mass through population intake to estimated health damage, along with its applicability conditions.

claims.text: Fine particulate matter with an aerodynamic diameter of 2.5 micrometers or less (PM₂.₅) is a size fraction defined by aerodynamic diameter, not a single chemical substance. Primary particles are emitted directly, whereas secondary particles form in the atmosphere from gaseous precursors. The 2011 method of Humbert et al. separately addresses primary PM₂.₅, coarse particulate matter between 2.5 and 10 micrometers (written PM₁₀–₂.₅ in the original paper), and the pathways from SO₂, NOₓ, and NH₃ to secondary fine particles. Particle size fraction, formation pathway, and emitted substance determine exactly which mass enters each subsequent calculation.
claims.scope: Aerodynamic size classification of fine particulate matter, primary versus secondary formation pathways, and the coverage of Humbert et al. (2011).

claims.text: A key quantity linking emissions to people is the inhalation intake fraction (iF): the cumulative particle mass ultimately inhaled by the exposed population divided by the mass emitted at the source. Humbert et al. define iF from the incremental ambient concentration caused by that source, multiplied by individual breathing rates and summed across all exposed people and time periods. Pre-existing background particle concentrations cannot be attributed to the modeled emission, and inhaled mass is not yet lung-deposited mass or internally absorbed dose.
claims.scope: Incremental-concentration definition of inhalation intake fraction (iF), population summation scope, and the boundary before lung deposition.

claims.text: A historical archetype illustrates the scale of this fraction. Table 3 of Humbert et al. (2011) reports an intake fraction of 44 mg/kg for urban ground-level primary PM₂.₅ emissions. Applied to 1 kg of such emissions, the exposed population collectively inhales 44 mg, or 0.000044 kg. The value 44 is expressed in parts per million by mass—neither 44% of the population nor an ambient air concentration.
claims.scope: Parts-per-million meaning and unit conversion of the urban ground-level primary PM₂.₅ intake fraction (44 mg/kg) in Humbert et al. (2011).

claims.text: When estimating intake fractions, the emission source and the inhaling population need not share the same location. The 2011 urban archetype counts both inhalation within the city and downwind inhalation after pollutants leave the urban area; "urban emission" identifies where the source sits, not where all exposure ends. Total inhaled mass is spread across many individuals, multiple locations, and an extended period, so it cannot specify how much any single person inhales.
claims.scope: Spatial boundary between emission-source location and cross-regional receptor population intake in the urban emission archetype.

claims.text: Next, the effect factor (EF) of Gronlund et al. (2015) multiplies the mortality response per unit of inhaled mass by a severity factor per death. Severity is expressed in disability-adjusted life years per death (DALY/death) and already incorporates non-fatal morbidity through the authors' proxy assumption; it is neither years of life lost per death (YLL/death) alone nor a standalone disability weight. The authors draw disease data from high-income North America and use the all-cause DALY/death ratio for each disease as a proxy for the fraction attributable to PM₂.₅. Multiplying iF by this severity-inclusive EF produces a characterization factor (CF) denominated per kilogram emitted; the resulting CF remains bounded by the included diseases, age range, and severity-proxy assumptions.
claims.scope: Scope of assumptions in Gronlund et al. (2015) for constructing a characterization factor (CF) by combining an effect factor (EF) with high-income North American cause-specific DALY/death severity proxies.

claims.text: Gronlund et al. publish a combined default effect factor of 78 DALY/kg inhaled PM₂.₅ for cardiopulmonary disease and lung cancer. They first calculate effects by age group and cause of death and then aggregate using World Health Organization (WHO) world standard population age weights. Inhaled mass in the denominator covers all ages, whereas health effects below age 30 are set to zero by model convention. That zero reflects the chosen model's coverage boundary and cannot be read as evidence that children face no health risk. Users applying the aggregated factor must also preserve its completed stratification and weighting sequence rather than reassembling rounded sub-table entries.
claims.scope: Default combined cardiopulmonary and lung-cancer effect factor (78 DALY/kg inhaled PM₂.₅) and the age-30 cutoff convention in Gronlund et al. (2015).

claims.text: Multiplying the intake fraction by the effect factor reproduces the characterization factor in this historical example. Converting the urban ground-level primary PM₂.₅ intake fraction of 44 mg/kg to 0.000044 kg inhaled/kg emitted and multiplying by 78 DALY/kg inhaled yields 0.003432 DALY/kg emitted. Inhaled mass cancels in the product, leaving emitted mass in the denominator; Table 2 of Gronlund et al. reports 0.0034 at its display precision. This arithmetic reproduces the published calculation, while the underlying health effect remains anchored to the source study's data and model.
claims.scope: Arithmetic reproduction of the urban ground-level primary PM₂.₅ characterization factor in Gronlund et al. (2015) Table 2 from intake fraction and default effect factor.
caveats: This worked calculation does not propagate parameter, structural, or input uncertainty from the original models; extra decimal digits reflect exact arithmetic on the listed inputs rather than equivalent empirical precision.
