claims.text: Applying the same effect factor to the rural ground-level archetype (iF = 3.8 mg/kg) yields 0.0002964 DALY/kg, while the remote archetype (0.1 mg/kg) yields 0.0000078 DALY/kg; the original table publishes 0.00030 and 0.0000078, respectively. Comparing the tabulated intake fractions directly (44 / 3.8) rather than dividing two already-rounded published CFs gives an urban-to-rural ratio of about 11.58. Because the effect factor is held constant, that difference stems entirely from intake fraction in this example and cannot be interpreted as a measured ratio of real-world urban versus rural health losses.
claims.scope: Recalculating rural and remote ground-level primary PM₂.₅ characterization factors under a fixed effect factor and bounding the urban-to-rural intake-fraction ratio.

claims.text: Pathways forming secondary particles begin with gaseous emissions. Because SO₂, NOₓ, and NH₃ form secondary fine particles that people subsequently inhale, a precursor iF simultaneously carries the mass identity of the emitted gas in its denominator and the inhaled particle in its numerator. The precursor intake fractions in Humbert et al.'s table already embed particle formation, atmospheric transport, and inhalation, so analysts must not multiply by a formation yield a second time. Moreover, aerosol formation depends on temperature and co-emitted precursors, so chemical stoichiometry alone never defines a universal particle yield across locations.
claims.scope: Denominator mass identity and gas-to-particle conversion boundaries for secondary fine-particulate precursor intake fractions of SO₂, NOₓ, and NH₃.

claims.text: Starting from an SO₂ emission, both the intake fraction and the final characterization factor are denominated per kilogram of SO₂ emitted, whereas the health effect factor is denominated per kilogram of PM₂.₅ inhaled. The urban SO₂ intake fraction is 0.99 mg inhaled PM₂.₅/kg emitted SO₂; converting milligrams to kilograms and multiplying by the same 78 DALY/kg inhaled effect factor yields 0.00007722 DALY/kg emitted SO₂, matching the 0.000077 reported at table precision. Applying the same procedure to the tabulated urban intake fractions for NOₓ (0.20) and NH₃ (1.7 mg inhaled PM₂.₅/kg respective precursor emitted) yields 0.0000156 DALY/kg NOₓ and 0.0001326 DALY/kg NH₃. These figures quantify damage estimated through secondary particle formation rather than direct gas inhalation; while they compare how the specified model characterizes each emission, they cannot by themselves compare products, whose delivered service and emission quantities must still come from the inventory.
claims.scope: Denominator alignment and product-comparison boundaries when reproducing urban SO₂, NOₓ, and NH₃ characterization factors in Gronlund et al. (2015) via secondary PM₂.₅ formation.

claims.text: Whereas the historical example above carries emissions all the way to DALY, current mainstream frameworks cut the same "emission → inhalation → morbidity/mortality → years of life lost" causal chain at three distinct points (Table 1). The 2011 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook defines a Level I midpoint in kg PM₂.₅ eq and recommends endpoints in DALY at Level I for primary particles and Level II for secondary particles. ReCiPe 2016 and LC-IMPACT share the 56-region TM5-FASST model and adult cohort slopes: ReCiPe 2016 expresses its midpoint as an intake-fraction ratio in kg PM₂.₅ eq and multiplies by a global default of 6.29×10⁻⁴ DALY/kg PM₂.₅ eq, whereas LC-IMPACT omits the midpoint and computes regional DALY/kg directly. The European Union Environmental Footprint (EF 2.0 to EF 3.1, distinct from the effect factor above) adopts the 2016 United Nations Environment Programme and Society of Environmental Toxicology and Chemistry (UNEP/SETAC) nonlinear model, retaining a midpoint label while advancing the indicator to "disease incidence" (8.96% weight, second highest among all 16 categories); Joint Research Centre report JRC109369 explicitly documents that the underlying metric is actually premature deaths, renamed in text without altering numerical values or adding non-fatal morbidity.
claims.scope: Aligning particulate matter indicator cutpoints and unit meanings across ILCD 2011 (Section 1 Tables 1–2, Section 3.4), EU EF 2.0–3.1 (EU 2021/2279, JRC109369 printed pp. 6–8 and 16, EF 3.1 particulate method package and global normalization/weighting workbook), ReCiPe 2016 (RIVM Chapter 5 and 2017 paper), and LC-IMPACT (2020 paper and Overall Report Chapter 6).
caveats: The three indicator units (kg PM₂.₅ eq, disease incidence counting premature deaths only, and DALY) cannot be compared directly in numerical magnitude; the exact cached EU EF 3.1 normalization reference in workbook cell D9 is 5.9536682112547822×10⁻⁴ cases/person.

The unit conflict between JRC109369 Table 1/Section 4.4 and Table 2 is an intra-source inconsistency in the official publication; citations must specify both the table referenced and the EF 3.1 particulate matter method package version.

Detailed framework parameters: ILCD 2011 combines European RiskPoll and US source–receptor models; ReCiPe 2016 and LC-IMPACT apply a 20% perturbation to year-2000 emissions in TM5-FASST paired with Krewski et al. (2009) relative risks for adults aged 30+ (1.013 for cardiopulmonary disease and 1.014 for lung cancer per µg/m³), an annual breathing rate of 4,745 m³, and WHO 2012 severity factors (ReCiPe's summary table rounds this to 6.3×10⁻⁴); JRC109369 Table 2 inconsistently printed the legacy PM₂.₅ mass equivalent (kg), while the method XML binds underneath to the generic "Number of items" flow property.

claims.text: Once an indicator cutpoint is selected, particle size-fraction disaggregation and emission-height tags at the package interface can still cause double counting, silent zeroing, or hundredfold jumps (Table 2). Three proxy rules are built into the EF 3.1 particulate matter package (983 factor rows): first, outside the high-altitude subcompartment (where both are zero), every PM₁₀ factor equals exactly 0.23 times the corresponding PM₂.₅ factor (assuming PM₁₀ is uniformly 23% PM₂.₅ and coarse fractions cause zero mortality); second, ultrafine PM₀.₂ and submicron PM₀.₂–₂.₅ copy the PM₂.₅ factor at 100%; third, although elementary flows exist for coarse PM₂.₅–₁₀ and particles > 10 µm, the method assigns zero factors to both. Consequently, splitting an inventory into PM₂.₅ and PM₂.₅–₁₀ silently zeros out the coarse fraction, whereas reporting both total PM₁₀ and its constituent PM₂.₅ double-counts fine particles (doubling the score exactly when the true share is 23%). Meanwhile, EF 3.1 equates "unspecified air" with the highest-exposure "urban close-to-ground" subcompartment—20.96× non-urban close-to-ground, 79.04× non-urban high stack, and 146.36× non-urban very high stack—so omitting site and stack height frequently amplifies scores far more than process-level abatement.
claims.scope: Verifying size-fraction scaling proxies, zero coarse-particle factors, and air-subcompartment multipliers from the EU EF 3.1 particulate matter method package and 12 size-fraction elementary-flow files.
caveats: The 0.23 multiplier is a generic built-in size-fraction proxy in EU EF 3.1 and does not represent the measured PM₂.₅/PM₁₀ ratio of any specific combustion or fugitive-dust source.

Assigning zero to coarse PM₂.₅–₁₀ in the EU EF 3.1 particulate matter package reflects a model-coverage boundary, not evidence that inhaling coarse particles has no physiological effect on the respiratory tract.

claims.text: Even for identical emitted mass, the distribution of emission heights can alter population intake. In Humbert et al.'s table, urban fine particles have a higher intake fraction than coarse particles at every individual source height; yet when each size fraction is weighted by its actual source-height mix, the ranking reverses because coarse particles are more heavily concentrated at ground level. This counterexample compares exposure and height-mix weighting—it neither proves that coarse particles are more toxic nor authorizes treating US source-height shares as universal across all products.
claims.scope: Conditional comparison of named urban fine and coarse particulate archetypes and source-height shares in Humbert et al. (2011).
caveats: The source-height factors themselves rely on the same anchoring relation; weighted agreement demonstrates internal consistency rather than independent empirical validation.

claims.text: Although intake fractions and health effect factors multiply cleanly, they rest on different tiers of evidence. Historical intake fractions synthesize models and literature with harmonized parameters, yet the unified table still spans heterogeneous sources and unquantified uncertainties. When Gronlund et al. cross-check emissions-based estimates against ambient-concentration estimates, both pathways share the same health relationship while differing in source–receptor aggregation boundaries, so discrepancies primarily test the intake estimate. Harmonizing inputs makes model outputs easier to compare, and agreement among models measures computational consistency; whether the health relationship itself is supported still depends on independent epidemiological observation.
claims.scope: Distinct evidentiary tiers underlying historical intake-model parameter harmonization and the dual-pathway US burden cross-check in Gronlund et al. (2015).
caveats: Model intercomparisons and dual-pathway consistency do not establish independent causal validation of health effects.

claims.text: The health-effect evidence used here comes from prospective population studies. Pope et al. (2002) followed adult mortality in the American Cancer Society cohort, assigning enrolled adults to metropolitan areas via enrollment addresses and three-digit ZIP codes, linking each area to regional monitoring averages, adjusting for smoking, occupation, diet, and other confounders, and testing spatial structure. Such a study evaluates associations between long-term ambient exposure contrasts and mortality; regional monitor averages are not each participant's lifetime inhaled particle mass.
claims.scope: Metropolitan monitoring-average exposure assignment and confounder-adjustment design of the American Cancer Society adult prospective cohort in Pope et al. (2002).

claims.text: The original study's early-exposure analysis reports adjusted relative risks separately for cardiopulmonary and lung-cancer mortality per unit PM₂.₅, whereas its smoothed exposure–response curve—nearly monotonic and linear over the observed range—comes from a separate analysis using the average of early and late exposure periods. The authors neither rule out flattening or steepening at higher concentrations nor eliminate residual confounding or post-enrollment behavioral shifts. Accordingly, later effect factors expressed in DALY/kg inhaled are derived quantities combining cohort associations with baseline mortality, breathing rates, and severity weights.
claims.scope: Observed concentration range of the smoothed cardiopulmonary and lung-cancer relative-risk curves in Pope et al. (2002) and extrapolation limits when converting them into effect factors.

claims.text: To perform that conversion, Gronlund et al. pair US mortality rates from a period and population close to the original risk study with concentrations and populations across 63 US metropolitan areas, stratifying responses by age and cause of death. Those 63 areas belong to the subsequent baseline calculation and cannot be merged with Pope et al.'s analysis subsets, which varied by pollutant and time period. WHO world standard population weights supply an age-aggregation standard; they do not transform a US cohort and North American disease dataset into independent national epidemiological surveys.
claims.scope: Baseline applicability of the 63 US metropolitan area populations and concentrations and WHO world standard population age weights in Gronlund et al. (2015).

claims.text: Estimating population intake also requires tracking whether particles move between indoor and outdoor air. Outdoor emissions infiltrate buildings, so where people spend time and how buildings ventilate and filter air all change cumulative intake; conversely, indoor emissions can exfiltrate outdoors and continue exposing people. Fantke et al. (2017) couple urban and rural indoor and outdoor air into a multi-compartment model that tracks transport, deposition, and inhalation simultaneously, enabling exposure modeling across the building envelope.
claims.scope: Scope of the coupled urban/rural indoor–outdoor multi-compartment transport, deposition, and population-intake model in Fantke et al. (2017).

claims.text: Before multiplying an intake fraction by a health effect factor, analysts must verify that both sides use compatible exposure definitions. If the intake model already accounts for time spent indoors, particle infiltration, and breathing rates, the health-effect conversion must adopt matching conventions—otherwise the same adjustment can be omitted or applied twice. Fantke et al. (2017) explicitly examine this coupling, and Fantke et al. (2019) likewise require consistent conventions across both sides. Consequently, swapping one newer number into the 2011–2015 worked example does not create an updated version of the same method.
claims.scope: Indoor–outdoor exposure-definition compatibility required when multiplying intake fractions by health effect factors in Fantke et al. (2017) and (2019).

claims.text: Population scope and modeled health outcomes must also match across both halves. Chapter 6 of LC-IMPACT v1.0 restricts the intake denominator to the population aged 30 and older and divides the concentration response by the same breathing rate in the effect step, so breathing rate cancels internally; its EF measures changes in cardiopulmonary and lung-cancer deaths per kilogram of inhaled PM₂.₅ and must then be multiplied by damage per death. By contrast, Gronlund et al.'s factor uses all-age inhaled mass in its denominator and already embeds severity. Neither shared symbols nor cancellation of an intermediate variable permits splicing half of one method onto half of another.
claims.scope: Incompatibility between LC-IMPACT v1.0 (age 30+ intake denominator, mortality-only EF) and Gronlund et al. (2015) (all-age intake denominator, severity-inclusive EF).

claims.text: Even after incorporating indoor–outdoor transfer, analysts must check which particles and emission sources the newer model covers. Fantke et al.'s 2017 coupled model covers primary PM₂.₅, with urban outdoor estimates grounded in ground-level emission data; elevated stacks, secondary inorganic aerosols, and secondary organic aerosols require further extension. Thus it demonstrates how to couple indoor and outdoor exposure more completely without replacing every precursor and source-height scenario in Humbert et al.'s 2011 table. Users must select methods by required capability rather than assuming a later publication year makes entire tables interchangeable.
claims.scope: Coverage boundary of the Fantke et al. (2017) coupled indoor–outdoor model (ground-level primary PM₂.₅) relative to the 2011 precursor and source-height table.

claims.text: The historical worked example above used a fixed effect factor. When the exposure–response relationship is curved, identical intake increments produce different health changes at different background levels. Fantke et al. (2019) construct effect factors from an age- and cause-specific Integrated Exposure–Response (IER) model combined with regional mortality rates, severity weights, and inhalation conventions; ischemic heart disease and stroke start from age 25, alongside adult chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer, and acute lower respiratory infections in young children. This changes both the mathematical shape of the response and the health-outcome coverage of the historical cardiopulmonary/lung-cancer example.
claims.scope: Changes to nonlinear slope behavior and health-outcome coverage introduced by the age-stratified five-cause Integrated Exposure–Response (IER) model in Fantke et al. (2019).
caveats: Age and outcome boundaries follow Section 2.2 of Fantke et al. (2019); Section 2.3.3 phrases the early-childhood age cutoff slightly differently, so uniform treatment of boundary age groups across all implementations is not claimed here.

claims.text: Reading a nonlinear curve requires separating current exposure from the theoretical minimum risk exposure level. Current exposure is the working point around which change is evaluated; the theoretical minimum risk exposure level is the counterfactual reference used to compute attributable burden and must never be mistaken from its name for a proven biological safety threshold or regulatory limit. Changing the counterfactual alters "relative to what" burden is measured, whereas changing the working point alters "starting from where" change occurs; both alter numerical results, yet they alter different relationships.
claims.scope: Functional distinction between the current-exposure working point and the theoretical minimum risk exposure counterfactual reference on a nonlinear exposure–response curve.

claims.text: For a given population with all other baselines held fixed, a marginal effect takes a small step near the working point—dividing incremental health burden by incremental intake to approximate the local tangent slope. An average effect spans the entire interval from the counterfactual reference to the working point, dividing the burden difference by the intake difference to form the secant slope connecting the two endpoints. Both slopes coincide on a straight line but diverge on a curve; sharing the unit DALY/kg inhaled PM₂.₅ never reveals which two endpoints were chosen.
claims.scope: Mathematical difference between a local marginal tangent slope at the working point and an average secant slope from the counterfactual to current exposure under fixed baselines.
caveats: This explains the ratio under compatible definitions without reproducing the mass-conversion typographical print verbatim; unresolved numerical discrepancies remain among the journal text, operational worksheet, and published summary.

claims.text: Consequently, if an exposure shift crosses a strongly curved interval, analysts cannot multiply the starting local slope all the way to the endpoint; nor does the average slope from counterfactual to current state automatically govern a transition from real scenario A to scenario B. Comparing A and B requires both the burden difference and the intake difference to match those two states. While Fantke et al. (2019) discuss attributional and consequential perspectives by study goal, perspective labels never substitute for explicit endpoint definitions. The local-versus-interval logic parallels that in acidification and nutrient enrichment, yet ecological targets and other references belong strictly within their own response systems.
claims.scope: Conditions for comparing finite exposure changes across curved intervals and distinguishing health counterfactuals from ecological response-system references.

claims.text: Understanding why the IER curve bends requires examining how its authors assembled exposure data from different sources. Burnett et al. (2014) placed ambient air pollution, household solid-fuel smoke, secondhand smoke, and active smoking within a single framework by converting exposures to a common inhaled-mass scale, assuming equal toxicity per unit inhaled mass and no interaction across exposure sources. At the high-concentration end, ambient-air cohort observations did not exist for every level; interpreting that segment therefore requires keeping in mind the scaling assumptions used to combine disparate exposure sources.
claims.scope: Equal-toxicity scaling assumptions used by Burnett et al. (2014) to combine ambient air, household solid-fuel smoke, and tobacco smoke in the IER model.

claims.text: The Global Exposure Mortality Model (GEMM) proposed by Burnett et al. (2018) instead relies exclusively on long-term outdoor-air cohorts, fitting a broader risk curve to nonaccidental mortality to estimate adult noncommunicable disease and lower respiratory infection burdens while also modeling five specific causes separately. Although GEMM reduces reliance on extrapolating outdoor risks from tobacco and household fuel smoke, it still requires evaluating counterfactuals, functional form, and sparse data at very high concentrations. Comparing GEMM with IER also involves overlapping cohorts, authors, and national exposure and mortality datasets; aligning covered health outcomes comes first, so wider disease coverage is not misread as higher risk per unit exposure.
claims.scope: Reliance on outdoor cohorts in Burnett et al.'s (2018) GEMM and dataset-overlap boundaries when comparing GEMM against IER.

claims.text: The Global Burden of Disease (GBD 2015) study underlying the UNEP/SETAC and EF nonlinear effect layer (Cohen et al. 2017, a 195-country assessment in The Lancet) illustrates the structural gap in age and cause coverage relative to adult-only cohorts. Combining satellite data, chemical transport modeling, and ground monitoring on a 0.1° grid with a 2.4–5.9 µg/m³ theoretical minimum risk reference, the study estimated 4.2411 million premature deaths globally attributable to ambient PM₂.₅ in 2015 (7.6% of all deaths) and roughly 103.07 million DALY—of which YLL accounted for 96.2% and years lived with disability (YLD) only 3.90 million. Among the five included causes, only lower respiratory infections (675,000 deaths) spanned all ages: children under age 5 alone accounted for 202,600 deaths and 17.4311 million DALY, or 16.9% of global PM₂.₅-attributable DALY. Because ReCiPe 2016 and LC-IMPACT use adult cohorts aged 30 and older, they zero out nearly one-sixth of global life-year losses occurring in young children. Meanwhile, the global age-standardized attributable mortality rate actually fell from 65.6 to 57.5 per 100,000 between 1990 and 2015; population growth and aging drove absolute deaths upward from 3.5 million to 4.2 million.
claims.scope: Five-cause breakdown, under-5 lower respiratory infection share, and 1990–2015 demographic-aging decomposition from Cohen et al. (2017) (GBD 2015), verified against the open-access Europe PMC full text (PMC5439030).
caveats: Original Tables 1–2 report point estimates and 95% uncertainty intervals in thousands of deaths and thousands of DALY (e.g., 4,241.1 thousand total deaths, 95% UI 3,698.0–4,776.7; 103,066.2 thousand total DALY, 95% UI 90,829.6–115,072.6); attributable totals depend heavily on cause-of-death registry quality and population age structure.

The 16.9% global DALY share for under-5 lower respiratory infections reflects high child mortality and large remaining life-expectancy weights in low- and lower-middle-income regions; cross-framework comparisons must align age and disease coverage first.

Additional GBD 2015 cause and country details: ischemic heart disease 1.5211 million deaths, cerebrovascular disease (stroke) 898,100 deaths (both attenuating with age from age 25), chronic obstructive pulmonary disease 863,600 deaths, and lung cancer 283,300 deaths; global population-weighted PM₂.₅ rose from 39.7 to 44.2 µg/m³ (+11.2%) over 1990–2015; in 2015, China (58.4 µg/m³) accounted for 1.1081 million deaths, India (74.3 µg/m³) for 1.0904 million, and the United States (8.4 µg/m³) for 88,400, while absolute attributable deaths still rose in Brazil, Russia, Indonesia, and Pakistan despite declining exposures.

claims.text: Three limitations explicitly noted by Cohen et al. (2017) define the empirical verification boundary for all of these models. First, like mainstream life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) methods, IER assumes equal toxicity per unit mass across all PM₂.₅ sources and compositions, without distinguishing sulfates, ammonium nitrate, traffic black carbon, and mineral dust. Second, large long-term outdoor cohorts were lacking in heavily polluted regions at the time, forcing the high-concentration curve to rely on secondhand smoke, household solid-fuel smoke, and active smoking—the direct motivation for introducing Chinese outdoor cohorts in GEMM (2018). Third, the model did not isolate mediated pathways via elevated systolic blood pressure or include low birth weight, preterm birth, asthma, or type 2 diabetes. Thus, whether using high-concentration-flattening IER, steeper sublinear GEMM, or log-linear cohort slopes, every curve rests on long-term residential exposure associations; no single-source engineering abatement quasi-experiment arbitrates which curve best captures real-world causal gains. Such background dependence appears not only on the health side, but also in the atmospheric chemistry governing secondary particle formation.
claims.scope: Empirical verification limits of IER, GEMM, and log-linear cohort slopes grounded in the stated limitations and printed equations of Cohen et al. (2017) (printed pp. 1909, 1916).
caveats: The printed IER equation on p. 1909 omits a minus sign in the exponential term; the immediately following statement that the high-concentration asymptote approaches 1 + α confirms the negative sign is required, and the typographical omission did not affect the actual GBD 2015 fitted curves.

The absence of prospective single-source causal arbitration does not question the human health hazard of fine particulate matter; rather, it clarifies that LCIA factors serve as conditionally consistent benchmarks of potential burden.

claims.text: Before health response even begins, secondary particle formation itself varies with atmospheric background conditions. Guo et al. (2018) constrained a thermodynamic inorganic aerosol equilibrium model with gas- and particle-phase observations at Cabauw in the Netherlands to test how precursor regimes alter gas–particle partitioning, while quantities such as particle acidity remained model-estimated. This asks how much inorganic ion mass stays in the particulate phase, not yet how much health damage those particles cause.
claims.scope: Scope of the gas–particle partitioning analysis in Guo et al. (2018) using Cabauw, Netherlands observations to constrain an inorganic aerosol thermodynamic equilibrium model.

claims.text: In the Cabauw annual-average and winter scenarios of Guo et al., holding all other inputs constant while lowering ambient total ammonia (NHₓ) produced weak responses in inorganic particulate ion mass concentration until reductions reached roughly 70%, whereas summer and northeastern US winter regimes behaved differently. That 70% threshold applies to total ambient NH₃ plus NH₄⁺ and cannot be rewritten as a rule that source NH₃ emissions must be cut by 70% before taking effect. It demonstrates that finite perturbations can cross distinct chemical regimes; extending a local sensitivity factor across a wide interval requires evidence matched to that gas–particle partitioning.
claims.scope: Nonlinear chemical operating-point limit in Guo et al. (2018), where ambient total ammonia (NHₓ) at Cabauw required roughly 70% reduction before inorganic particulate mass responded strongly.

claims.text: Before applying any factor, analysts must check whether it is formulated per unit emitted mass, inhaled mass, or ambient concentration. The outdoor scheme documented for the Global Consensus Life Cycle Impact Assessment Method (GLAM) of the UNEP Life Cycle Initiative first computes receptor-grid PM₂.₅ concentration changes per unit emission rate, multiplies by health-loss rates per unit concentration change, sums across receptors, and adds a simplified long-range fate term beyond 250 km paired with a global average effect to yield DALY/kg emitted. Inhaled mass need not appear explicitly as an intermediate variable; the quantity labeled EF here carries a different denominator than an EF per kilogram inhaled, so analysts must trace equations and units directly.
claims.scope: Equation structure in the UNEP GLAM outdoor framework combining gridded concentration increments and a simplified fate term beyond 250 km to derive DALY/kg emitted directly.

claims.text: Spatial averaging in regional factors also requires checking how the average is constructed. The GLAM outdoor scheme calculates impacts by source location and height, receptor, and background, then computes regional averages; its documented spatial mean is not weighted by population density or actual emission intensity. That spatial aggregation sits at a separate level from both the counterfactual-to-working-point average along a health curve and the source-height emission-share average in the historical example. Country, urban, or rural tags group the emission sources while receptors span wider areas; a single country label never reconstructs a specific smokestack or industry's emission profile.
claims.scope: Distinguishing spatial regional aggregation in the GLAM outdoor framework from the other two averaging operations in this chapter.
caveats: Spatial aggregation, health-response averaging, and source-height weighting do not become the same operation merely because all three use the word "average".

claims.text: Published release entries show that even the ordering between average and marginal factors within the same method can flip across scenarios. In the raw factor sheet of GLAM V1.0.2024.10 for Australian ground-level primary PM₂.₅, the average factor is lower than the marginal factor in the urban scenario but higher in the rural scenario. All four entries are already characterized damage factors and must not be multiplied again by the historical effect factor. This bounded check refutes any blanket rule that "average always exceeds marginal", while the table entries alone cannot attribute the reversal to a specific step among curve shape, background concentration, or spatial aggregation.
claims.scope: Qualitative ordering comparison across four named Australian ground-level primary PM₂.₅ entries in GLAM V1.0.2024.10.
caveats: This ordering applies solely to the specified release, substance, source height, country, and scenarios, without attributing the difference to an unverified internal generation step.

claims.text: Even after column headers are corrected, verifying how a published factor was computed remains a separate task. In Fantke et al. (2019), a formal erratum corrected the column labels for average and marginal effect factors (per kg inhaled PM₂.₅), yet unresolved discrepancies persist between the operational formulas, column documentation, and published city summaries in the revised supplementary workbook. Fixing a lookup label does not verify that the full computational chain has been reproduced. Citing published factors requires retaining exact version and scenario metadata, and explaining an operational model cannot rely on a single result column in place of its equations and inputs.
claims.scope: Distinguishing the formal column-label erratum in Fantke et al. (2019) from documented operational-versus-summary discrepancies in the revised workbook.
caveats: No claim is made here regarding the root cause of the discrepancy, which result should supersede the other, or full reproduction of the native generation code.

claims.text: Which factors are actually usable also depends on which worksheet in a release workbook is queried. In the GLAM particulate workbook, the raw factor sheet contains multiple outdoor slope variants and indoor primary-particle scenarios, whereas the software flow-matching sheet exports only outdoor average health-damage factors. Selecting a flow name, worksheet, and mapping therefore selects a subset of the method; capabilities described in a methodology paper cannot be assumed to exist in the factors loaded by LCA software.
claims.scope: Difference in usable scope between the multi-scenario raw factor sheet and the outdoor-average-only software flow-matching sheet in the GLAM particulate workbook.

claims.text: Australian ground-level PM₂.₅ entries illustrate the gap between those two sheets. On the raw sheet, Australian ground-level primary PM₂.₅ average factors differ between Urban and Rural scenarios; on the flow-matching sheet, however, both urban and non-urban ground-level "particles (PM2.5)" rows carry the exact same factor with the scenario field set to Unspecified. The category labels preserve an urban/non-urban distinction, yet the original numerical contrast is gone. Readers must inspect the exact matched row actually applied; this worksheet comparison neither deduces the underlying matching algorithm nor verifies any specific software execution.
claims.scope: Comparison of urban/rural differentiation on the raw sheet versus identical matched rows for Australian ground-level PM₂.₅ in the GLAM V1.0.2024.10 particulate workbook.
caveats: This observation is restricted to the cited worksheets and rows; it does not infer the generation algorithm, generalize to all mappings, or assert equivalence across software runs.

claims.text: Uncovered pathways must also be reported alongside results. PM₁₀ cannot simply be multiplied by a PM₂.₅ factor based on size proximity; GLAM recommends determining the PM₂.₅ mass fraction first and applying its named default fraction only when specific data are lacking—a methodological data-processing choice. Particles of differing chemical composition are still tallied by mass under a uniform mass-response relation, while selected secondary organic aerosol pathways and certain health outcomes remain excluded. Judging what a score covers requires separating these three treatments; when an inventory contains emissions without matching factors, the sum reflects only the characterized portion, and a missing factor never means zero impact.
claims.scope: GLAM boundaries covering default PM₂.₅ fractions for PM₁₀, equal-toxicity mass-response assumptions, and unmodeled secondary organic aerosols and health outcomes.

claims.text: Bringing aerosol chemistry and health response back into factor tables, inclusion switches for secondary inorganic precursors (SO₂, NH₃, and NOₓ) first determine which emissions are visible at all (Table 3). ReCiPe 2016 encodes evidence strength across three cultural perspectives: Individualist counts primary PM₂.₅ only and sets all three precursors to zero; the default Hierarchist adds only the most robust precursor, SO₂ (0.29 kg PM₂.₅ eq/kg), keeping NH₃ and NOₓ at zero; Egalitarian includes all three, ranking SO₂ (0.29) > NH₃ (0.24) > NOₓ (0.11) globally. Although LC-IMPACT shares the same TM5-FASST source–receptor model, it defines only two tiers: "certain effects" retains primary PM₂.₅ alone (6.29×10⁻⁴ DALY/kg) with no SO₂-only intermediate tier, while "all effects" adds all three precursors at once, preserving the global ranking SO₂ > NH₃ > NOₓ. Inventories rich in agricultural ammonia and combustion nitrogen oxides therefore score zero for secondary particulates under ReCiPe's default, yet show substantial contributions as soon as analysts switch to Egalitarian or LC-IMPACT all effects.
claims.scope: Comparing secondary-precursor inclusion switches and global weighted rankings across ReCiPe 2016's three perspectives (RIVM Report Tables 5.1–5.2 and 2017 paper) and LC-IMPACT's certain/all tiers (2020 paper Section 2.7/Table 3 and Overall Report Chapter 6 Sections 6.4.2 and 6.5 Table 6.2).
caveats: Setting NH₃ and NOₓ to zero in ReCiPe's Hierarchist perspective is a methodological evidence-tiering convention and does not imply that ammonium nitrate or ammonium sulfate aerosols fail to form in the atmosphere.

claims.text: In contrast to ReCiPe and LC-IMPACT global means ranking SO₂ above NH₃, EF 3.1 uses no perspective switch yet ranks ammonia above sulfur dioxide under generic and rural conditions (Table 3). In EF 3.1 unspecified air, NH₃ (2.1×10⁻⁵ cases/kg) is 2.625× SO₂ and 13.125× NOₓ; switching to the "non-urban/high stack" subcompartment drops SO₂ and NOₓ by roughly 87% (to 9.9×10⁻⁷ and 2.1×10⁻⁷) while NH₃ rises from 1.4×10⁻⁵ (urban close-to-ground) to 2.1×10⁻⁵—reaching 21.21× SO₂ and 100× NOₓ in that subcompartment. Driven by these factors, ammonia accounts for 23.16% of EF 3.1's global normalized burden (951,000 cases), roughly twice SO₂ (11.55%) and nine times NOₓ (2.52%). Comparing an abatement of 1 kg rural agricultural NH₃ (Option A) against 2 kg high-stack SO₂ (Option B), ReCiPe Hierarchist (0 vs 0.58) and Egalitarian global means (0.24 vs 0.58) both favor Option B, whereas EF 3.1 non-urban reverses the verdict, scoring Option A (2.1×10⁻⁵) 10.61× higher than Option B (1.98×10⁻⁶).
claims.scope: Recalculating EF 3.1 subcompartment precursor ratios, global normalization shares, and the cross-framework rank reversal between rural ammonia abatement and industrial desulfurization from the EF 3.1 particulate package and normalization workbook.
caveats: Options A and B represent a fixed-mass marginal abatement sensitivity test; actual product comparisons require complete multi-pollutant inventories under a shared functional unit.
Abating NH₃ and NOₓ simultaneously alters terrestrial acidification, ground-level ozone, and aquatic and terrestrial eutrophication indicators examined in Acidification and Nutrient Enrichment.

claims.text: Even within ReCiPe 2016's own 56-region TM5-FASST tables (Annex Tables S1.1–S1.2), atmospheric chemistry backgrounds and baseline mortality rates trigger three spatial reversals. First, although global means rank SO₂ above NH₃, ammonia-limited regions of Europe and East Asia push NH₃ midpoints 5× to 6.3× above SO₂ (Switzerland 1.70 vs 0.27; Benelux 1.04 vs 0.19; South Korea 1.59 vs 0.32), whereas ammonia-rich India reverses back to SO₂ (1.26) 4.85× above NH₃ (0.26)—explaining why Europe-calibrated EF 3.1 weights ammonia so heavily. Second, in New Zealand and the Pacific Islands, long-range gaseous SO₂ (midpoint 0.15) exceeds rapidly depositing primary PM₂.₅ (0.02) by 7.5× at midpoint and by 9.1× to 11.7× at regional endpoint. Third, because baseline cardiopulmonary mortality varies nearly fourfold across regions, South Korea's primary PM₂.₅ midpoint (2.15) is 1.65× Romania's (1.30), yet at the regional endpoint (yr/kton, numerically equal to 10⁻⁶ DALY/kg), Romania (1.7×10³) overtakes South Korea (7.0×10²) by 2.43×. At national scale, a single global midpoint-to-endpoint constant no longer preserves ranking.
claims.scope: Three spatial reversals verified from RIVM 2016-0104 Annex Tables S1.1–S1.2 (printed pp. 121–124): Europe/East Asia vs India NH₃/SO₂ flip, island secondary-over-primary inversion, and South Korea vs Romania midpoint-to-endpoint reversal.
caveats: Table S1.2 prints endpoint units as yr/kton (years of life lost per kiloton emitted, numerically equal to 10⁻⁶ DALY/kg); comparing with DALY/kg tables requires verifying the 10⁶ scaling factor.

These regional reversals reflect year-2000 emission backgrounds and historical national mortality baselines and cannot be extrapolated as fixed elasticities after deep future desulfurization, denitrification, or demographic shifts.

Island regional endpoint details (yr/kton): New Zealand SO₂ = 1.1×10² vs primary PM₂.₅ = 9.4 (11.7×); Pacific Islands (including Papua New Guinea) SO₂ = 1.0×10² vs primary PM₂.₅ = 1.1×10¹ (9.1×). Similarly, Chile (midpoint 1.92, endpoint 6.6×10² yr/kton) reverses against Ukraine–Belarus–Moldova (midpoint 0.84, endpoint 1.3×10³ yr/kton).

claims.text: Auditing software tables against official packages also requires recognizing several structural quirks and intra-source discrepancies. First, beyond its 83 locationless flows, the EF 3.1 particulate matter package expands 25 nitrogen and sulfur precursor flows across 36 European codes into 900 location rows whose values are 100% identical to the locationless generic rows—preventing unmatched country-tagged flows rather than performing country-level source–receptor modeling. Second, the high-altitude subcompartment assigns zero to primary PM₂.₅, SO₂, and NH₃, while retaining 2.1×10⁻⁷ uniquely for NOₓ, NO₂, and NO; meanwhile, the global normalization workbook assigns 52.1% of global airborne ammonia mass to the lower-factor "urban close-to-ground" bin (1.4×10⁻⁵). Third, printed equations and tables in RIVM (Dutch National Institute for Public Health and the Environment) Report 2016-0104 (p. 50 and Table 5.3), JRC130796 (Table 10 sign and Table 13 duplicated column), and XML header metadata all contain documented intra-source anomalies (detailed in the caveats). Aligning indicator cutpoints, particle size and emission height, population age scope, precursor switches, and regional baselines prepares analysts to diagnose why results diverge across studies.
claims.scope: Structural package details and intra-source discrepancies across the EU EF 3.1 particulate package and normalization workbook, RIVM 2016-0104 (printed pp. 50, 123–124), LC-IMPACT Overall Report (printed p. 67), and JRC130796 (printed pp. 21–22, 30).
caveats: The EU EF 3.1 particulate matter XML metadata also misspells exposure–response as "Emission Response Function (ERF)", reports 50 inventory items under completeness (fewer than the actual 83 elementary flows and 983 factor rows), and points its permanent Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) to a different identifier (72ce3013); header audits must recognize these fields verbatim.

Documenting intra-source anomalies preserves audit reproducibility against original releases and does not authorize modifying standard factor packages or official normalization constants without upstream errata.

Detailed intra-source anomaly log: (1) EF 3.1's 36 European codes include the retired Serbia and Montenegro code CS, while 48 primary-particle flows and 10 NO/SO₃ flows carry no location rows; high-altitude NOₓ contributes 599.69 cases in the global normalization inventory; (2) RIVM 2016-0104 p. 50 misprints the numerator of the global primary PM₂.₅ midpoint-to-endpoint weighting equation as NOₓ emissions, and Table 5.3 omits "6.29×" in the Egalitarian column leaving only bold "10⁻⁴"; Annex Table S1.2's global mean SO₂ (183.2 yr/kton) matches LC-IMPACT Table 6.2 (1.83×10⁻⁴ DALY/kg), whereas NH₃ (149.2) and NOₓ (70.1) sit slightly below LC-IMPACT's 1.61×10⁻⁴ and 7.62×10⁻⁵; (3) JRC130796 text describes the particulate normalization-reference change as a "0.003% decrease", Table 10 prints positive "0.0034%", and Table 13 repeats 608 across two columns.

claims.text: Once a single framework is chosen, multiplying each characterization factor—whether in kg PM₂.₅ eq/kg, disease incidence/kg, or DALY/kg emitted—by its matching inventory emission and summing across covered primary particles and gaseous precursors estimates the potential health burden captured at that cutpoint and reveals each emission's relative contribution. Even when expressed as disease incidence or DALY, the result neither identifies any specific affected individual nor guarantees that the exact same count of cases or lost life-years occurs in reality. Estimating actual burden in a specific locality requires local exposure distributions, population age structures, disease baselines, counterfactual references, and time horizons; historical default tables cannot simply be relabeled as site-specific measurements.
claims.scope: Interpretive boundaries for population-level statistical burden estimates formed by multiplying and summing particulate characterization factors across three cutpoints, and requirements for site-specific burden assessment.

claims.text: Particulate matter characterization translates emitted mass into estimated potential population health burden at a chosen causal cutpoint. When results differ, analysts can trace the gap along five links of the causal chain: indicator cutpoints and precursor switches, emission-height and air-subcompartment distributions, population exposure and age baselines, nonlinear exposure–response curves, and the exact flow-matching sheet and package version applied. Comparing two products delivering the same service therefore requires specifying that shared service first and then verifying particle-size and precursor coverage, receptor scope, health outcomes, marginal versus average references, and release-package versions before interpreting modeled health burdens or emission contributions. Asking how much health gain a specific abatement delivers—and to whom—still requires explicit change scenarios and prospective causal evidence. The next chapter turns to water consumption, examining how water withdrawal, consumption, and watershed availability reshape scarcity potentials and damage judgments.
claims.scope: Five-dimension causal-chain comparison checklist for particulate characterization factors, boundaries on abatement-policy extrapolation, and transition to water consumption.

claims.text: An inventory entry stating "3 m³ of water consumption" specifies a volume, but it does not yet establish water scarcity potential. Which watershed supplies the water, whether and when it returns, what hydrological background the characterization factors represent, and what reference baseline the equivalent unit expresses all determine what question the final score can answer. The Available WAter REmaining (AWARE) model draws on local water availability to evaluate the potential for a given volume of consumption to deprive other human or ecosystem users of water. A worked two-location calculation will show why identical volumes of water consumption can yield markedly different indicator scores.
claims.scope: Structuring the explanation from water volume to scarcity indicator using AWARE's named definition and characterization relationship.

claims.text: The first distinction separates water withdrawal from water consumption. In the 2018 AWARE paper, withdrawal records water entering the product system, whereas consumption records the portion no longer available to users in the original watershed—for example, through evapotranspiration, incorporation into a product, or discharge to another watershed or the ocean. Water withdrawn and returned to the same watershed cannot all be counted as consumption, although the paper cautions that localized impacts may still occur between the withdrawal and return points. Interpreting any cubic-meter total therefore requires knowing where water originates and where it returns; an aggregate volume alone conceals those flows.
claims.scope: Water withdrawal, consumption, and original-watershed users as defined in §3.2 of the 2018 AWARE paper.
caveats: These definitions are attributed to the named paper rather than substituting for original ISO standard clauses.

claims.text: AWARE frames a narrow, explicit analytical question: what is the potential to deprive another human or ecosystem user when consuming freshwater at this location? The original paper characterizes it as a proxy midpoint indicator. It does not directly estimate endpoint damages to human health or ecosystem quality, nor does it account for impacts from water-quality degradation. An AWARE score therefore expresses potential along a specific quantity-deprivation pathway and cannot stand in for all water-related impacts.
claims.scope: The quantity-focused proxy midpoint question defined in the 2018 AWARE paper.

claims.text: To distinguish hydrological contexts, AWARE evaluates remaining water availability per unit area and time after human and aquatic ecosystem demands are met. Within the uncapped range before model cutoffs apply, less remaining availability relative to the reference produces a larger characterization factor, allowing the same 1 m³ of consumption to generate different scarcity potentials depending on where it occurs. The model links consumption to its hydrological background, but it does not convert that volume into observed ecological damage; ecological water requirements and underlying hydrological datasets also carry their own modeling assumptions.
claims.scope: The positive Availability Minus Demand (AMD), uncapped characterization interval in the 2018 AWARE paper.

claims.text: Before computing remaining availability, one must check whether the input flow already deducts human water use. The 2025 AWARE 2.0 paper defines ActAvail as actual water available after human intervention—already incorporating human water consumption and water management—and then subtracts environmental water requirements (EWR) and divides by watershed area to obtain Availability Minus Demand (AMD) per unit area. Reviewing the 2018 method, the same paper notes that ActAvail was implemented using actual discharge at watershed outlets, which likewise already reflects upstream human activity. In this formulation, "available water" is not pristine runoff untouched by human use.
claims.scope: Input variable and AMD definitions in §1.1 of the AWARE 2.0 (2025) paper, without replicating all hydrological implementations.
caveats: This review passage should not be generalized to every AWARE 2.0 watershed implementation; endorheic basins use separate approximations.

claims.text: A simple algebraic ledger clarifies how double counting arises. Let A_0 denote water availability prior to deducting human consumption H, so post-deduction availability is A_1 = A_0 − H. Then A_0 − H − EWR equals A_1 − EWR, whereas writing A_1 − H − EWR deducts H twice. This identity isolates the relationship between pre- and post-deduction quantities; how regulated flows, upstream processes, and other hydrological interventions shape actual water availability must still be verified from the underlying model and data documentation.
claims.scope: Explaining double counting through an explicitly assumed simplified water ledger, without evaluating or replicating official 2018/2025 implementations.
caveats: The A_0, A_1, and H illustration assumes a single watershed, time period, and accounting basis; it does not claim that official implementations actually double-count.

claims.text: Placing AWARE (Boulay et al. 2018; updated in 2025 as AWARE 2.0) in methodological history shows that building a proxy midpoint from remaining water is only one of three structural routes (Table 1). The first route embeds scarcity at the midpoint with no endpoint layer: the 2011 International Reference Life Cycle Data System (ILCD) Handbook rejected simple withdrawal summation (Methodology for Ecodesign of Energy-using Products, MEEuP) and scarcity-free Cumulative Exergy Extraction from the Natural Environment (CEENE, where exergy measures thermodynamically available energy), recommending instead the 6-class Swiss ecological scarcity method (Level III); the EU Environmental Footprint (EF 2.0 through EF 3.1) retained this single-level structure while adopting AWARE (capped at 0.1–100). The second route restricts the midpoint to consumptive volume and defers scarcity to endpoints: ReCiPe 2016 assigns a uniform Water Consumption Potential (WCP) of 1 m³/m³ to net blue-water consumption, then models malnutrition health, terrestrial plants, and estuarine freshwater fish at the endpoint level. The third route bypasses midpoints to quantify global damage directly: LC-IMPACT (Verones et al. 2020) publishes damage-level health factors across 11,050 watersheds and wetland species-extinction risk factors on a 0.05° grid. Before reading any water indicator, one must check whether it stops at volume, a scarcity proxy, or endpoint damage.
claims.scope: Structural comparison of four major life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) frameworks (ILCD 2011, EF 2.0/3.0/3.1, ReCiPe 2016, LC-IMPACT) and where each places regional scarcity and socio-ecological vulnerability along the cause-effect chain.
caveats: Although ReCiPe 2016 WCP (no scarcity weighting at midpoint) and EF 3.1 AWARE (scarcity-weighted proxy) are both loosely referred to as "water footprint" or "water use midpoint" indicators, the former measures only freshwater volume lost from the original watershed while the latter measures user deprivation potential relative to a world reference; their values and rankings are not interchangeable.

The LC-IMPACT wetland ecological endpoint assigns 50% weight each to vascular plants and animals, multiplied by International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List threat status and range-size vulnerability factors, expressed as global irreversible potentially disappeared fraction of species (PDF·yr/m³).

claims.text: Before any regional scarcity weight is applied, the ledger rules converting withdrawals and return flows into net consumption can alter effective water consumption by an order of magnitude. The official EF 3.1 water-use method file (2,310 lines: 11 water-related elementary flows across 210 geographic entries) relies on same-country algebraic cancellation: 7 withdrawal flows carry +c and 4 return flows to freshwater or unspecified water bodies carry −c (green water, rainwater, seawater, fossil water, and discharges to seawater are excluded, effectively scoring 0), treating groundwater extraction and surface-water discharge within the same country as nettable from a single reservoir. ReCiPe 2016 (RIVM Report 2016-0104, Table 10.2) instead sets withdrawal-to-consumption conversion ratios by water source and sector: agricultural irrigation defaults to 0.44 (national range 0.16–0.70), and industrial or domestic surface-water withdrawals use 0.1 (reflecting 90%–95% return flow); industrial and domestic groundwater withdrawals, however, receive a ratio of 1 because return flows normally discharge to surface rivers rather than the source aquifer and cannot be deducted without artificial recharge. Thus, a plant withdrawing 10 m³ of groundwater and discharging 9 m³ of compliant effluent to a surface river in the same country registers 1 m³ of net consumption in EF 3.1 but 10 m³ in ReCiPe 2016—a 10:1 divergence before multiplying by any regional factor.
claims.scope: The 10-fold quantitative divergence between EF 3.1's 7-positive/4-negative algebraic flow cancellation in official XML and ReCiPe 2016's source- and sector-specific withdrawal-to-consumption conversion ratios.
caveats: This 10:1 divergence arises when raw inventories report groundwater withdrawal and surface return separately (or report only industrial groundwater withdrawal using Table 10.2 defaults); where hydrological evidence confirms artificial recharge into the same aquifer and the inventory is modeled on a net-consumption basis, practitioners should explicitly depart from Table 10.2 defaults.

EF 3.1's 7 positive withdrawal flows are freshwater, groundwater, lake water, river water, cooling water, turbine water, and unspecified water; its 4 negative return flows are unspecified freshwater discharge, cooling return, turbine return, and unspecified water-body discharge. ReCiPe 2016's agricultural irrigation ratio of 0.44 carries a standard deviation of 0.14.

claims.text: Monthly factors in characterization tables also carry specific historical data baselines. The 2018 AWARE paper derived water availability from 1960–2010 climate records and represented human water consumption using 2010 data. The 2025 AWARE 2.0 update shifted the reference period for actual water availability to 1990–2019 and adopted 2019 human consumption, while retaining the 1960–2010 naturalized hydrology baseline for environmental water requirements. Consequently, a monthly factor captures seasonal variation without necessarily reflecting hydrological conditions during the exact year of a product inventory. Publication year, hydrological reference period, and inventory year must be read as three distinct dates.
claims.scope: Hydrological and consumption reference periods reported in the 2018 and 2025 AWARE papers and their distinction from inventory timing.
caveats: This records the input baselines stated in the papers and does not verify the data chain of arbitrary subsequent factor release packages.

claims.text: During characterization, each watershed-month consumption flow is multiplied by its matching factor to yield results in m³ world-eq. Here, world-eq. denotes a relative indicator scale anchored to a reference baseline—not an additional physical volume withdrawn, a count of water-deprived people, or a measure of species loss. Because averaging remaining water first and then taking its reciprocal differs mathematically from averaging characterization factors directly, an unknown location cannot be assigned a factor of 1 merely because the unit says "world-eq." The two-row worked example below demonstrates that arithmetic distinction.
claims.scope: Relative scale of m³ world-eq. and averaging order in the named AWARE method.

claims.text: When an inventory lacks watershed or monthly resolution and provides only national annual totals, coarser aggregated factors bridge the gap. The agricultural and non-agricultural aggregations in the 2018 AWARE paper reflect the spatiotemporal distribution of water consumption within each sector rather than separate local laws of hydrology. While such aggregations make use of available background data, they cannot reconstruct lost watershed or seasonal detail; whenever an inventory already specifies watershed and month, that resolution should be preserved through characterization.
claims.scope: Local watershed-month resolution versus agricultural and non-agricultural aggregations in the 2018 AWARE paper.
caveats: Sector-aggregated factors must not be interpreted as distinct local hydrological laws for each industry.

claims.text: Two distinct water-consumption quantities operate simultaneously in this calculation: background consumption, which characterizes existing water use in a watershed to generate the characterization factors, and product-inventory consumption, which is the flow being evaluated. Standard AWARE factors rest on a marginal applicability condition—namely, that the product inventory is small enough not to alter local water availability significantly, so the given background remains valid. If an activity is large enough to shift the hydrological background, linear extrapolation with existing factors no longer holds, and any change to the background requires documenting the revised model conditions.
claims.scope: Marginal applicability condition and the separation of background and product-inventory consumption in §1.1 of the 2025 AWARE 2.0 paper.
caveats: No universal percentage threshold is specified here, nor is a non-marginal characterization method implemented.

claims.text: This also bounds what "marginal" means in water scarcity assessment. In *Acidification and Nutrient Enrichment*, a marginal effect factor represents the slope of an ecological response curve at a given operating point; here, the marginal applicability condition states that the product inventory does not significantly alter local water availability. Although both concepts address small perturbations around a background state, they do not share the same response model, and satisfying the inventory-scale condition here does not specify the target or operating point of an ecological response curve.
claims.scope: Contextual contrast between AWARE's inventory-scale marginal condition and UNEP (2019) ecological marginal effect factors.
caveats: This contrast does not rule out mathematical links between the two usages; it prevents inferring identical model layers or calculation rules from a shared term.

claims.text: Default spatiotemporal settings and domain cutoffs can both flatten geographic structure and zero out endpoints for entire regions (Table 2). Although AWARE offers seven spatiotemporal and sectoral resolutions (including watershed-by-month and agricultural versus non-agricultural), JRC109369 prescribes national annual unspecified-use factors as the default for EU Product and Organization Environmental Footprint (PEF/OEF) studies. EF 3.1 country factors span three orders of magnitude—Aruba 100, Egypt 98.4, Spain 77.7, China 42.4, the United States 33.8, and India 29.4 (global default 42.950), down to Brazil 2.17, Germany 1.36, Switzerland 1.34, and Norway 0.634 m³ world-eq./m³—while the global per-capita normalization reference remains 1.15×10⁴ m³ world-eq./person. In ReCiPe 2016, by contrast, the Pfister et al. (2009) Water Stress Index (WSI, bounded on 0.01–1) adjusts dry-season stress using a 1961–1990 precipitation variation factor; the human development factor (HDF) governing health vulnerability is fitted to the 2001 Human Development Index (HDI) and forces HDF = 0 whenever HDI > 0.88; and the freshwater fish endpoint excludes all watersheds outside 42° N–42° S latitude. Consequently, water consumption in Nordic countries or Canada yields positive scores in EF 3.1 but zero for both human health and freshwater fish endpoints in ReCiPe 2016.
claims.scope: Spatiotemporal mismatch between PEF/OEF national annual unstratified defaults and ReCiPe 2016's cross-era hydrological baselines, HDI > 0.88 socioeconomic cutoff, and 42° latitude biogeographic cutoff.
caveats: Setting malnutrition health damage to zero for countries with HDI > 0.88 and excluding freshwater fish outside 42° latitude represent domain cutoffs of specific ReCiPe 2016 endpoint equations, not evidence that water consumption in high-income or high-latitude regions has no aquatic ecological or water-supply cost impacts.

Water use ranks first in the EF 3.1 single overall score in 121 of 2,752 official datasets (versus 125 in EF 3.0; 0% rounded change). ReCiPe 2016 specifics: WSI multiplies strongly flow-regulated watersheds by √VF and non-strongly regulated watersheds by VF (Table 10.1 marks Individualist as "high" regulation without printing the De Schryver et al. 2011 sub-equation; Table 10.3 reports 2010 consumption-weighted global WSI of 0.698 for Individualist and 0.657 for Hierarchist/Egalitarian); HDF equals 1 for HDI < 0.30 and declines quadratically over 0.30–0.88; terrestrial vascular plants combine Nemani et al. (2003, 1982–1999 net primary productivity, NPP) with terrestrial species density 1.48×10⁻⁸ species/m², while freshwater fish use aquatic species density 7.89×10⁻¹⁰ species/m³.

claims.text: Even more revealing is how the algebraic position of a value choice reverses cultural-perspective ordering (Table 2). In climate, ozone, radiation, and toxicity categories, ReCiPe 2016 Individualist (I) damage factors are typically no higher than Hierarchist (H) and Egalitarian (E) factors; for water-consumption human health, however, the Individualist global mean reaches 3.10×10⁻⁶ disability-adjusted life years (DALY)/m³, roughly 40% higher than the Hierarchist and Egalitarian mean of 2.22×10⁻⁶ DALY/m³. The cause lies in the denominator of the effect factor: the model estimates displaced irrigation water as WSI times the agricultural withdrawal share, then multiplies the health effect factor HDF / WR_malnutrition (yr·person/m³) by per-capita malnutrition damage of 3.68×10⁻² DALY/(yr·person). Assuming more efficient agricultural water use, the Individualist perspective lowers the minimum annual dietary water requirement per person (WR_malnutrition) from 1,350 to 1,000 m³/(yr·person). Because WR_malnutrition sits in the denominator, displacing 1 m³ of irrigation water affects 1.35 times as many person-years, which—together with a slightly higher WSI (0.698 versus 0.657)—pushes the Individualist health factor upward. Ecological endpoints move in the opposite direction: Individualist zeroes terrestrial ecosystems due to weak correlation in high-diversity watersheds, LC-IMPACT's certainty set excludes groundwater-dependent wetlands, and freshwater fish factors are identical across all three perspectives while remaining about four orders of magnitude smaller.
claims.scope: The counterintuitive I > H = E ordering (3.10×10⁻⁶ vs. 2.22×10⁻⁶ DALY/m³) in ReCiPe 2016 water-consumption human health caused by placing per-capita dietary water requirement WR_malnutrition in the denominator, alongside opposing value-choice shifts in terrestrial, wetland, and aquatic endpoints.
caveats: Because Individualist raises the human-health factor while zeroing terrestrial ecosystems, switching cultural perspectives in single-score weighting simultaneously alters the internal health-versus-ecosystem share of water impacts and cross-country rankings.

ReCiPe 2016's terrestrial-ecosystem cutoff excludes high-diversity watersheds exceeding 2,000 species per 10,000 km² (Hierarchist and Egalitarian mean 1.35×10⁻⁸ species·yr/m³); for freshwater fish (Table 10.6), the global watershed median is 6.04×10⁻¹³ and the country area-weighted mean is 1.74×10⁻¹² species·yr/m³.

claims.text: Computing a product's water scarcity potential requires summing consumptive contributions across all watersheds in its supply chain. Water Use in Life Cycle Assessment (WULCA) application guidance illustrates how water consumption at each stage is first scaled to a single product reference and then multiplied by its matching spatiotemporal factor, ensuring upstream raw-material stages are included alongside on-site operations. A single factor at the manufacturing site therefore cannot substitute for upstream locations. The tomato-juice demonstration in that guidance explicitly uses AWARE 1.2 to illustrate this accounting structure; its numerical values do not automatically carry over to other products or method versions.
claims.scope: Product-reference scaling and supply-chain aggregation in WULCA's AWARE 1.2 application guidance.
caveats: Actual characterization factors and tomato-juice data from the demonstration graphic are not adopted here.

claims.text: A completely hypothetical dataset makes this relationship concrete. Suppose two non-overlapping inventory contributions have both been scaled to delivering 1 kg of a specified product: on-site operations in watershed X during month M withdraw 10 m³ and return 8 m³ to the same watershed in the same period, while upstream material production in watershed Y during month N withdraws 4 m³ and returns 3 m³ in the same period. Under these closed assumptions, water consumption equals 2 m³/kg product on-site and 1 m³/kg product upstream. No inter-basin transfers, storage changes, or unspecified return flows occur; X, Y, M, N, and all volumes are illustrative labels and assumptions, and omitted supply-chain contributions are not assumed to be zero.
claims.scope: Two hypothetical, non-overlapping water-consumption contributions sharing a 1 kg product reference.
caveats: This example illustrates calculation structure rather than a complete functional unit or full life cycle inventory of a real product.

claims.text: Assign these two hypothetical contexts characterization factors of 2 and 8 m³ world-eq./m³ under a single fixed background. Both can be written in the uncapped ratio form of the 2018 AWARE paper: given an externally fixed positive reference r, setting AMD_X = r/2 and AMD_Y = r/8 yields r/AMD_X = 2 and r/AMD_Y = 8, keeping both well inside the uncapped bounds. Here r is not recomputed as a world average from these two product rows, nor are the two AMD values real hydrological measurements; the construction simply keeps the numbers consistent with the proportional relationship being illustrated.
claims.scope: Hypothetical positive AMD ratios under a fixed external reference r, without reconstructing real watershed factors.

claims.text: Characterizing each row separately yields an on-site contribution of 2 × 2 = 4 m³ world-eq./kg product and an upstream contribution of 1 × 8 = 8 m³ world-eq./kg product, for a total of 12 m³ world-eq./kg product, while total physical water consumption remains 2 + 1 = 3 m³/kg product. The smaller upstream volume generates the larger indicator contribution because the two flows face different scarcity contexts. The figures 3 and 12 answer different questions: the 12 m³ world-eq./kg product must not be misread as 12 m³ physically withdrawn, an observed count of water-deprived people, or an estimated ecological loss.
claims.scope: Row-by-row characterization and summation of the two hypothetical inventory rows using their respective fixed factors.

claims.text: Changing only the on-site characterization factor from 2 to 8—while holding both consumptive volumes fixed at 2 and 1 m³/kg—doubles the indicator score to 2 × 8 + 1 × 8 = 24 m³ world-eq./kg. This single-parameter sensitivity check demonstrates that identical physical volumes do not determine identical scarcity potentials. It does not establish that relocating a real factory would alter only this factor, nor does it justify siting recommendations; what else changes during an actual relocation requires separate empirical evidence.
claims.scope: Sensitivity contrast varying a single hypothetical context factor while holding consumptive volumes and product reference fixed.

claims.text: Returning to the original factors (2 and 8) with the same hypothetical inputs exposes the effect of averaging order. With external reference r fixed, AMD_X = r/2 and AMD_Y = r/8 carry consumption weights of 2/3 and 1/3. Computing the consumption-weighted average AMD first gives 3r/8; taking the relative reciprocal produces a factor of 8/3, which multiplied by total consumption of 3 yields 8—whereas row-by-row characterization followed by summation yields 2 × 2 + 1 × 8 = 12. The discrepancy stems from the nonlinear reciprocal step: the factor of an average remaining availability is not equal to the average of the characterization factors. These weights describe only the two inventory rows here; they do not redefine the world reference or constitute national aggregation factors.
claims.scope: Order of reciprocal transformation and consumption-weighted averaging in the uncapped positive two-row example.
caveats: This contrast does not invalidate aggregation approximations used for their stated purpose; it shows that such an approximation cannot substitute for row-by-row characterization when locations are known.

claims.text: The same known inventory can nevertheless be summarized by an average factor that reproduces the exact total. Weighting the two established characterization factors directly by consumption yields (2/3) × 2 + (1/3) × 8 = 4 m³ world-eq./m³; multiplying by total consumption of 3 m³/kg product recovers 12 m³ world-eq./kg product. That value of 4 summarizes only these two rows and their specific weights—it cannot serve as a national or global default, and valid aggregation can compress known contributions without ever recovering missing watershed or monthly data.
claims.scope: Consumption-weighted average characterization factor and exact total reconstruction for the two-row inventory example.
caveats: Weights from this two-row product inventory do not replace agricultural, non-agricultural, or geographic aggregation conventions in published factor sets.

claims.text: Moving from hypothetical arithmetic to real national factor tables for 1 m³ of blue-water consumption in EF 3.1 and ReCiPe 2016 (Table 3, restricted to countries with English initials A–C to avoid the corrupted section of Table S6.2 noted below) reveals multiple cross-country rank reversals. Comparing arid, high-income Australia with humid, low-income Bangladesh: ReCiPe midpoint assigns 1 m³ to both; EF 3.1 AWARE (72.1 versus 2.43, ~29.7×) and ReCiPe terrestrial ecosystems (~15.3×) both rank Australia higher; at the human-health endpoint, however, high-HDI Australia triggers the cutoff and retains only a 10⁻¹⁸-order residual while Bangladesh reaches 1.95×10⁻⁶ DALY/m³—flipping the ranking by more than eleven orders of magnitude—and freshwater fish also reverses slightly toward Bangladesh. Comparing Chile with China: EF 3.1 AWARE (80.1 versus 42.4) and physical WSI (0.773 versus 0.539) both rank Chile higher, yet all three ReCiPe endpoints consistently reverse to rank China higher; converting 10 m³ of irrigation withdrawal via Table S6.1 ratios (0.2 for Chile versus 0.36 for China) even reverses midpoint consumption to China higher. Which country shows the larger water impact depends on whether one asks about remaining water depth, vegetation productivity, or food-security vulnerability.
claims.scope: Multiple rank reversals for 1 m³ of blue-water consumption across real national factor tables (Australia vs. Bangladesh; Chile vs. China) between EF 3.1 AWARE midpoint and ReCiPe 2016 endpoints.
caveats: National-scale factors reflect consumption- or area-weighted domestic averages; for facilities or farms in hyper-arid northern Chile, humid coastal Australia, or the North China Plain groundwater depression cone, national averages cannot replace watershed-by-month site characterization.

RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table S6.3 prints species-eq·yr/m³ in its header, synonymous with species·yr/m³ in the main text. Under the Individualist perspective, human-health factors are 6.69×10⁻¹⁶ vs. 2.69×10⁻⁶ DALY/m³ (Australia vs. Bangladesh) and 1.07×10⁻⁶ vs. 4.08×10⁻⁷ DALY/m³ (China vs. Chile), while terrestrial ecosystems are 0 for all.

claims.text: Even when stripped back to pure physical hydrology with no population or species parameters, cross-country rankings still invert (Table 3). On ReCiPe 2016's physical WSI, densely populated, industrialized Belgium (0.686; Individualist 0.900) scores roughly 6.29 times higher than Canada (0.109; Individualist 0.181); on EF 3.1's national AWARE factor, however, Canada (7.40 m³ world-eq./m³) scores roughly 5.40 times higher than Belgium (1.37). The reversal reflects different physical independent variables compounded by nonlinear aggregation: WSI feeds the dimensionless ratio of total withdrawals to available water (∑WU/WA) into a logistic curve, so Belgium's heavy industrial and cooling withdrawals inflate WSI even when most water returns to surface rivers; AWARE deducts net consumption to compute remaining water per unit area (AMD) and takes the relative reciprocal (r/AMD), so humid Belgium retains ample post-return availability while Canada's net consumption concentrates in semi-arid prairie watersheds whose high local reciprocals pull the consumption-weighted national default above Belgium by more than fivefold. What share of runoff is withdrawn and how much water remains per unit area where consumption occurs are fundamentally different hydrological questions.
claims.scope: Physical hydrological mechanism driving opposite Belgium–Canada rankings between WSI (withdrawal-to-availability ratio ∑WU/WA) and AWARE (consumption-weighted reciprocal remaining water per unit area r/AMD) even without socioeconomic or species parameters.
caveats: WSI builds stress from total withdrawal before multiplying consumption, whereas AWARE deducts net consumption and normalizes by watershed area; the divergence is sharpest in industrial regions dominated by once-through cooling.

At the ReCiPe 2016 endpoint level, Belgium and Canada (both north of 42° N and above HDI 0.88) score 0 for human health and freshwater fish, leaving only terrestrial ecosystems (Hierarchist/Egalitarian: Belgium 2.14×10⁻⁹ vs. Canada 1.27×10⁻⁹ species·yr/m³).

claims.text: Interpreting an applied study also requires pinning the method name to its exact version and factor file. Although the 2025 AWARE 2.0 release updates hydrological inputs and several computational steps, it continues to restrict regular factors to small-scale inventories that do not significantly alter local water availability, and retains explicit limitations regarding non-renewable water stocks, inter-basin transfers, and model uncertainty. Inventory locations and timing, the exact characterization factors applied, and unrepresented impact pathways should always be reported alongside the calculated results.
claims.scope: Updates, marginal applicability conditions, and non-renewable stock and inter-basin transfer limitations reported in the 2025 AWARE 2.0 paper.
caveats: Actual geographic factor packages, non-marginal models, and uncertainty distributions are not selected or verified here; shared author or institutional lineage does not constitute independent empirical replication.

claims.text: Extending version verification into machine-readable release packages and report appendices uncovers two source-internal defects that cannot be smoothed away by intuition. First, in the official EF 3.1 water-use method file (1,268,239 bytes, version still stamped 03.00.014), withdrawal and return magnitudes match exactly across all 209 country codes, yet the unspecified-country default assigns +42.950 to all 7 withdrawals, −42.95 to the 3 freshwater returns, and −42.955 to the "unspecified water body" return—generating a spurious −0.005 m³ world-eq. net credit from withdrawing and returning 1 m³ without a country code; the same file assigns 0.00 to Greenland (GL), below the 0.1 lower cutoff. Second, and far more severe, RIVM Report 2016-0104 Appendix Table S6.2 (pp. 166–169, listed alphabetically A–Z) obeys WSI ∈ [0.01, 1] and HDI > 0.88 zeroing through row 52, but from row 53 (Fiji) through Zimbabwe—the entire F–Z block spanning more than 100 countries—severe row-and-column misalignment corrupts the table, printing out-of-range WSI values such as 34.7 and 7.28×10⁴ while assigning positive malnutrition damage to high-HDI countries like Sweden and the United States. Additional unit and text-versus-appendix discrepancies are logged in the accompanying caveats; appendix tables must never be transcribed without range verification.
claims.scope: Five groups of page- and byte-verified source-internal discrepancies and typesetting corruptions across EF-v3.1.zip water XML, JRC reports, RIVM Report 2016-0104 text and Table S6.2, and the LC-IMPACT paper.
caveats: Printed figures in RIVM Report 2016-0104 Table S6.2 pp. 167–169 from row 53 (Fiji) through Zimbabwe (alphabetical F–Z block) are typesetting-corrupted artifacts and must never be cited or used as real ReCiPe 2016 national parameters; studies requiring F–Z countries must verify the uncorrupted original spreadsheet against WSI ∈ [0.01, 1] and HDI > 0.88 zeroing.

Complete five-group audit log: (1) EF 3.1 water XML (1,268,239 bytes, v03.00.014, source record citing "Boulay et al. 2016 submitted manuscript"): the unspecified-water-body return flow XML writes integer "1" for mean volume (the other 10 write "1.0"), Greenland (GL) is 0.00 across all 11 flows, the completeness field claims 36 items versus 11 actual, and the English description contains a missing space; (2) unit and flow-property drift: JRC109369 Table 1 misprints "kg world eq. deprived" and Table 2 prints mass unit group "(kg)", JRC130796 Table 1 prints "m3 world eq. deprived water" and Table 10 prints "m3 water eq. of deprived water/person", while the XML reuses generic Volume (m3); (3) RIVM 2016-0104 Chapter 10 internal mismatches: pp. 74 and 77 mis-cite Tables 10.1 and 10.3 as Tables 9.1 and 9.3, p. 78 text gives minimum dietary water requirement as 1,530 m³/(yr·person) whereas Table 10.1 and summary Table 1.3 print 1,350, and summary Table 1.5 rounds Tables 10.4/10.5 to two digits while keeping only Table 10.6's watershed median 6.0×10⁻¹³ and omitting the country mean 1.74×10⁻¹²; (4) RIVM Table S6.2 pp. 167–169 corrupted F–Z sample rows: WSI prints Fiji 4.64×10⁻³, Germany 34.7, Senegal 7.28×10⁴, United States 8.20×10⁻⁷, while health damage prints 0.00 for Iran, Kenya, Niger, Nigeria, Senegal, Sudan, Uganda, and Zambia yet positive values for Sweden (2.40×10⁻⁶) and the United States (9.80×10⁻⁷); (5) LC-IMPACT paper Table 1 labels water-stress health as "average" while §2.3 on the same page states both average/linear and marginal sets are provided (the p. 11 case uses marginal factors).
